WHOSE CHOICE? Some faces are supinely fair, Some sparkling in their splendour; Some are demure and debonaire, And some divinely tender. Some win us with one fatal glance, From eyes too brightly beaming; Some smile that smile that brings a trance, Till life is lost in dreaming. Some flit before us, sweet and gay, - To fill our hearts with laughter; Then fade as fancies fade away, And leave no achings after. And some—some faces, sorrow-kissed, When holiest thoughts are thronging, Come back, come always in that mist Of everlasting longing. So faces come and faces go: Some make existence sweeter; And some, they make iLe sad, we know, , Yet being sad, completer. Until one face comes up at last (Heaven knows each heart: don't doubt it)— The Future fades, the Past is past! • We cannot live without it! We ask not if men call her sweet, Or fair, or wise or clever: We ask, we passionately entreat, Will you be mine for ever?" .
WILFRED WOOLLAM, B.A.
THE TUNE THE OLD COW DIED OF.

rPhe rhyme about the old cow called "The Tune the Old Cow Died of" is the first of the following verses. The conclusion of the story is added in a similar style.] There was an old man, and he had an old cow, But he had no fodder to give her; So he took up his fiddle and played her a tune— " Consider, good cow, consider! This isn't the time for grass to grow; • Consider, good cow, consider ." "And when you have nowt,' Lay the blame on the drought, , . Consider, good cow, consider, That you've something to chew While I'm singing to you; Consider, good cow, consider! "You cut up so rough, • ' This food might be tough— Consider, good cow, consider! Just fancy 'Lis meat, And get fat on the treat; Consider, good cow, consider !" The cow looked queer— Do you wonder, my dear? She faintly cried " Boo!" For food when told to "consider," As the old man did sue— " Consider, good cow, consider!
"The gass will grow Some time, you know; Consider, good cow, consider! You're not going to go While I'm pleasing you so; Consider, good cow, consider!
"Now stop that sad lowing; Can't you he,, r the grass growing? Consider, good cow, consider! Kindly turn round your head— Oh! my poor cow is dead! She wouldn't my song consider !"
Varittico.

When is a young lady like a poacher? When she has her hair in a net. Old anglers say that if you wish to catch a fine fish, you must throw your bait directly at him. Young ladies, take notice_ Men are moral alchemists; itrests with themselves to change their moments into golden hours or to let them burn out like slags in a furnace. A young married lady who moved into the country from a city home considered the keeping of hens as a pleasant and profitable duty. As she became more ab- sorbed in the pursuit her enthusiasm increased, and hens and their care were the favourite subject of her thoughts and conversation. During one of her animated descrip- tions of her success a friend inquired," Are your hens good hens ?" "Oh, yes," she replied, in a delighted tone, "they haven't laid a bad egg vet !" A LOVING SON.—A man and his son were fishing one day near New York. Suddenly the boat capsized: and they were both thrown into the water. The man could not swim well, but he tried at once to save his son, who could not swim at all. By-and-by, as the boy saw his father getting exhausted, hessaid earnestly, "Never mind me, father. Save yourself, for mother's sake." Such love had the reward which it deserved, and the noble- hearted boy w.as saved, as well as his father, by some sailors from the shore.—" Little Folks" Magazine for September. It is not true that private thoughts affect no one but the thinker. In one sense indeed there is nothing truly private—nothing that does not send forth an influence more or less direct upon the world. Certainly thought is all powerful in this direction. It shapes the life, whether we will or not. The strong and earnest thinker is usually the strong and earnest worker, while he who indulges in idle and dreamy reveries will be equally self-indulgent when he approaches the business of life Pure, sweet and generous thoughts develope involun- tarily into purity and generosity of life while the impure desire or the evil passion that is cherished in the heart can by no means be restrained from leaping into action. Thus it is thought, through the life, that is constantly acting upon the world for good or for evil. A coloured justice of the peace was about to open court in Alabama. The case to come on was between two coloured men, one of whom charged the other with having stolen a hoe. There were neither lawyers nor jury, but the judge called up the plaintiff, and said, "Mr. Burrows, how many witnesses have you got that Mr. Bunker stole dat hoe?'" " Two, sah." "Mr. Bunker, how many witnesses have you got dat you nebber took dat hoe nowhere ?" " Fo', -sah." "Den I shall dismiss de case, an' Mr. Burrows must pay de costs. Ebery one -knows dat fo' witnesses kin sw'ar harder dan two wit- nesses, an' it am no use gwine ahead to take up 'de waluable time ob dis court.' Mr. Burrows paid about 3 dollars cost, and as he was going away his Honour con- tinued, "Next time you is gwine ter sue a man you want mo' witnesses dan he's got, or you are gwine to be :left." _ _

THE Yorico IDEA.—" How did you understand the foreign languages?" was asked of an uncultured traveller. "Oh, wherever we went there was an interrupter," was the reply. The minister relating this incident expressed the hope that pastors and teachers may not prove inter- ..rupters rather than interpreters of the truth. "Interest the young by all and any means," would appear to be too often the inward feeling. Of course we do not ex- pect the children of the present day to be like their pre- -decessors, who listened patiently to incomprehensible -discourses till afflicted with "pins and needles." The present age has its sermonettes, its object lessons, its picture aids—lumdreds are striving to render divine and moral teaching attractive to the juvenile heart; but beware of erring on the other side. Avoid wearying, certainly, but do not foster a constant craving for novelty and excitement. Some of the children are quite critics :as to the means employed for their improvement, and decline to be gratified save by something that is quite a change. This is an unhealthy feeling, and leads on to trouble. Happy those whose delivery is in itself such a spell that the children listen fascinated, asking, per- chance, as one did of a humble old man who could en- thral a roomful of juveniles, "Is he a bishop ?"—" The .Quiver" for September. OUTt ILIPORTED WILD PLANTS.—I doubt whether the stinging-nettle, which renders picnicking a nuisance in England, is truly indigenous: certainly the two worst kinds, the smaller nettle and the Roman nettle, are quite recent denizens, never straying, even at the present day, far from the precincts of farm-yards and villages. The shepherd's purse and many other garden weeds of cul- tivation are of Eastern origin, and came to us at first with the seed-corn and the peas from the Mediterranean region. Corn-cockles and corn-flowers are equally -foreign and equally artificial; even the scarlet poppy, seldom found except in wheat-fields or around waste places in villages, has probably followed the course of tillage from some remote and ancient Eastern origin. There is a pretty blue veronica which was unknown in England some thirty years since, but which then began to spread in gardens and is now one of the commonest -and most troublesome weeds throughout the whole country. Other familiar wild plants have first been brought over as garden flowers. There is the wall- flower, for instance, now escaFed from cultivation in 'every part of Britain, and mantling with its yellow bunches both old churches and houses, and also the crannies of the limestone cliffs around half the shores of England. The common stock has cimilarly overrun the sea-front of the Isle of Wight; the monkey-plant, Originally a Chilian flower, has run wild in many boggy spots in England and Wales; and a North American balsam, seldom cultivated even in cottage gardens, has managed to establish itself in profuse abundance along •the banks of the Wey about Guildford and Godalming. One little garden linaria, at first employed as an orna- ment for hanging-baskets, has become so common on old walls and banks as to be considered a mere weed, and exterminated accordingly by fashionabde gardeners. Such are the unaccountable reverses of fortune, that one age will pay fifty guineas a bulb for a plant which the next age grubs up unanimously as a vulgar intruder. White, of Selborne. noticed with delight in his own kitchen that rare insect, the Oriental cockroach, lately imported; and Mr. Brewer observed with joy in his garden at Reigate the blue Buxbauna speedwell, which is now the acknowledged and hated pest of the Surrey agriculturist. SORE SIIOULDERS.—There is one thing on the farm, that is a sore shoulder on a horse, for which there is no excuse. Not the thinnest-skinned horse that ever lived need have a sore shoulder. If the animal is thin-skinned it is well to bathe the exposed places with tannin to toughen the hide,which is better than salt water for this purpose. Care should also be taken to have the collar well dried when it is taken off the horse. GAS LIME.—" A. H. P." asks for experience of gas lime for pasture land, when best applied, and how much per acre.—Gas lime is largely used on poor Has pastures near Bristol and elsewhere. It is there the custom to "grip," that is, plough or cut furrows in the fields, which thus gradually assume a ridged condition of surface. The turf is carted to a compost heap, and then re-mixed at the rate of, perhaps, sixty bushels of gas lime per, acre of the extent to be dressed; aud the compost, having been turned in winter, is spread in early spring. THE LAND PURCHASE Bars—The first sale of landed property under the Land Purchase Bill of 1835, or under what is known as Lord Ashbourne's Act, took place at Kiirush recently. It was the sale of an estate at Clonna- killa, by Mr. John J. Keatinge, of Kilrush, to the tenants. The area of the estate is 252 statute acres, the original rent £llO, reduced rent £B5. The estate was sold to the tenants at £1,330, or nearly 14i years purchase on the reduced rent. The tenants will have to pay the Govern- ment £4O annually for 49 years at 4- per cent. About 40 years ago this property was bought for £l,BOO, and, en the original lease expiring, the landlord was paid £6OO fine. THE HARVEST.—Harvest work is now in full swing throughout the midland, southern, and eastern counties, and this week it is becoming general in many parts of Yorkshire. All over England there has been a fortnight of the kind of hot, still, harvest weather that arable farmers were wishing for, so .that a considerable im- provement must be reported in the general outlook. In the earlier districts there has been a grand opportunity for cutting and carrying a lot of wheat in good condi- tion, and just as it was in the right condition for the , reaper. DOGS IN Cllt RCH.—Talking of the dogs suggests another great improvement made in the church. There were no doors on the seats, and nothing but a narrow deal in each as a footboard, and no separation below between them. The planking on the passages was very deficient, a great dear of the earthen floor was thus exposed, and it can easily be imagined that when the shepherds from Ettrick, as well as from Yarrow, came to church, each shepherd as regularly acccompanied by his dog as encased in his plaid—no matter what the weather or the season—what frequent rows there were. On the

slightest growl they all pricked up their ears. If a couple of them fell out and showed fight, it was the signal for a general melee. The rest that were prowling about, or half asleep at their masters' feet, rushed from

their lairs, found a way through below the pews, and among the feet of the occupants, and raised literally such a" dust" that fairly enveloped them. Then the strife I waxed fierce and furious, the noise became deafening-, the voice of the minister was literally drowned, and he was fain to pause, whether in preaching or in prayer. Two or three shepherds had to Itave their places and use their nibbies unmercifully before the rout was quelled, and the service of the sanctuary resumed. These scenes were more unseemly than a solitary cur, with some rude ear for music, joining in the psalmody, and were of old standing in Yarrow. Old Mr. Scott, of Eldinhope, used to relate how Dr. Cramond bade the old beadle, Sandy Rae, put out the noisy delinquents, and got for answer, "I dinna like to meddle wi' the folk's dogs, sir;" some- what more polite than another rejoinder, "I'm no 0-aun to get mysel' bitten; they may put them out °that brought them in." The appearance of a strange dog in church was the signal for the whole fraternity holding a conclave; and if not satisfied with its appearance, giving it no peace during the service, unless it could find an open door to beat a retreat. So much, indeed were the curs recognised as a regular portion of the congregation, that the closing arrangements were made with reference to them. The going round of the elders with the ladies put them all on the qui rive, and for peace's sake, the congregation sat still till the blessing was pronounced. Their rising was attended by a perfect storm of barking, a general canine jubilee. A clergyman from a distance, who one day officiated, was struck with this singular peculiarity and seeming irreverence of the congregation, and was told in explanation that it was "to cheat the dougs." The flooring of the church, and fitting the seats with doors, by which each shepherd could keep his fidue Achates beside him was the first blow to the long- established order of things, the almost weekly collie- shangies. The shepherds began to perceive that their dogs were not so very indispensable to them on the Sabbath as they supposed. The divisiGn of the parish lessened the number still more. And as at the opening of Kirkhope Church I had requested the cor:gregation to keep their dogs at home, and stand at the blesSing, their example in regard' to the latter practice, when they came over to the Communion, was followed by the Yarrow hearers too.—"Renziniscences of Yarrow," by Jariles Rus- sell, AD. "Thou rain'st in this bosom," as the chap said when a basin of water was thrown over him by a lady he was serenading. • The Rev. Dr. Strong, of Hertford, and Rev. Dr. Mason sometimes visited each other. On one of these occasions, while Dr. M. was visiting in Hertford, the two doctors one day took a walk together. Now, the step of Dr. Strong's residence was of freestone, and constructed after the old pattern; that is, two stone slabs of sufficient thickness to form a step, laid upon each other, the upper being smaller than the lower. It so happened that a corner of the lower stone had been broken and laid up loosely; so, when the two clergymen returned from their walk, and were ascending the steps, Dr. Mason stepped upon the broken corner, which turned over with him, and caused him to stumble. "Brother Strong," he ex- claimed, "why don't you mend your ways ?" "I would," said Dr. S., "if I were a Mason." THE HOUSE IN THE ROCK.—Last century there lived a blacksmith, George Paterson by name, in the village of Gilmerton, near Edinburgh, who became locally a famous man for a singular exploit. The sandstone near his dwelling being soft and easily worked, he hit upon the singular notion of hewing a house and shop out of the rock with his own hands. This task he began in 1720; and after five years of continuous work he had com- pleted it. In addition to a smithy with its fireplace (or forge), this rock-hewn house contained a dining-room- 144ft. long, 71t. broad, and 61t. high—with a bench all round, a table, and a bed recess; a parlour, somewhat larger, a kitchen a cellar, 71 t. long, and a wash-house. There was a skylight window in each room, and the dwellinc, was properly drained. Paterson lived and worked for 11 years in this underground home, which was visited by holiday folk and lovers of the curious, and he, no doubt, made a good deal of money out of this strange handiwork. As a sign of approval of his in- dustry, the local authorities freed him from land-tax and other public rates.—" Little Folks" Magazine for September. THE PARROT'S POWERS Or SPEECIT.—Just as the monkeys have been placed at the head of the Mammalia on account of their high development, so the parrots, from their general cleverness, and especially on account of the facility with which they can talk, have been con- sidered the highest order of birds, and placed at the be- ginning of the class. It is impossible for some people to avoid the conclusion that these birds think and reason, and the a propos or sometimes mal A propos way in which they introduce speeches, coupled with the look of wisdom which they assume while being spoken to, seems to show that the brain is being employed in thinking. A friend in Manchester told the writer of a parrot show in the North of England, where the talking powers of each bird were made the subject of a prize competition. Several of the birds had exhibited their prowess, and at last the cover was removed from the cage of a gray parrot, who-at once exclaimed, on seeing the company to which he was suddenly introduced, "By Jove! what a lot of parrots !" an observation which gained him the prize at once. nib' MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY. MORE ABOUT POULTRY-HOUSES. With the majority of our readers it is an absolute ne- cessity that the poultry they keep should cost as little as possible for what we may call the permanent fixtures of the establishment, for where there is one keeper of fowls who can spend as much as he desires upon houses and fixtures, there are a hundred if not a thousand who are not in this position. Therefore, when there are buildings already standing which can be adapted as poultry-houses, an opportunity is afforded for a very welcome saving of first cost. It is indeed surprising what we have known to be utilised in this way. But it is very often the case that there are old sheds, unused stables, and even unoccupied cottages which can very easily be adapted as poultry-houses. As a rule these buildings have one very manifest advantage, namely, that they are better built than is usually the case with houses specially erected for fowls, and this is no slight benefit, giving the additional warmth that is so welcome in the winter season. It is a mistaken policy, but it is nevertheless a common one, that fowls are sheltered in houses which no one would think of putting a horse or a cow into, because of the want of ventilation, or of the other requisites for proper housing. Therefore, when a house has been built for what we may term the superior animals, and can be given to the fowls, the opportunity should be very gladly welcomed. Properly fitted up, it will make a. splendid poultry-house. When a stable is placed at the disposal of the poultry keeper there is usually very little to be done, as it is generally in good order, roomy, well drained, and pro- perly ventilated. If a single or two-stalled stable, when fitted with perches, and a hole is made for the exit of the fowls, it is all ready for the occupants. But if a larger building, it is desirable that there be made a divi- sion, so that the fowls are not kept in too great numbers. We have before stated that not more than fifty fowls should be kept in. one house and run. The reason for this is that larger numbers do not answer, and the aver- age production of a flock of one hundred fowls is con- siderably less than when half that number is in one house. Why this should be so we have never been able to discover, but the fact is there nevertheless, and that is sufficient for our purpose now, though it would cer- tainly be more satisfactory if a reason could be given for it. The additional cost of dividing any large building need not be very great, and it will repay itself by the greater results attained. It is most desirable that the partition made be a good one, for if not so, if disease attacks the inhabitants of one part of the house it will certainly spread to the other. Under any cireumstances it may be difficult to avoid this, but it will be impossible to do so if the partition be a thin and incomplete one. We once visited a six-stalled stable that was tem- porarily fitted as a poultry-house, and in a way which we thought most complete. Three stalls were on each gide, with the usual passage between, the door being at one end. Each stall was wired over the top to prevent the birds "getting to each other, and movable frames, the lower half wood and the upper half netting, with a. small door fitted in, formed the fronts of the compartments. Trap holes were made through the walls to afford communication between the house and the runs outside. The stable in this way was made to accommodate a hundred and fifty fowls, that is twenty- five in each compartment.. Of course, there was the ob- jection which has been already noted, namely—that any disease attacking the birds in one run would be sure to be taken by those adjoining; but under the circumstances it could not be avoided, and the house could be trans- formed into a stable again at a very short notice. To many this would be a great convenience, as it might not be desirable to give up to the fowls entirely a stable which might be required again for its original purpose. This is a point that ought always to be borne in mind when houses are being adapted, and it is worth a little more expense at the outset to make the fittings capable of being easily removed. To this end the perches should not be made fixtures, but have the inclined side sup- ports, which ,give them the ladder-like appearance so familiar in many poultry-houses, especially on farms. The supports are formed of a plank at either end, with slots cut therein, into which the perches are made to fit. Perches so made are easily removed, and the supporting planks are also movable when required. Barns are sometimes available for making into poultry houses, but with them more is needed than with stables, for there are no stalls to form the sides of the compart- ments. These can be provided, but the expense will necessarily be greater. Still it is worth incurring if the place is likely to be given up to the fowls for any reason- able length of time. There is another method of arrang- ing which may recommend itself to many of those who have a few portable houses for putting out on the fields after harvest—namely, to place these houses within the barn itself, and by means of a few boards, or a little wire netting, make a covered run, conducting from the house to the trap communicating with the open run. We have often seen some hundreds of fowls herding together in a large barn, and apparently irt good health and condition. This plan has the decided merit of simplicity, but, for the reason already given, it is not to be recommended. What are most desirable on any farm when there are a number of small buildings that can be adapted for the purpose of poultry houses are buildings which will each hold from 20 to 50 birds. Fortunate indeed is the breeder who has these at his command, for he need go to very little expense in adapting them to his use, and they can be more easily put to their original or any other purpose than is the case with a larger erection. But there are very few indeed who are in such a happy posi- tion. The chief danger to be avoided in the adaptation of existent buildings as poultry houses is that they are either damp, badly ventilated, or badly built. If any of these be the case they must be remedied if success has in any way to be achieved. We have before said what we think about the evils resultant from imperfect venti- lation, and it is not necessary that we should say any- thing more on that question at this time. There is one thing, however, that the worst ventilated house can be made right in this respect if the proper means be adopted, so that ill ventilation need not be an impassable barrier to the adoption of any house. Dampness is much more difficult to remedy; it is generally found in old buildings, in which it seems to have got a firm hold upon the walls. Into a house like this it would be most dan- gerous to put any living thing, and certainly it would be fatal to success with poultry. How to cure dampness in walls is a question which cannot be settled off-hand, as it puzzles builders greatly. Something can be done by beat drying, but even that is not a perfect cure. We have known coating the walls both outside and inside with tar effect the purpose, but we have also known that plan to fail, and it seems almost impossible in some cases to find a real cure for dampness, as the moisture has got right into the walls, and appears to attract mois- ture from wherever it is to be found. Not nearly so serious is it when a house is badly built, for that can generally be put right, either thoroughly or sufficiently for the requirements of the fowls. SEASONABLE HINTS. It is often found at this season of the year that chickens are troubled with diarrhcea' chiefly resulting from the green food eaten by them, though sometimes a too rich diet is the cause. As a preventive there is nothing better than bone meal, pf which a little should be put in the soft food every day. It has a most bene- ficial effect upon the stomach, and at the same time pro- vides material for building up the frame of the bird, supplying just those qualities which are often wanting, and which if in a state of nature the fowls would be able to obtain for themselves. Should diarrlicea declare itself, a little more bone meal may be mixed in the soft food, •
and if that does not stop it a drop of chlorodyne should be given in water twice a day.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

Now that all Strawberry plants needful for making fresh beds have been secured, the most barren portion of the old plants should be destroyed. This we do by pushing the spade over the surface of the ground under each plant till the whole are severed, leaving the root in the ground to be turned into the bottom of the trench when we come to perform that operation, which is always done before another crop is put in the ground. Old Strawberry plants left for another year should have all the runners and some of the lower leaves removed and taken into some convenient corner with the plants destroyed to be burnt in conjunction with weeds and any other refuse, for the purpose of making as many wood ashes as possible, which is most useful as a fer- tiliser, or to scatter over seed beds to protect the seed- lings from various kinds of insect pests. The surface of the ground between the rows should be disturbed with the fork an inch or two in depth in order to admit some air and rain into its otherwise impenetrable body, the unavoidable results of the work of gathering the fruit, which involves continuous movement of the feet, ren- dering stiff soils in time like a cemented pathway. If after breaking the surface, a coat of manure is applied, say a couple of inches thick, there is no doubt the plants would greatly benefit by it, and the mulch would be the means of roots emitting from the old naked stems, and act as additional feeders. We cannot understand the action of those persons who ruthlessly strip most of the leaves off their plants and take the additional trouble of digging several inches deep between the plants. Ad- mitting that they have ordinary success, the extra labour they incur is something serious and if reckoned up must tell disastrously on the profits. From our experience we feel sure that the Strawberry plant prefers the soil firm, and on light land the forking we have recommended may be dispensed with; if the hoe and the rake are run between the plants they will do all that is requisite. Cauliflowers: We are so pleased with our success in wintering these with very slight protection, and the advantages derived from it are such that we strongly urge our readers to practice autumn sowing for an early crop. Two or three old window sashes inclined against a wall, with a bed of light soil under them to prick the plants in, are all that is wanted to protect scores of plants. By sowing Early Erfrut or Early London and Veitch's Autumn Giant at the present time a long succession may be secured next year. We sow our seeds in drills six inches distant, which are made with the corner of the hoe, about an inch in depth. If at the time of sowing the ground should be dry—which it can only be a short distance down,—we would, in pre- ference to watering it at this season of the year, turn it over a few inches deep, and so bring moist soil to the surface to receive the seed. This is of importance, as the soil in many gardens to a depth of about two inches is so dry that the seeds would not germinate in it, and every day's delay just now means time lost, equal to a week in the summer. Lettuce: Another small sowing of these may be made, and the plants, after being pro- perly thi,ined, may remain in the seed bed over the win- ter, and those sown in August should when large enough be pricked out in beds. THE FRONT GARDEN.—Aster amellus is one of the earliest flowering of Michaelmas daisies. It has been in flower for three weeks, and likely to continue to the end of this month or the middle of October. Surely such a long-owering plant should be grown in every garden, and it is not too vigorous for those of limited area. It grows about 21t. high, and seldom requires any support. The flowers are pale blue, and are produced in open corymb, and defy sun wind, or rain to mar their beauty. Carnations: Layers of these should be sprinkled every evening during dry weather, using for the purpose a can with a fine spreader, so as not to wash the soil away from them and expose the cut parts. THE GREENHOUSE.—AII Chrysanthemum plants will by now have filled their pots with roots, and will require • feeding until the colour of the flowers is visible. Growers • do not confine themselves to any particular kind of fertiliser, and most of them use soot-water and that in which horse or sheep manure has been steeped and stirred a few times before using,. Clay's Fertiliser we • found to have a beneficial effect; also guano applied about once a week, and more than once we have pro- duced good blooms with little else than sulphate of am- monia, at the rate of half an ounce to the gallon of clean water' but better results are secured by using two or three different kinds of fertilisers. Some of the old . growers depended chiefly on sheep droppings and hen and pigeon manure. There is no doubt as to the efficacy , of these latter, and as they are within the reach of most growers, they are doubly valuable. Care must, however, be taken to well dilute the water in :which these ma- terials have been soaked, and the safest plan is to put • only as much of it in the watering-pot as will discolour the clear water and gradually strengthen it. There is a tendevy to conclude that because a manure has proved ; good, the more of it that is given the better. This, how- ever, is a fallacy that many have proved to their sorrow; , weak and often is the rule with good gardeners.

• • WESLEYAN B.PCO-iNITION MEETING. On Monday evening a public tea and recognition meeting to welcome the Rev. George E. Young, ' the new superintendent of the Warrington Wes- leyan circuit, were held in the Bewsey-road Chapel. At the tea there were about 150 persons present, while at the meeting the body of the chapel was filled. The chair was taken by the Rev. G. E. Cut- ting, and there were alio present on the platform— the Rev. G. E. Young, the Rev. J. Howell Jones, Messrs. E. J. Guest, J. 13., F. Wright, W. Silcock, Knowles (Appleton), Beaman, John Bennett, and , Richardson. The meeting having been opened in the usual way, the CHAIRMAN, in a few introduc- tory remarks, said there was one grand thing he could assure. Mr. Young of, and that was that they had peace in that circuit. (Hear, hear.) They had had two general elections in Warrington, but they had come and gone, and all was peaceful in their borders. As citizens they could do what they liked and say what they liked, but as lgethodists they were neither Liberals nor Conservatives. They could look in the face of the world and rejoice for that. But4if they were neither Liberals nor Conser- vatives as Methodists, yet at the same time he wan- ted them to be both Liberal and Conservative. He wan- ted them to be Liberal in getting the people blessed. and he wanted them to be Conservative in holding tenaciously to the good they had got. (Hear, hear.) —Mr. W. SILCOCK, one of the circuit stewards, said he wished all of them to give Mr. Young a very hearty welcome. (Applause.) There was nothing that killed more than indifference. (Hear, hear.) There was many a noble spirit, and many a true heart had been killed by indifference. Indifference is death, and if they wanted a successful church they must work. It was one of the characteristics of Mr. Spurgeon's church that it was a working church. and where was there a more success- ful Nonconformist church than that .of Mr. , Spurgeon? In the name of the meeting *he gave their esteemed superintendent a very hearty wel- come. (Applause.)—Mr. F. WRIGHT, mission sec- retary, gave Mr. Young a hearty welcome on behalf . of Padgate. He was glad to say that in Padgate they had had additions to the church. (Hear, heag.) They had also enlarged their Sunday School, and the enlargements would soon be open for the reception of children. He also mentioned that the Rev. Chas. Garrett had promised to preach at Padgate on the 13th October.—Mr. KNOWLES having given a cordial welcome to Mr. Young, said he was sorry to say that they did not prosper so very much in Ap- pleton, though they were able to hold their own. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. BEAMAN remarked That, as the Chairman had said, Mr. Young came into a very peaceful church. He had also come into a working church, for there were signs of life amongst them. Life in a Methodist church did not stagnate for want of action; there was room for all in a Metho- dist church. (Hear, hear.) He believed Mr. Young's advent amongst them would be signalised with great blessing. (Applause.)—Mr. E. J. GUEST said he was glad to throw out the right hand of fellow- ship to Mr. Young, and to see him amongst them. But there was something of sorrow to him in meet- higs of that sort. He remembered those who had left them. (Hear, hear.) It was to him a great deal when their late suFerintendent left that cir- cuit, and he should ever remember him with the sincerest affection. He was sure they would never have anyone who would more conscientiously do his work than the Rev. Jas. McTurk did in that cir- cuit. (Applause.) For his (Mr. Guest's) own part, he should have been glad had it been possible for Mr. McTurk to be permanently stationed in that circuit, but at present the law of Methodism is as the laws of the Medes and Persians, unalterable. He did not know whether unalterable or not, but at any rate unaltered. Perhaps it would be altered in days to come. (Hear, hear.) But whilst he regretted Mr. McTurk's removal from that circuit, he rejoiced in the advent of Mr. Young, and looked forward to three years of great prosperity under his reign. (Applause.)—Mr. BENNETT, who, the chairman said, represented the 'agricultural interests, and Mr. RICHARDSON, who was said to represent the trade interests of the. circuit, next gave short addresses, and heartily welcomed Mr. Young.—The Rev. J. HOWELL JONES, who was called upon by the chair- man as his "young man "—(laughter)said he could assure Mr. Young that he had come amongst a sympathetic and loyal people, a people who would do all in their power to make him comfortable and to further the great cause in the interest of which he had come amongst them. Having alluded to the pro- cress that had been made during the past tWo years, Mr. Jones said there was Still a great work before them in Warrington. He thought their position in this town did not at all represent their

position as a church amongst the other Protestant churches. Instead of having two chapels like that they ought to have four, and their motto during the coming winter should be "extension within the limits of the town itself." They had a number of beautiful country chapels, but if they excluded Sankey Bridges they had not kept pace with the ' increase of the population of the town. The nor- mal growth of the population of Warrington was 1,000 a year, and they were not keeping pace with that normal growth. They must remember that as a church they were the strangest Protestant church in the world, but he believed that in Warrington there were six churches for every chapel. Now the Church at England bore no comparison with them as a body of Christians in the world, and if their position in Warrington was to be at all in keeping they must extend within the town itself. (Hear, hear.) They had not laid hold of the people of their towns as they ought to do, and he was afraid thLy should not until they complied with the conditions of success. Theirduty was to Christianise the masses of the country, and lie believed that as Methodism came between England and the horrors of revolution in the last century, so it might do again. With the end of reaching the masses Mr, Jones urged that modifications ought to be made in the present itineracy system, such as were being made in Scotland. (Applause.)—The Rev. G. E. Young, who was very cordially received, said that Mr. Silcock had remarked that indifference killed. There was nothing which would sooner kill him than indiffer- ence manifested by the friends. He rejoiced that there had been no signs of indifference, and he had every reason to believe in their hearty and prayer- , ful co-operation. :(Ifear, hear.) It had been no' small trialsto leave his old circuit. He .should never forget it, and it was with the deepest•emotion that he bade farewell to their friends the other day. (Hear, hear.) There was somethin,r very hard about the itineracy system, but he felt that he had not come among total strangers. (Applause.) Mr. Young having mentioned that he felt the deepest interest in the village Methodism to which he owed his own Methodism, and having spoken in favour of adapting their methods of working to their sur- roundings, he concluded amidst applause. The meeting was brought to a close by the singing of the doxology.—lt may be mentioned that on Sun- day Mr. Young preached the anniversary sermons in Bold-street Wesleyan Chapel, there being a large attendance morning and evening.

div.head: GENERAL PEWS.
div.p: GENERAL PEWS.

DESTRUCTIVE FIRE.—A destructive fire occurred on Tues- day at Red Rouse Farm, Amesbury, Wilts. Most of the farm buildings were destroyed, together with a vast quan- tity of corn, 100 sheep, a valuable carthorse, a bull, and other live and dead stock.

BRITISH ANNEXATION IN SOUTH AFRICA.—It is officially announced that the Queen has directed Letters patent to be passed under the Great Seal of the United Kingdom for the annexation at the Cape of Goad Hone of certain territory known as the Nesibt Country. LORD SALISBURY AND LORD HARTINGTON.—Losd Salis- bury visited Lord Hartington at Devonshire House, on Tuesday, remaining with him nearly half an hoar. The present position of affairs in Ireland, and more particularly the bill about to he introduced by Mr. Yarnell on the Irish land question, are believed to have occupied their atten- tion.

THE 1885 ELECTION.—A. Parliamentary return regard- ing the general election of 1884, issued on Saturday, shows that there were then 5,693,753 electors on the register. There were 3,734,693 votes polled in England and Wales, at an average cost of 4s 61; 447,588 in Scotland, at an average cost of 5s Bd, and 451,456 in Ireland, at an average cost of 2s 9d.

§r,PICIOUS DEATIL—The body of an old woman has been found in a shed in a brickyard at Ewyaa Harold, Hereford, under circumstances leading to the supposition that she had been murdered. The deceased had gone to the shed to see if there were any tramps there, and as she did not return search was made, and she was found lying in a pool of blood. Two tramps have been arrested on suspicion. A NEW LIBERAL " WHIP."—Mr. William Summers, who formerly sat for 6talybridge, and now represents Hudders- field, has been asked to undertake the duties of an additional " whip "to the Liberal party, The hon. gentleman, who has 'acceded to the request, is thoroughly popular with all sections of Mr, Gladstene's followers, and especially with what may be termed the advanced or Radical party. CUTTING A WIFE'S THROAT.—JOim Garriety was charged at Buckingham, on Saturday, with attempting to murder his wife by cutting her throat. Prisoner had been separa- ted from his wife ten years. Finding her with a Highland piper at Bicester, on Thursday, he followed them on to Buckingham, and found them at a lodging. house, where be cut the woman's throat. Prisoner was remanded.

GERMAN COTTON TRADE.—The German cotton spinning trade seems to be, like the iron industry, in a rather difficult position. According to a despatch received by the Foreign Office from Mr. O. Strachey, the British chara d'affaires, at Dresden, a meeting of the Saxon Cotton Spinners' Asso- ciation was held at Chemnitz on August 18, when a resolu- tion was passed to the following effect :—" There Leing a loss on spinning at ruling prices, those present declare their readiness to reduce their yarn outpat, provided the other spinners of Germany are prepared to take a similar course, the chairman to negotiate immediately in this sense with other German associations."

_ A Riser, HERO.—Mr. Carnegie has sent a letter to Dun- fermline, in which he intimates a subscription of £lOO to a monument proposed to be erected to the memory of the young man Hunter, who lost big life in the Town Loch while attempting to save a person who was drowning. Mr. Carnegie says :—" The false heroes of barbarous man are those who can only boast of the destruction of their fellows. The true heroes of civilisation are those alone who save or greatly serve them. Young Hunter was one of these, and deserves an enduring monument. Dunfermline has had no son of whom she could be prouder, or in all her annals is there an act on record of nobler heroism." A MISSIONARY STATION BURNT TO THE GROUND.— Letters from Stanley Pool, South Airiest, contain particulars of the destruction by fire of the Baptist mission at that place. On June 24th, a grass fire came through the bush, and the sparks ignited one of the store housee. Seven other store houses caught fire, aud the fire was not got under until the whole mission station had become a com- plete wreck. The key. T. J. Comber states that the loss is simply appalling. All the goods ready for three up-river stations have been destroyed, and this alone means ever £lOOO. All the gear, Jtc., of the mission steamer Peace. of which no correct value can be estimated, all the barter stock, and all the persoaal property of the missionaries— food, stores, clothing, books, &c.,—have been lost, and Mr. Comber questions if £3OOO will cover the loss. ESCAPE FROM A REFORMATORY.--011 Sunday /1ig111.41 boys escaped from the Warwickshire County R4ormatory, at Weston, near Leamington. Directly after prayers in the dining hall the boys were dismissed to their dormitories, and when the monitor in charge threw open the yard gate the lads escaped. No violence was used, and the officers were completely taken by surprise. The boys had been twice te church, their conduct had been exemplary, and there had been no premonitory signs of insubordination. The alarm bell was instantly rung, and officials and villagers, who speedily assembled, set off in chase of the fugitives across the country. It was getting dusk, and penult was difficult, but ten boys were captured in the neighbourhood of the re- formatory. On Monday, the surrounding country was scoured, and 10 more boys were apprehended at Coventry, where some of them belonged. This party, when surrounded in a garden, offered violent resistanc?, and a constable was severely injured. Ten more boys were secured at Bedworth, and on Monday night only five remained uncaptured. TRE NORTH WALES TITRE AGITATION.—The Rector of Llanarmon on Saturday, through his agent, Mr. Osbert Edwards, solicitor, Ruthin, levied a distraint upon the stock of Mr. James Lawton, of Saithdaran, who occupies a moder- ately large farm, situated abont one mile from Llandegla, in the parish of Llanarmon. The amouet of tithes that Mr. Lawton owes is X 0 12s 2d, and the costs of serving the writ is 2s 6d, bringing the sum up to £6 14s Bd. The bailiff was offered no actual violence, but Mr. Lawton seemed greatly exasperated against him, for he eeized him by the collar and said he had a very good mind to duck him in the trough that stood conveniently near. The bailiff quietly waited till the storm had blown over, and then he proceeded to seize two brindle cows grazing in the fields. The tithe payers recently appealed to the vicar of Mold, the Rev. T. Jones, for a reduction of 15 per cent., on the ground of the depressed state of agricultnie, but when the rev, gentleman ex- explained that although Broncold was his parish he received only a very small portion of the tithes, the tenant farmers, with a few materials, all paid the amounts due from them. HEAVY TRUNDERSTORMS.—A DESTRUCTIVE WATERSPOUT. At Swansea, on Saturday evening, a waterspout burst over Kilvey Hill, a mountain at the bottom of whieh stands a portion of Swansea known as Foxhole. The water rushed I down the precipitous sides of the mountain at different points, bringing with it many thousand tons of earth and Irocks, which plunged at a fearful rate on to the houses. In most cases the walls of the houses remained intact, but the earth, much diluted with water, burst through back doors and windows, carrying both furniture and people before it, and so continued on to the next row of houses. Two chil- dren were swept out of a room and carried down the hill. A man tried to save them, and him94ilf got dragged in, and while the children were stopped by some rocks, the man was washed 200 feet, and only saved his life by clinging to the top of a lamp post. A fish woman was standing at the back of a house when the avalanche caught her, dashed her in through the door and into the corner of the front room, and she was found standing in the corner covered to the neck with mud and boulders, which so closely encircled her that the use of crcwbars and picks was:necess try for half an hour before she could be extricated. In a similar way in about 50 houses rooms were filled with earth piled up to the ceilings. The utmost distress prevails, but the Mayor (Mr. Reed) and Captain Colquhoun, the head constable, have made temporary provision. Three roads were covered with earth to the depth of six feet. On Saturday, thunderstorms of great severity were experienced in various parts of the country. At Cheltenham several shops and houses were flooded. A deluge of rain fell in Glasgow en Sunday after- noon. In some dwellings water rose three feet.

On Wf dnesday the Duke cl Connaught left this country for India, in order to take up his command at &Iva Pindee. At Leicester on Wednesday the inquest on Mr. J. G. Lowe, wlicse dead buoy was lately found in a carriage 00 the Midland Railway, was concluded, the jury finding that death was due to a revolver shot. and that there was not sufficient evidenco to show by whom it was fired. FATAL ACCIDENT AT NORTHWICII—On Saturday a young man named Walter Coe, who was employed by the Weaver Navigation Trustees at the improvement works, carried nn at Barrow I_,cks., near •Northwich, met his death. While crossing a gangway placed over a deep dry rock he lost bis foothold, and fell to the bottom bead foremost. Medical aid was at once procured, but the poor fellow died almost immediately.

A FATAL QUARREL.-A fatal quarrel between lovers Oc'' curred in Citeaps;de, Birmingnam; on Saturday. A young man named Ganlk,y quarrelled with a young woman nail Murphy, with whpin he had been keeping companY,; struck her on the head with his fiat. She cried " Oh, fell to the ground. A bystander found her insensible ant. bleeding from a cut on her right temple, and she died before the doctor arrived. Ganley has• been arrested, and will be charged with causing the girl's death. HOME RULE FOR SCOTLAND.—In their annual report the Committee of the Scottiah Liberal Federathan spedif7,9: number of reforms needing to be undertaken, and place Pry minently amongst them the establishment of a statute*" Scotch Parliament for the transaction of all eiv xcluselV Scotch affairs. The Csmmittee refor with satisfaction the increase in the number of Gladstonian Liberals return" for Scotland in spite of the Unionist split, and express IT opinion that it would be for the public advantage, as,w„e as to the benefit of the szcAers, if they would contin" their alliance with the Tory party. t SUPPLYING ARMS TO THE ENEMY.—For some time has been a mystery to the officials in Burmah how tho Dtb; mese now fighting against our troops obtained the itVelle,na arms they have. In the north they were supposed to he been obtained through the Chinese, but the Chinese in 1" adjacent province of Yunnan have no arms to spare, all' indeed are but poorly armed themselves. The EnYaterilti; however,has now been solved. The Winchester repeater w which the Dacoits were armed were sold by a. firrn in °tie cutta (the name of which is known), and by some incredlu negligence were suffered to pass freely through the R4o'o Cnstusa-Housa.

BAILIVAY ACCIDENTS._.I railway guard, named Fete:. Lamb, belonging to Tweedmouth, while engaged in BhPura tog waggons at Chathill Station, on the North-Easte„d Railway, on Saturday, was pitched from a waggon,„„e;, • broke his neck.—Two trucks and a van of the Soutb-we: tern goods train leaving Tavistock for Devonport on day afternoon, ran off the rails near Yelverton Statioo,olll' ing the line to be blocked for over t,,v) hours, occasiorull great inconvenience t 3 a very largq number al passengerias Waterloo being heavily laden. They were each del39 the 3-15 a.m. excursion train and 9 a.m. ordinary train e about an hoar. The minute states that it would be ts_ duty of the commission to investigate the causes of thel changes, and especially to inquire whether they are due (ti. to depreciation of silver, or (2) to the appreciation of 07 or (3) to both these Causes. TileV would next inqaire ! has been the bearing of the changes—first, upon retnittan.cel 9! of the Government of India for payments on old or /100 contracts, for payments on new or current contracts, upc!.., the persons in India who have to make remittances horse 7f gold; upon the producers, merchants, and taarlaYer6l,,, India ; upon merchants and manufacturers at home v.i4, trade with India. Secondly, upon the trade of the i Kingdom with other silver-using countries ; upon the for4n6_7 trade of the United Kingdom generally; upon the interne+. trade and industry of the United Kingdom. If the CO mission come to the conclusion that the aforesaid chang_. in values are causing permanent or importuit evils or To conveniences to any of the interests above referred to, it Wit be their duty to inquire whether it is possible to suggest 00- remedies and the precise form they should take within tber power of the Legislature, or of the Government by itself, 0 in concert witn other Powers. DOUBLR MURDER AND SUICID33 AT OLDRAM.-0(1 Trier

day morning, at Oldham, Margaret Dawson, 35 years of egs' drowned two of her children and committed suicide. iltire. Dawson is a widow, her husband having died suddenly e year ago. She had three children and kept 2:grocer's OOP in Heywood-street. The ages of the children were 13, °e' and six years. The names of the last two are respective', George Handel and Emily, and they were the children Whe were murdered. At ten minutes past eight on Tueedaf morning the mother left the house with the two young° ehildren, to each of whom she gave an apple, telling 011 to accompany her. The eldest seta she directed to raj?, the shop while she was away. The mother and the cble dren went in the direction of Strinesdale Waterworks; Shortly afterwards they were seen sitting on the bank s' one of the reservoirs. Meanwhile Mrs. Dawson's sister, knowing the former's depressed state of mind, became IVY easy at her continued absence, and went in search of her' She first found the woman's shawl, and, pursuing her seater discovered the unfortunate mother and two children float" ing in the filtering lodge at the Waterworks. An alert:110 raised, and the bodies were recovered. In each case life 10.1 quite extinct. The bodiea were laid upon the bank preparations had been made for their removal. When th'' had been done, the deceased persons were cenveyed horn° amid a great crowd, who evinced the greatest sympatl3/ with the relatives. It is stated that the death of her bCfr band, coupled with the loss of money through giving crech" has preyed on the woman's mind and led to the melancholl occurrence. On Wednesday an inquest was heid at Waters head on the bodies of Margaret Dawson and her two cb dren. It was clear that the mother, who bad been vel, low-spirited for some time, had drowned her children ail afterwards jumped into the water herself. The jury fou that she murdered the boy and girl and they oeueniitteu suicide, and that Mrs. Dawson was at the time mentaill deranged. THE BRITISH ASSOCIATION.—AII the sections of the British Association, with three exceptions, the Math'," matical, Geographical, and Anthropological, met on Satre' day morning, but only for short sittings. There were 11 road and rail more than a dozen excursions in Warwick' shire, Staffordshire, and Worcestershire. and for the rne_,,st part the limited number of tickets for each excursion o' been issued. On Monday a paper was read on "River Ec.: trances," by Mr. If. R. Mill, who said that the only Britian river fully investigated had been the Forth. Interesting, papers were also read in the other sections. The Geoelel Committee of the Association met in the afternoon to elect officers for the ensuing year, and to. fix the place of meeting for 1887. Sir W. Dawson presided, and stated that there were invitations from Melbourne, Sydney. and Bath. S'r Saul Samuel gave an invitation for 40 or 50 members of the association to attend the centenary of the colony. The meeting resolved to accept the invitation to send 50 repre' sentativea to Sydney. An invitation was received frorn Bath to holj the ordinary meeting of the association there in 1888. This was at once accepted, on the motion of Sir R. S. Ball, seconded by Professor Cayley. bit. H. E. Roe" coe, F.R.S., was then elected president for the meeting to be held next year at Manchester. In the evening a lecture was given in the Town Nall by Professor Rutherford on the sense of hearing.—On Tuesday, in the Geology Section, after papers by Sir Wm. Dawson and Professor Williamson, some notes on the recent earthquakes in the United States, including a telegraph despatch from Major Powell, Director of the United Geological Survey, were read by Mr. W. TopleP President of the Geological Association. in the Economic Section of the committee appointed to inquire as to the teaching of science in elementary schools reported. Geogra- phy showed a falling off, and elementary science seemed to be losing the footing which it had. The impettance of technical instruction was making rapid progress in popular estimation. In the Anthropology Section, a large audience assembled to hear Sir George Campbell discourse on What is an Aryan?" He arrived at the conclusion that the AryacS were to be distinguished by feature and colour as much es by language. In the Geography Section Mr. J. Thompen° described his researches on the Niger and in the Central Soudan. As to European influence on the natives in Wee! Africa, he said for every negro missionaries had influence by Christianity a thousand had been driven into deeper degradation. On Wednesday one of the most interesting papers read in the Mechanical Science Section was that eon' tributed by Mr. J. Sturgeon, giving an account of the Bir- mingham scheme for supplying motive power in the form of compressed air, laid on in pipes in the streets like water or gas, in order to drive the various smaller engines required in manufacturing districts. At the closing meeting, held ac Wednesday afternoon, it was announced that the gathering in Manchester next year will commence on the 31st of August.

div.head: FOREIGN NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.

THE CRISIS IN BULGARIA. ABDICATION OF PRINCE ALEXANDER.—SPEECH TO THE ARMY. SOFIA, SATURDAY (Delayed in transmission).—Prince Alexander has received a telegram from Prince Bismarck recommending his Highness to abdicate in order to save Bulgaria. SOFIA, SUNDAY.—A meeting, attended by representatives of all parties, was held yesterday afternoon, under the presi- dency of Prince Alexander, to consider the position of affairs and decide what course should be pursued. Its deliberations have resulted in the election of five members—namely, MM. Stambuloff, Radoslavoff, Karaveloff, Gueshoff, and Stoiloff --charged to treat with Russia and the other Powers in regard to the settlement of the present crisis. A citcular has been issued inviting the deputies to assemble in ordinary aeasion to discuss the abdication of the Prince. The officers here unanimously declare that they are ready for any sacri- fice rather than allow the Prince to depart. Fears are enter- tained of the outbreak of civil war should his Highness quit the Country. PESTS, SATURDAY.—Telegrame giving full particulars of Prince Alexander's return to 'Sofia state that his Highness, On arrival at the parade ground where the troops were re- Viewed, rode up te Colonel Alutkuroff and saluted him with a kiss. On entering the city the Prince rode a magnificent charger with gold-mounted trappines. Among the dignitaries 1 Who met his Highness at the gates were the Metropolitan, b!gr. Mirikoff, who deliverel a speech!, in which he thanked God for the return of the Prince, who was, he said, the Pride of the Bulgarian nation and the beloved of the people. The Metropolitan at the conclusion of his address kissed his Highness on the cheek. PARIS SATURDAY.—A message which has reached here from Sofia states that fifty Russian officers have arrived there, and held aecret consultations with the Zenkoff fol- lowing. The officers, it is stated, reached Sofia singly or in Small parties. Prince Peter, of Oldenburg, is openly named as Prince Alexander's successer among the Ruseophils at &fig. BERLIN, SUNDAY.—Prince Alexander's abdication has been received here as another triumph of Russia over Germany and Austria, and also over England. This latest develop - =ant of the Bulgarian entbroglio would, it is considered, have been uvoided had the Prince received a single word of encouragement from Austria or Germany to persevere in his task, but from dynastic and political reasons the word was never spoken. PARIS, SUNDAY.—A telegram from Berlin states that Prince Bismarck will make some statement concerning the policy of Germany in the Eastern Question during the debate on the ratification of the Treaty of Commerce with Spain. RUSTCRUIC, MONDAY.—It has transpired that it was by the advice of the Russian Consul here that Prince Alexander sent his submissive telegram to the Czar. DRPARTURE OF PRINCE ALEXANDER.—PROCLA- MATION TO THE BULGARIAN PEOPLE. SOFIA, TUESDAY.—Aclording to present arrangements Prince Alexander will leave here at four o'clock this afternoon. His Highness has received the foreign repre- sentatives in farewell audience, and will receive the offi- cers and Government officials immediately before his de- parture. SOFIA, TUESDAY.—Prince Alexander left at four o'clock this afternoon for Lom Palanka. As soon as the news spread that the Prince was going to eet out to-day the palace was surrounded by crowds pressing in all directions to see him, and as the appointed hour of his departure drew near the throng in the streets became so great that foot passengers found it almost impossible to move about. Outside the town the scene was very impressive. The Prince drove by, stand- ing up in his carriage, and saving "Good bye brethren," in the Bulgarian language to the people gathered on both sides of the way. Tears were visible in many eves, and numer- ous were the hearty wishes expressed for his return. Before his departure the Prince issued the following manifesto to ' the Bulgarian people " We, Alexander 1., by the grace of God and the national will, Prince of Bulgaria, being convinced of the sad truth that our departure from Bulgaria will contribute to her liberation, and having received the, assurance of His Imperial Majesty the Czar of Russia that the independence, liberty, and tights of our country will remain intact, and that no- body will interfere with its internal affairs, we inform our beloved people ;hat we renounce the Bulgarian throne, wishing to prove in'the sight of all how precious, how dear to us are the interests of our country, and how for its good and independence we are ready to sacrifice all, even that which is more precizes to us than life. Expressing Our sincere and heart, gratitude for the feelings Of affection and attachment which the whole of Our people have cherished for us both in the happy and sad times thiough which the country and throne of Bulgaria have passed since we first entered Bulgarian territory, we now set out for the frontier of the principality, offering up, as we shall continue to the end of our days, the most heartfelt prayers to Almighty God to shield, defend, and help Bulgaria. May ebe become great, powerful, fortunate, complete, and independent. We have appointed as Regents MM. Stephan Strstbuloff, Petro Kara- veloff, and Colonel Sava Mutkurpff, and we invite all Bal. garian subjects to submit to and carry out all their orders and regulations. The Regency and Ministry appointed by us will preserve order and peace, so that the position of our country, alre.id v so difficult, may not become more complica- ted. God save B Algeria. Given at our capital September 7, 1886. ALEXANDER.
