div.p: THE NEW MINISTRY.

Sorra, TresDAvT2T- rie.--"Rege-Wc-Y-h-a-s been appointed, and I consists of M. Stambuloff, M. Karaveloff, and Colonel Mut- 1 kuroff. The Ministry resigned this morning, and a new Cabinet has been formed as follows :—M. Radoslavoff, ' Premier and Minister of the Interior ; M. Nacevics, Minister of Foreign Affairs ; M. Storloff, Minister of Justice ; M. Ivanchoff, Minister of Education ; Colonel Macolaief, Minister of War. THE MOBILISATION OF TURKISH RESERVES. BRIROUT, TUESDAY.—Great excitement has been caused throughout this district by the calliug out of the army re- serves and the drawing of men for the conscription. Several thousand men have been taken and have arrived at Damascus. WEDNESDAY.—The Porte has des- Patched a fresh note to its representatives abroad on the Bulgarian question. In diplomatic circles here the belief Is entertained that the Bulgarian Sobranje will re-elect Prince Alexander. THE PRINCE IN ROUMANIA. Prince Alexander, accompanied by MM. Stanabouloff and Karaveloff, and nearly.all the Bulgarian Ministers, arrived at Turn Severin on board his yacht at two o'clock on Thurs- day morning. A detachment of Roumanian troops vr as drawn up at the landing-stage to receive the Prince, and soldiers also lined the roads to the railway station, where his Highness took .an affecting leave of the Ministers and officers. A Bulgarian aide-de-camp accompanied the Prince. Loel PALANKA, WEDNESDAV.—Prince Alexander arrived here to-day accompanied by his brother, Prince Francis Joseph, Baron Riedesel, M. Stambuleff, and several of the 1 Ministers. A crowd received the Prince at the entrance to the town, where a triumphal arch had been erected. • The Vice President of the National Assembly made a speech, in which he said that the Bulgarians were greatly affected at the departure of Prince Alexnder, and that they could not forget that they owed everything to him. They would con- tinue to consider him as their ruler although he left the country. They hoped for his speedy return. The Prince made the following reply : " I cannot forget the people among whom I lived eight years. I shall be happy when the Bulgarians are content, and I am ready to assist them when they are in need." Finally, his Highness expressed the hope of seeing them soon again. The children of the schools strewed flowers on his path amidst enthusiastic cheers. TURN SEVERIN, THURSDAY, 3 A.m.—Princa Alexander,

accompanied by MM. Stambuloff and Karaveloff and near- ly all the Bulgarian Ministers, arrived here on board his yacht this morning. A detachment of Roumanian troops was drawn up at the landing-stage to receive the Prince, and soldiers also lined the road to the railway station, where His Highness took an affecting leave of the Ministers and officers. A Bulgarian aide-de-camp accompanies the Prince, who will leave at four o'clock direct for Darmstadt.

-- The Patriotic Association is circulating throughout the country a form of petition to Lord Salisbury urging upen the Government the necessity for prompt and energetic ac- tion with regard to the crisis which has arisen in the East. The petition says it is of vital importance that Russian troops should be excluded from the Balkan Peninsula, and above all that Constantinople should be preserved from Russian control. The Government are, therefore, begged to support Prince Alexander of Bulgaria in every possihle way, and to resist the occupation of Bulgaria or East Rou- melia by Russian troops. RUSSIA AND CENTRAL ASIA.—WARLIKE RUMOURS IN INDIA,. CALCUTTA, SUNDAY.—Rumours are coming in of distur- bances in the Punjaub. It is currently reported that the Ameer is raising new regiments and making warlike pre- parations on a large scale, either for the purpose of resisting a Russian attack, or, as some reports put it, with a view of subjugating Kafiristan. A Lahore newspaper states that there has been widely circulated in the Punjaub an anony- mous vernacular proclamation calling upon the natives of the province to sink minor differences and to combine to throw off the yoke of Ferinehee tyrants. The document goes on to announce the arrival of a large Russian army at Herat en route for India. SUNDAY.—The Bonerwall tribe on the Punjaub frontier, near Peshawur, whose predatory incursions on British territory were under the consideration of Government last January, have again made a raid across the ftontier. The Government is contemplating the despatch of an expe- dition to punish the Bonerwals as soon as the cold weather sets in. BOMBAY, TUESSDAY.—A band of the blockaded Litirani tribe on the Dora Ismail Khan border have issued from the Bhandhwan Pass and attacked a neighbouring village, kill- ing several of the inhabitants and capturing a number of cattle. ' The raiders succeeded in escaping with their booty, but were pursued for several miles. DOUBLE MURDER IN BURMAH. RANGOON, MONDAY.—A dreadful murder was committed at Moultuein on Saturday night. While Father Biet, a catholic priest, and a man named Ramos, were seated to- gether in the latter's house, two Burmese and a Chinaman entered, and stabbed both to death. The motive of the crime is unknown, but it is supposed that the assassin only in- tended to kill Ramos, who is a money lender, and murdered the priest to prevent him being a witness against them.

EGYPT AND THE SOUDAN. CAIRO, MONDAY.—Spies who have succeeded in making their way to Dongola, and have now returned thence, report the existence of a frightful famine in that place, the scarcity of food being so great that the inhabitants are said to have been driven to acts of cannibalism. Eight thou- sand rebel troops, with their families, are stated to be con- gregated at Dougola, and to be almost entirely without food or ammunition. The whole province has been laid waste, and bands rendered desperate by famine are pushing north.

FIGHTING IN THE SOUDAN. • STURM, WEDNESDAY. Col. Kitchener, the newly ap- pointed Gownor-General of the Red Sea Littoral, accom- panied by Els staff, arrived in her Majesty's ship Dolphin yesterday, and was received with the customary selute. After holding are official reception, Colonel Kitchener formally took up his duties. The rebels in Tamai recently attempted a sortie, but were sharply repulsed, with the loss of 150 killed, by the friend- lies, who are investing the place. Deserters, through hun- ger, from the rebel camp are daily coming in. The heat is slightly abating. DISTURBANCE IN SPAIN. MADRID, MONDAY.—A. serious riot occurred at Corunna yesterday, some of the inhabitants protesting against pay- ment of local taxes. The rioters burned the tax collector's books, and threatened to set fire to his offices. The military were called out, and after some resistance succeeded in dis- persing the mob, a few persons on both sides being wounded.. This morning the disturbances were renewed. Troops were again compelled to interfere, and finally dispersed the rioters. The official telegrams relating to the affair announce that tranquility has been restored. OUTRAGE IN AMERICA. NBIV YORX, SATURDAY. A. hut near Williamsport, On the North Branch of the Pennsylvania Railroad, inhabited by Hungarian labourers, has been maliciously set On fire. All the inmates, nine in number, were burnt to death. THE EARTHQUAKES IN AMERICA.—MORE SHOCKS. —MESSAGE FROM THE QUEEN. NEW Yortx, SATURDAY.—The confidence which the peo- ple of Charleston were beginning to regain owing to the cessation of the shocks has again been completely shattered. The town was to.day visited with fresh shocks of earth- quake and showers of pebbles. This fresh visitation has produced the utmost consternation, and the inhabitants are paralysed with fear. A body of military engineers has been sent to examine the buildings yet standing, and report as to their security, and a supply of tents has bees despatched for the houseless. The harbour has remained quite unaffected by the eartlequeke, the depth of water remain the same in all parts. The captain of a coasting steamer reports that he heard a terrible rumbling, which lasted a minute and a half, while his vessel was off Port Royal, Jamaica. Some anxiety is felteregarding the Bermudas, which lie directly in what is supposed to have been the path of the earth- quake. WASHINGTON, SATURDAY.—A telegraphic message ad- dressed to the President from the Queen of England ex- presses her Majesty's profound sympathy with the sufferers ley the recent earthquake. The Queen awaits with anxiety fuller intelligence, which she hopes will show that the calamity has been less disastrous than reported. • PHILADELPHIA, SUNDAY.—At Columbia South Carolina, a vigorous shock was felt, lasting 20 seconds, at one o'clock yesterday morning. Savannah, Georgia. was shaken at in- tervals for several hours after eleven on Friday night. Fears are felt of the possible effect of the earthquake at the Ber- muda Islands, lying in the supposed path of the most violent agitation, their physical features warranting the fear that they have experienced h disaster. The annual September gale due is greatly feared. NEW YORK, MONDAY.—Gr,at alarm prevailed among the inhabitants of Charleston yesterday, and open air services were held in various parts of the city. Slight earthquake shocks were felt ha Charleston and Augusta at eleven o'clock last night. Another distinct shock of earthquake was felt at Columbia, South Carolina, at eleven o'clock last night, accompanied by the ueual roaring sounds at intervals. Five minutes after the shock two remarkably large and brilliant meteors shot across the sky from north to south. About one-third of the population of Charleston are being aseisted by the Relief Committee, who continue to receive contribu- tions from all. parts in aid of the sufferers. Some of the walls damaged by the shock fell to-day. At the meeting of the New York Chamber of Commerce to-day steps were taken to send assistance to the sufferers by the earthquake at Charleston. Preaident Cleveland has sent the following telegram to Queen Victoria :—" Your Majesty's expression easyrnpathy is warmly appreciated and awakes grate- ful response in American hearts." Intelligence from Bermuda states that nothing was felt of the earthquake in that Island. Intelligence received in New York states that several springs have recently appeared in the vicinity of the vil- lage of Cuba del Ague, near Habana, Cuba. The water has formed a large lake, which threatens to inundate the village. Several plantations and factories are already submerged. The springs are increesince in volume, and there are now three feet of water in the place. Some of the inhabitants have been compelled to leave their homes. Two slight shocks of earthquake occurred on Wednesday at Augusta, Georgia. There was also a sharp shock at Savannah, and a number of slight pulsations were felt during Thursday. At Charleston there were three perceptible shocks on Wednes- day. It is estimated that 40,000 persons are now compelled to sleep in the streets and squares of the city. FURTHER EARTHQUAKE SHOCKS IN GREECE. ATHENS, TrESDAY.—Fresla shocks of earthquake were felt here, at Katavryhe, and at other places, at three o'clock, this morning. Renewed seismic disturbances also occurred at a quarter to three yesterday morning in many towns and villages of the Peloponesus. MALTA, WEDNESDAY.—Her Maj,sty's despatch vessel Iris has proceeded to Navarino with stores, tents, blankets, and other necessaries for the relief of the sefferers from the re- cent earthquakes in Greece. THE CHOLERA. ROME, WEDNESDAY —The cholera returns for the last 24 home are as follow : Torre del Annunziata, 20 cases, 8 deaths ; Castellamare, 1 case. 1 death; San Marco in Lemis, 4 deaths : Putignano, 23 cases, 12 deaths ; San Gionanni Rotondo: 5 cases, 3 deaths ; Ferrara, 10 cases, 18 deaths ; , Padua, 6 cases, 2 deaths ; Stradella, 3 Cases, 1 death.

THE WEATHER AND THE HARVEST—The broken weather of the past week has seriously interfered with harvest opera- tions throughout the country. The drenching showers of raid, followed by bursts of sunshine and sultry weather, will also cause the grain to sprout in parts where the crop is heavy. The thunderstorms have beaten down the corn, and the use of the machine is impossible ; this will make a serions addition to the laboar bill. SAD BOATING ACCIDENT.—On Thursday afternoon two young gentlemen named Frederick Bell, of Keswick, and William Rathbone were sailing on Lake Derwentvater, when their small yacht was seen to capsize. Boats were at once despatched irorn the shore, but though the yacht was found floating bottom upwards there was no trace of the occupants. Mr. Rathbone was the eldest son of the member for North Carnarvonsbire, and only arrived at Keswick on Thursday morning for a holiday. EXTRAORDINARY CAPTURE OF AN ALLEGED MURDERER. —A desperate scene was witnessed on Thursday in Biriaing- ham, when a young man named John Clent was arrested by tke police on a charge of murdering a companion, Walter Henry Langley. On Wednesday night the two men had bean playing at billiards. Clent lost his temper, and blows were exchanged. Some time afterwards Clent took a knife out of a bag he was carrying and stabbed Langley to the heart. He escaped, and early this morning the police went to his houze, which they found barricaded. The murderer offered a recklees resistance, throwing all sorts of missiles at the officers, and offering to fight the wliole lot of them. Eventually the window was forced open, and after a sharp struggle Clent was secured. He was brought before the magistrates this morning and remanded for a-week.
IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. The House met at 4-15. In the absence of the Lord Chancellor, the Duke of Buckingham took his seat on the woolsack. There being no business beyond the advancement of a few private and provisional order bills, the House adjourned at 4-40. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 4-0. Tine SILVER QUESTION: ANOTHER COMMISSION.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, in reply to Mr. Montague, said the Goverament have decided to appoint a Royal Commission to inquire into the recent changes in the value of precious metals. He hoped to be able to state to the House in a day or two the names of the Commissioners, and would lay upon the table of the House a minute setting forth the causes of the appointment of the Commission and the terms of reference. Trill AFGHAN BOUNDARY.—Mr. BRYCH asked for infor- mation with regard to the movements of Sir W. Ridgway and the return of the British members of the Afghan Boundary Commiesion. Sir James Ferguson: The Afghan Boundary Commission will return to India as soon as the necessary arrangements have been made—certainly in the course of the present month, and Sir W. Ridgway will con- fer with the Ameer of Afghanistan at Cabul on his road.

THR BULGARIAN CResrs.—Mr. BRYCE, asked whether Prince Alexander of Bulgaria had abdicated, and whet steps were being taken to appoint his successor. Sir J. FERGUS. 13CiN : As far as her Majesty's Government are informed no act of abdication has been performed by Prince Alexander. With regard to the future, any arrangements can only, ac- cording to public law and international engagements, be made upon the basis of the Treaty of Berlin—(cheers),— which gives no separate or exclusive right to any one Power. Hee Majesty's Government have no separate en- gagements, duties, or interests in Bulgaria. Their engage- ments and duties are held in common with the Great Powers, whose assent to the election ef k Prince must be unanimous. (Hear, hear.) They had hoped much from the ability and great qualities of Prince Alexander. (Cheers.) They deplore the treachery and violence by which his reign was interrupted—(renewed cheers).—and they would hear with regret that be had finally abandoned the task he had undertaken. (Cheers.) THE ARMY ESTIMATES. The House having gone into Committee of Supply, the CHANCRLLOR of the I.xcetEeeniert rose and said: I beg to move that Mr. Leonard Courtney take the chair. (Cheers) —Mr. Courtney was about to take the chair when Mr. Sex- ton, interposing, asked, ‘• Who puts the motion? "—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER understood that should any member rise to speak to the motion the Speaker would resume his place in the chair.—No hon. member rising, Mr. Courtenay took his seat at the table amid cheers, and the consideration of the Army estimates was proceeded with. The balance of £30,800 for divine service in the army and of £17,600 for the administration of military law were voted without discussion. On a vote of £173,000 to complete the estimate for army medical establishments, .Colonei DUNCAN called attention to certain grievances under which he stated the Army Medical Department laboured, mentioning in par- ticular the extreme disproportion of foreign to home service —Mr. W. 11. SMITH agreed that the medical staff of the army was deserving of all encouragement, and promised that their grievances should have his careful attention. I On the vote of £285,000 to complete the vote for the militia, Mr. LLEWELLYN called attention to the unsatisfac- tory condition of shooting in the militia, pointing out that volunteers bad opportunities of practice which were denied I to the militia.—Mr. LADWOHERIi stated that the vote in- eluded regimental bands, and he desired to know to what length the instructions issued by the.department as to the employment of these bands at political demonstrations went. —Mr. W. H. SMITH concurred in the views expressed by Mr. Campbell-Bannerman. No military uniform should be allowed to appear in party. politics, but the military and naval forces of the country should be kept altogether free from the question of party. (Hear, hear.) His inflaence would be used to secure that no person in the Queen's uni- form attended a party demonstration of any kind. He had no control over bandsmen not in uniform. The vote was agreed O. 'On the vote of ,£36,000 for the Yeomanry Cavalry, Mr.l LABOUCHERB maintained that this was a perfectly useless expenditure, and that the money would be far better em- ployed in increasing the capitation grant to the Vol leers. He opposed the vote.—Upon a division, it was carried by 155 to 64. On the vote of £300.500 for the Volunteer Corps, Sir W. HARTTRLOT inquired whether the Secretary of State bad yet been able to consider the question of increasing the capita- tion grant.—Mr. JOHN CONNOR asked the right hon. gentle- man to seriously consider the establishment of a Volunteer force in Ireland. He moved the reduction of the vote by £l6,ooo.—Mr. W. H. SMITH pointed out that there was no legal power to institute a volunteer force in Ireland.- He should be glad when the state of the country was such that her Majesty's Government would be able to propose an alteration of the law in this respect. Mr. O'Connor's amendment was on a division rejected by 150 votes to 55, and the vote was agreed to. On the vote of £260,200 for commissariat and transport services, a long discussion occurred, and the vote was agreed to. The House adjourned at 1-40. HOUSE OF LOB.DS.—TUESDAVe The Duke of Buckingham and Chandos, in the absence of the Lord Chancellor, took his seat on the woolsack at 4-15. , The Prince of Wales, the Duke of Connaught, the Duke of Manchester, and the Earl of Bradford took the oath and subscribed to the roll. Seven private bills and the same number of provisional order bills were read a third time and passed.. Several other provisional order bills were forwarded a stage. Their Lordships adjourned at 4-40. • HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. THE IRISH CONSTABULA.RY.—Ansiveriag questions from Colonel Sendys and Mr. Hooper, Sir M. Hecies•BExcer gave the general strength of the Royal Irish Constabulary as 275 officers, 249 head constables, 2,536 sergeants and acting ser- geants, 9,750 constables. The distribution of religious per- suasion was approximately 50 Roman Catholic officers, 216 Episcopalians, and 10 Presbyterians; 1,801 Catholic ser- geants and acting sergeants. 650 Episcopalians, and 115 Presbyterians ; 7,318 Catholic constables, 1,963 Episcopa- lians, and 429 Presbyterians. BULGARIA.—Mr. HOWARD VINCENT asked if the Govern- ment were in possession of any confirmation .as to the alleged contemplated partition of South-Eastern Europe by the triple alliance, and whether the occupation of Bulgaria by Russian troops, or the administration of that Princi- pality by a Russian Governor, would be in accordance with existing treaties, or consistent with the integrity of the Ottoman Empire and the safety of Constantinople.—Sir Jeans FERGUSSON said: Her Majesty's Government are is possession of no such information as is mentioned in the first question. The second suggests a hypothesis of separate action on the part of one of the Powers, which Her Majesty's Government could not assume as possible. MISCELLANEOUS.—In reply to Mr. Pulleston, the CHAN- CELLOR of the EXCHEQUER said that the constitution of the Currency Commission would be as follows:—Mr. J. Balfour, Seeretary for Scotlacd (chairman); Mr. Jos. Chamberlain, Mr. L. Courtney, Mr. L. Cohen, Mr. W. H. Houldswortb, Sir J. Lubbock, Mr. E. M. Berber (Secretary to the Govern- ment of India in the Department of Trade), Mr. Bowel (director of the Bask of England), Sir Thomas Farrar, the Hon. C. W. Freemantle (Deputy Master of the. Mint), and Mr. J. R. Bowen Smith (member of the Council of India).— In reply to Mr. Labouchere Mr. W. H. Smith said that his attention had not been called to a placard announcing that the band of the Bedfordshire Regiment would perform at a Primrose, meeting at Longford, in Herts, but he would take care that the Queen's regulations on the subject were at- tended to. (Hear, hear.) SUPPLY.—ARMY ESTIMATES. In Committee of Sapply, on the vote of £1,650.000 to cemplete the sum required for warlike and other stores, Mr. Moaaciv drew attention to the complaints that had been made as to the the quality of these stores, and asked what were the intentions of the Secretary for War on this subject. —Sir W. BA.RTTELOT said the country demanded a thorough investigation into this important question, which involved the whole question of our defences, including that of our coaling stations abroad.—Mr. BRADLAUGH said he had been requested by some private soldiers, who were aware that he had himself been a soldier—(hear, hear)—to lay before the House their statement that daring the time they were serv- ing in Egypt they were left on different occasions without medicine and without two days' rations, because those things could not he conveyed in conseqaence of the trans- port carts leaving broken down by reason of the rotten con- dition of the harness.—Captain PRICE referred to the charges brought by the press against the action of the Ord- nance Committee, and arguea that the result of the recent inquiry showed that the whole system respired revision.— Captain SELWYN asked whether it was intended to issue a new and improved rifle to the army, and suggested that in any new weapon attention should be paid to the lowering of the trajectory, and the issue of cartridges that would not Jane in the barrels.—Mr. Woodall said the question of a new rifle had of late engaged considerable attention, and the new and improved arm that had been decided upon was in pro- cess of manufacture and distribution, the weapon baying been tried at Wimbledon to the great satisfaction of the skilled volunteers who had used it. Admiral Sir J. COMICERELL thought the country bad a right to ask how it was that OM' naval guns were in such a condition that the men who had to work them felt they would be safer in front of them than behind them. (Hear, hear.) The debate was continued by Colonel HUGHES HALLETT, who moved the reduction of the vote by .£5,000. —Sir E. J. REED said there was a feeling abroad that there was too great an intimacy between some of the public de- partments and certain private firms, and expressed a hope that the Government would exercise great caution in regard to this matter.—Mr. W. H SMITH said the hon. gentleman had for six months been a member of the late Government, and during that time had said nothing as to the condition of things be now denounced.—Sir E. J. REED said he had more than once called attention to the matters referred to.— Mr. W. H. SMITH, referring to the recent charges against the Ordeance Department, reminded the House that he had challenged anyone who had any definite information to give, or any case to adduce as to malversaton, corruption, fraud, or conduct disgraceful to any officer or gentleman, to bring the matter to his knowledge at once, and he would undertake to find a tribunal to investigate the charge. ellear, hear.)—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL denied that there was anything in the vague and indefinite charges that had

div.head: EXA ‘IINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 11, 1886_
div.p: THE EXA ‘IINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 11, 1886_
recently been promulated in regard to the action of the Ordnance Department. After some discussion, the CRAW- .
CELLOR of the EXCHEQUER said !.t should be remembered that the Government had only been in office for a
short time, and so large a change as they had in-

dicated with regard to the transfer of the navy ord- nance to the Navy Department could not be expected to take effect until after the lapse of a reasonable time. The discussion, in which Mr. Cawhell-Bannerman sympa-
thised with the Government view, was continued until half- past ten, when the vote on which it arose was agreed to.—
After this the remainiug votes were more rapidii, dispesed
of, and soon after midnight the whole of the Army votes obtained, and they were ordered to be reported to the
House. THE BELFAST RIOTS.—On the orar for the second read- ing of the Disturbance at Belfast Inquiry Bill, Mr. SEXTON moved that _publicity of the proceedings of the proposed

. . court was indispensable, and that the—arrangements for procuring evidence were not sufficiently stringent.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL for IRELAND replied that the Irish Government intended the court to be open to all interested, and that the Commissioners would have the same power as the High Court to compel the production of evidence. He

defended the appointments of Commissioners already made, and could not consent to the suggested addition.—The Bill was read a second time on the understanding that the composition of the Commission would be further dis- cussed.
The House adjourned at 15 minutes past two. HOUSE OF COMMONSI—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at ten minutes past twelve. HOMELESS POOR IN LONDON.—Mr. PICICERSGILL asked
the President of the Local Government Board whether his
attention had been called to the fact that a large number of homeless poor, comprising men, women, and children slept

nightly on the Embankment and other open spaces of the metropolis.—Mr. Lona replied that the Board had no infor- mation beyoud what appeared in the newspapers with res- pect.to the number of persons who slept in the open spaces _ _

of the metropolis. Having referred that morning to the report of the Superintendent Visiting Officer of Vagrant Wards, he had found that there were only three wards in which admission had been refused to vagrants. The

refusals were five persons in two cases, respecting both of which the Board had asked for explanations. In all cases of refusal, if the applicants were women or chil- dren, care was taken to ascertain that they were in a fit state to move on.
THE NAVY ESTIMATES —On the Order for Committee of
Supply on the Navy Estimates, Sir E. REED complained of the manner in which naval returns were made to The House.
Criticising particularly a recent one, he pointed out that it made our fleets appear more powerful than they were, whilst representing foreign fleets at leas than. their real

strengtb.—Mr. BRADLAUGIti giving instances of the waste of stores, pressed the Government for an assurance that such mismanagement should not recur.—Admiral Com- MBRELL and others complained of the condition of the navy,
aud Lord GEORGE HAMILTON admitted that with regard to
guns there had been some failitres.—The vote for miscel- laneous services was under consideration when, at a quarter
to six, progress was reported, and the House resumed. The Report of Supply un Army Estimates was brought up
• and agreed to, with the exception of two votes, which stand over.
The House adjourned at seven minutes to six o'clock.
HO USE OF LORDS.—TIitIPSDAY. The Duke of Buckinglaam and Chandes, in the absence of
the Lord Chancellor, —took his seat on' the Woolsack at

twenty minutes atter four o'clock. PRINCH ALEXILNDER.—EarI Ds Li WARR inquired whether Her Majesty'a Government had any information to give the House with regard to the reported abdication of the Prince of Bulgaria, and the steps which had been taken in
consequence by the European Powers.—The Earl of Inns- No doubt the arrangements that will have to be made in consequence of the abdication of the Prince will be
made in accordance with the Treaty of Berlin and the ar-

rangements that were made subsequently at the Conference, and I du not think there would be any advantage in entering into any speculation with regard to the course which will be pursued by He( Majesty's Government. (Hear, hear.) LAND TENURE IN IRELAND. - The Earl of LEITRIM moved—That in the opinion of this House all leaseholders in Ireland who at the natural expiration of their leases will come under the Land Act of 1881, or who way be subject to a fluctuation of rent during the term of their lease, should have access to the Land Commissioners for the adjustment of their rents.—The Earl of Hovrra did not wish to obstruct legislation in favour of leaseholders, but held that this was not a fitting opportunity for attempting to bring about a change in the law. There had not been sufficient time given for the consideration of the motion.—Earl CADOGAN, reply-

_ lug for the Government, pointed out that the resolution, if adopted, would go far beyond the Act of 1881. He there- fore trusted that as the resolution was one which the Government could not accept the noble earl would withdraw it.—The resolution was withdrawn.
Their Lordships adjourned at a quarter to six until Monday. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TXURSDLY.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. QUESTIONS.—At the opening of business, Mr. Summers having given notice of a motion to be brought forward next session by Sir Henry Roscoe with reference to the open- ing of art galleries on Sundays, Mr. Caleb Wright suc- ceeded in obtaining an answer to his long-pending question from the Chancellor of the Exchequer, who promised to sub- mit to Parliament next year an estimate of the charge for a gratis supply of Parliamentary documents to free libraries. Mr. Wright's notice appeared twice amongst the ques- tions, and helped to swell the number to a total of sixty-two. An unusual number of them de- manded the attention of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, and Lord Randolph Churchill exerted himself to please the House and satisfy curiosity on a variety of subjects. Hay- ing with unaccustomed modesty disclaimed a full know- ledge of the gold currency question, he jocosely told Sir John Lubbock, with regard to the possible appointment of a Minister of Education, that any change in a public depart- ment involving increased charge upon the public purse

sessed in his eyes an " incurable defect." Peculiar significance was detected in his reply to Mr. Pickersgill. The latter wished to know whether, as he had given a day for the consideration of the bill to relieve the Irish tenantry, he would off 3r similar facilities for a measure in the interesto of the poor rate- payers of London. Lord Randolph sarcastically commented ou the analogy suggested between the Irish tenants and the London ratepayers, which be thought would be made use of during the forthcoming discussion on Mr. Parnell's bill, but he asserted that the Government saw no reason for alter- ing their decision not to initiate legislation themselves, or to encourage it on the part of private members daring the present session. CIVIL SERVICE ESIIMATES.

Upon the order to go into Committee of Supply, for the first time, upon the Civil Service Estimates, which was called on at a quarter past five o'clock, Mr. Pickersgill proposed to assail a regulation of the Local Government Board affecting metropolitan unions, but he discovered to his confusion— and the House roared over his disappointment—that he was precluded from going on with his prepared speech because he had himself already brought in a bill to deal with the same matter. As Mr. Tuite was prevented from adverting to the Barbavilla murders, notwithstanding Mr. Sexton's interposition on his behalf, cheerful expectations arose that the work of voting Supply might be resumed without delay. Mr. Conway was free to make his protest against the treatment of denominational schools under the present School Board system,but be by Bo means abused his opportunity, and he received such warm expressions of sympathy, not only from the Vice-President of the Council, but also from Lord Cranborne and others of the Tory party, that he was easily persuaded not to press his amendment, especially as Lord I Cranborne went across the floor to confer with him. In this as In other matters the Government trusted to a Royal Commission to help them out of a difficulty, and the subject was disposed of is a very short time. Mr. Tuite was again baffled in his endeavour to promote controversy, and Mr. Biggar was foiled in an attempt to raise an irrelevant de- bate, but still no resentment was displayed by the Irishmen, and it was in the qnietest possible manner that Mr. Dillon touched upon the subject of the Royal Irish Constabulary as connected with the enforcement of evictions. That sub- ject being once broached opened the floodgates of Irish rhetoric for a time, and in spite of a mild remonstrance from Sir M. Hicks-Beach, Mr. Edward Harrington persisted in discoursing on the theme for the greater.part of an hour. Mr. 1. D. Pyne demanded a count in order to ensure an adequate audience for his friend Mr. B. Kelly; and after Mr. Labouchere had interpolated a brief reference to the mismanagement of the Department of Woods and Forests, with the result of obtaining satisfactory pledges of investi- gation from the Government, M. Pyne himself took up the topic of the Irish constabulary, and startled and amused a thin House by one of the most eccentric displays of Hiber- nian oratory that have yet been produced by the Parnellite party. At the same time he seemed to be thoroughly in earnest, and an appearance of sincerity saved him from suspicion of any deliberate obstructive design. When his harangue ceased, Dr. Tanner presented himself from under the side gallery to continue the debate; but he received a sudden check from the Speaker, and failed to protract his remarks beyond ordinary limits. Mr.O'Hanlon was literally "brought to book" by Mr. Tomlinson, who had long been studying a small volume bearing upon the rules of proce- dure; and as it was now half-past nine o'clock, and nearly • five hours had been frittered away, the Irish members al- lowed the House to go into Committee of Supply. On the Civil Services Estimates, Mr. Labouchere moved that the vote of £15,978 for the salaries and expenses of the officers of the House of Lords be red nced by the sum of £l,7oo.—After discussion the Committee divided—For Mr. Labouchere's amendment, 98; against, 173; majority against, 75.—0 n the vote of £23,560 for the Treasury. Mr. LABOUCHERE moved its reduction by £3,000, a portion of the salary of the Chancellor of the Exchequer. The noble Lord had made many speeches in the House on the subject of economy, and it wtmld be a proof of his desire for economy if he were to agree to this reduction of his salary. Allowing that the noble Lord was the equal of Prince Bis- marck, if £2,400 was sufficient for him, then the noble Lord, who received £5,000, was surely over paid. (Laughter.) The total salary of the present Ministers was about £160,000, and of that sum £llO,OOO was received by peers and peers' sons.—The Committee divided without discus- sion, and Mr. La6ouchere's motion was rejected by 181 to 66. Progress was afterwards reported, and the House re- sumed. The report of Wednesday's Supply was adopted. —On the report of Tuesday's Supply, Mr. SEXTON com- plained of the sale of Government powder at cost price to

rifle eiubs in Ireland.—Mr. W. H. SMITH promised to look into the subject.—The report was agreed to. i-aron H. DE WORMS brought in a bill to amend the sub- marine Telegraph Act, 1885. The House adjourned at ten minutes to two.

div.head: GHASTLY MURDER IN PARIS.
div.p: GHASTLY MURDER IN PARIS.

A horrible crime was committed on Weinesday afternoon in the Rue Albouy, at Paris. A young woman, named Loa Heritier, aged 28, came to Paris two years ago as servants. She was seduced, and be- came the mistress of a man named Blanc, aged 28, who professed to be a cook, but who really belonged to the most disreputable class of scoundrels in Paris. He told her that he meant to make her keep him, and when she refused he struck her unmercifully and took her dresses and trinkets from her and sold them. Lea lodged a complaint with the police, and in March last Blanc was condemned to four months' imprisonment. On leaving prison, on July 24, he threatened to be revenged on Lea. He went to the house where she lived, but the concierge refused to allow him to go upstairs, and, presenting a revolver, compelled him to retire. Blanc then became a frequent visitor of a pub- lic-house which communicates by a back entrance with the staircase leading to Lea's room. Taking advantage of the absence of the concierge yesterday, he found his way to it. He knocked at the door, and when it was opened by Loa he told her be had come to settle her affair. He produced a long knife in a wooden handle. She at first begged for mercy, then she screamed "Help," and "Murder," but before there was time for assistance to come he had seized his victim by the hair, thrown her on the ground, and cut off her head. A neighbour had been trying to get in, but found the door fastened, and had to escape, as Blanc was armed with a revolver and threatened to shoot him. Meanwhile, a crowd had assembled before the window, at which the murderer appeared with the head. He hung it by the hair to the handle of the shutter. Just as the door was burst open by the police Blanc shot himself in the breast with his revol- ver. The two bodies were removed to the Morgue after the legal inquiry, which was necessarily brief, ha.' been completed.

ST. HELENS RECREATION V. STONYCROFT - Played at Stonycroft on Saturday last, with the following result : Recreation, 113 ' • Stonycroft, 39. WARRINGTON VICTORIA V. WARRINGTON v. WM- —Warrington took a fairly, strong team to Werneth on Saturday, an owing to the good batting of Clarke, J. J. Crosfield, Lawton, Ford, and Louis, they succeeded in keeping up tbe wickets until time was called. The two Crosfields went in first, and S. M. having been caught by Bottomley at 11, Clarke joined J. J. Cros- field. At 80, the latter retired for a well played 36, and Denton, who came next, stayed while 100 runs were put on, of which be made 20. Moggeridge was beaten by a good ball from Bent, and J. C. Lawton came in. Clarke, at 103, gave a difficult chance in the slips, and did not seem to steady down again. He was taken at long slip at 213, or 202 runs on while he was at the wicket. His performance was an excellent one, and he was warmly applauded. C. G. Lawton hit with freedom, and he was ably seconded by Ford and Louis. Yates bowled the most successfully. In all eight bowlers were tried, and some had several at- tempts.

NOTES BY THE WAY.-

At Southampton on Siturday the Surrey Eleven did a capital performance against Hants, heating the latter county at the finish by ten wickets. Much of thia brilliant result was due to the splendid bowling of Lohmann, who fol- lowed up his achievement in the first innings, when he had Stye wickets for 64, by an even better one in the second, when he obtained seven wickets at an average of three runs apiece. In the match he took twelve wickets for 85 runs. The Colts gained an easy victory over the Eleven in the Derbyshire Colts match which concluded at Derby on Tues-flay in beautiful weather. As on the previous day the bowlers had matters all their own way, Cropper and David- son bowling unchanged throughout the second innings of Colts, whose 'batting calls for no special mention. The Eleven required 128 to get to win, but only Cropper played the bowling with any confidence, and the total reached 36. Hulme, who bowled successfully on Monday, took five wickets without a ran being obtained off him, and Derby- shire appear to have found in him a good left-hand bowler ao4 a dangerous hat. The cricket at Bradford on Wednesday was neither im- portant nor interesting. The position of the game between Eleven of Eogland and the Australians over night left little hope of finishinz the match, and the weather was so cold, windy, and dull that but few people visited the Park Avenue ground. The Australians were batting from ten minutes past twelve until a quarter past four, when rain caused the players to seek shelter. It was soon apparent that further cricket was impracticable, and the game was eventually abandoned. The Australians with eight wickets down, were then 235 runs on. Trumble had hurt his knee and 'would not have goue in. The bast innings of the day was played by Jones, whose excellent 50 consisted of eight fours, two threes, four twos, and singles. rougher, despite his lameness, was very successful with the ball. After promising to end in a draw, the third and last match of the Scarborough festival was on Wednesday won by the M.C.C. by 133 run!, at a quarter to four. With 246 runs to get to win, and no possibility of making such a number in the time remaining for play, the Yorkshire men went in for their second innings. Everything pointed to the game being left unfinished, but Bates, I.llyett, and Hall were got rid of for 18 runs, and despite a fine innings of 42 by Mr. Hawke and some very plucky cricket by Peel, the eleven were all out at a quarter to six for a total of 112. The M.C.C. gained their victory by first-rate all round cricket, and thoroughly deserved to win. Some capital bat- ting by Messrs. J. G. Walker, Page, and Paravicini in the early part of the day put the game in such a position that the club could not lose, and in Yorkshire's second innings the good bowling of Barnes and Mr. Grace was backed up• by brilliant out-fielding. The two bowlers divided the wickets equally between them, but Mr. Grace, who con- stantly bowled for catches, was much the more expensive. The chief honours of an excellent tnatch belongel to Barnes and Mr. Walker, the former taking eleven wickets for 120 runs and scoring 30 and 7, and Mr. Walker playing two ad- mirable innings of 55 and 65 not out.

div.head: SAD DEATH AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: SAD DEATH AT EARLESTOWN.

Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an in. quest at the Prince of Wales Hotel, Earlestown, on Monday afternoon, respecting the death of Joseph Lythgoe, whose dead body was on Friday evening discovered in a well in the neighbourhood. De- ceased, who was 68 years old, was very popular, and was known throughout the district. Formerly he , was for a number of years a member of the Newton Board of Commissioners, and was also responsibly concerned in large contracts, under a contractor living in the neighbourhood. He had, however, for some years given up active business, and his house. the Prince of Wales, was managed by his son. De- ceased was of robust constitution, but for some months past his nervous system had been seriously affected, and he suffered at times great pain. He was also subject to dizziness. It is supposed that on Friday he was looking at the well, which is only protected by a low wall, and, being seized with dizziness, fell in. The following evidence was taken:— '

Richard Lythgoe, of the Prince of Wales Inn, said that the deceased was his father, and was 68 years of age last July. In answer to a question whether deceased had of late been in a depressed state of mind, witness said that for the last six or seven months one of his servants had slept with de- ceased, and had kept him company night and day. Deceased had been attended by Jr. Fatersen for nervous debility and hallucinations. Witness last saw him alive at nine o'clock on the previous Friday morning. They had then just had breakfast, and deceased went out by the front door, but did not say where he was going to. Wit- ness supposed that he was going for his usual walk as he had been accustomed to do for the last few months. In answer to Sergeant Commins, witness said that his father, on going out, remarked "Good morning, lam going for a walk." Replying to a question from the Coroner, witness said deceased had not been subject to fits, but sometimes he had put his hand to his head and stumbled as though he were giddy. William A.spinall, cooper, Vitriol-square, said that at about five o'clock on Friday evening he met Richard Lythgoe, who said that his father was mis- sing. They went in search and found a stick that belonged to deceased near the well in question. The body was afterwards recovered. In answer to questions, witness said that the well was on private ground, but there was a road through which was commonly used. The cottage of a friend of the de- ceased's named Craven, was about thirty yards dis- tant from the well.

Mary Ann Craven, wife of George Craven, Sankey paper mills, Earlestown, said that her husband was a postman. Deceased came to her house at about ten o'clock on Friday morning and inquired for Cra- ven, -who was not at home. Deceased said that he had come down to have a chat with Craven and then, remarking that he would have a look round, went away. In her opinion the well was a danger- ous one, and one that anyone might tumble in. The paper mill, had belonged to a company, but it was not working now. She and her husband acted as ! caretakers. There were a great many children in. the neighbourhood. George Aspinall, cooper, Vitriol-square, said. that on Thursday night deceased asked him about the depth of the well, when witness met him in the Prince of Wales. Witness said he believed it cost £12,000. and deceased said "Sadly too much." That was not the well from which the body of the de- ceased was recovered. _ _ _ _

This was all the evidence.—The foreman, Mr. Ed- wardson, expressed the opinion that the well, which is only encircled by a low wall, was a dangerous place.—The jury, after a few moments conversation, came to the conclusion that the deceased acciden- tally fell into the well, and returned a verdict to that effect. They also expressed the opinion that tho well should be properly covered over.

MR. LYTHGOE'S CAREER. • By the death of Mr. Joseph Lythgoe, Earlestewn has lost one of its oldest, and most prominent inhabitants. It may, indeed, be said that the growth of Earlestown, from a a mere hamlet of a few houses, hie been coincident with the life of Mr. Lythgoe, so interwoven is Ir'cal history with the labours of that 0-^f,eman in the vicinity. Mr. Lytilgos, who attained the 68th anniversary of his birth oh the 20th July laSt, was horri at, INgh, where Dit Wit! I.4otlght up until his marriage, exactly 50 years at a fortnight, ptior to the accident which brought so long and useful a life to such an unfortunate termination. At Leigh he had been employed in mining and similar occupa- tions, and two years after his marriage he journeyed to France, where he pursued his avocation with such credit that after about seven years stay in that country he re- turned to Leigh with several testimonials as to his efficiency. At his native town be com- menced business as contractor for tunnelling and builders, dc., but in a very short time he he was engaged by the late Mr. Thomas Stone. of Newton, as superintendent foreman over the bricksetters, builders, &c. This post he occupied for a great number of years, and this brought him into close connection with Earlestown, or Warrington Junction as it was more generally called. About that time the London and North-Western Railway .Company purchased the small foundry, owned by Messrs. Jones and Potts, and in the course of a few years carried Out extensive alterations and additions, and transformed the place into what is now known as the Viaduct Works, the great waggon making depot of the company. The contract for these extensions was secured by the late Mr. Thomas Stone, of Newton, and the work was carried out under the personal superintendence and directions of Mr. Lythgoe. The erection of cottage property for the work- men of the company was also commenced, and these buildings virtually made Earlestown what it is at the present moment. In those days Earle-street, Market-street, Queen-street, and Bridge-street, the present thoroughfares of the town, were unknown, and, in fact, had not been projected; but the dwelling-houses, built also under the supervision of Mr. Lythgoe, rapidly gave son.e semblance of a town to the district. Among other works carried out by the late Mr. Stone and superintended by Mr. Lythgoe were the erection of the present Mersey Mills, Wartington, built for Mr. James Fairclough. In 1863 Mr. Lythgoe succeeded the late Mr. Melling as the tenant of the tiriffin lon, Earle-street, which he kept for a period of 12 years. After a short retirement to private life he moved to the Prince of Walas Inn, Earle-street. This was in the year 1876, and ha remained here up to about 18 months ago, when the business was transferred to his son Richard, who had for some time previously managed the busi- ness for his father. Since then the deceased has lived on the premises and took an active interest in the huslness up to the day of his death. Daring the time he occupied the ariffin Inn and the Prince of Wales Inn, Mr. Lythgoe was frequently consulted by local gentlemen upon building and other matters requiring skilled attention, and in recognition of his ability and excellent workmanship he was presented with many testimonials. In other directions Mr. Lvthgoe was equally well known and esteemed. He was generally understood to be the old- est Oddfellow, in the town, as for over 50 years he was a member of the Royal Alfred Lodge, whose headquarters were at Leigh. In connection therewith he bad occupied every post in turn with the exception of that of secretary. Though not a member of any Earlestown branches he has officiated as treasurer for the local lodge of Foresters, and other similar institutions. He was also one of the prime movers in the establishment of the Earlestown Mineral Waters Company, and had taken an active interest in it as one of the managing directors. For a neriod of about a den years he occupied a seat as one of the im- provement Commissioners for the township of Newton. In politics be was a consistent Liberal and was one of the sub- scribers to the first and every succeeding Liberal Club in the district. He was of a generous disposition, and in re- ligious opinions was a Churchman. The deceased's wife died about two years ago. Of the marriage there were 12 children, but only two sons (Richard Lytbgoe, who succeeda,his father at the Prince of Wales Inn), and James Lythgoe (of the Oddfellows Arms, Legh- street), and one daughter survive. The deceased did not enjoy good health for some time prior to his death, and was attended by Dr. Patterson for about eight months, while during the last three or four months he had also consulted Dr. Smith, of Warrington. The an- nouncement of the death of Mr. Lythgoe, under circum- stances stated in our report of the ineluest, created a sensa- tion throughout the district, and there were icepreseions of sympathy and regret on every band, FUNERAL.

The remains of the deceased gentleman were interred in the graveyard attached to Emmanuel Church, Wargrave, on Tuesday afternoon, and the funeral cortege, which con- sisted of hearse and seven coaches, was fully representative of the esteem in which the deceased was generally held. In, the first each was Mr. James Lvtbgoe and Mr. Richard Lythgoe (sons of the deceased), Mrs. James Lythgoe, Mr. Thomas Lythgoe (nephew), Miss Nancy Lythg‘e (niece), and Mr. Richard Aldred (Leigh). The second coach con- tained Mrs. R. Aldred and Mrs. Collier, Dr. J. N. Patterson, 1 Mr. William Melling, and Mr. Henry Houghton ; in the third were Mr. William Williamson (late foreman at Vulcan foundry), Mr. James Tinsley and Mr. Edward Kay (repre- sentatives of the Bedford Brewery Company), and Mr. I. Craughton and Mr. J. Fairclough (representing Messrs. Stone, of Newton); - the fourth coach contained Mr. Richard Barclay, Mr. John William Webster, Mr. Peter W. Bent, Mr. Edward Edwardson, Mr. W. D. Hurdle (on behalf of the Earlestown Liberal Club), and Mr. Thomas Howard. A large num;)er of other friends at- tended, among whom were—Mrs Fairhurst, Miss Lea, Mr. George Aspinall, and Messrs. Edward and William Aspin- all. Messrs. John Walker, L. Jones. P. White, and J. Appleton were present as carriers. Along the route many 1 persons congregated and a large number of blinds in i dwelling-houses were drawn. The funeral service was con-. 1 ducted by the Rev. Canon Whitley, rector.

RUNCORN ATHLETIC CLUB V. SUTTON FREE WANDER- ans.—These clubs played their opening match at Sutton on Saturday, before a fair number of spectators. The Ath- letics scored one try and two minors, against the Wanderers five minors.

RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB .—A football match took Place on Saturday evening on the ground of the Runcorn Football Club, betwem the teams of Mr. H. Hughes and Mr. J. Wilson. The Runcorn captain placed 17 men on the field asainst 20 opponents. Both sides were pretty evenly matched, and a good game was played. Both first and second team men displayed admirable form, and they will evidently want beating -during next season. The game re- sulted in one try being scored by H Hughes' team against two touchdowns. CARRINGTON lsr TEAM v. JUNIORS.

Football is such a favourite game in Warrington that the seasons of the Warrington Football Club end late and com- mence early. It seems only a short time since the vic- torious first team brought home the coveted, well-fought- for challenge cup too ards the end of a season's play, which was in every respect a successful one, and one in which the Club raised its prestige to a very high point, while on Sat- urday another season may be said to have been iniated by a match between the first team, numbering fourteen, and a team of nineteen juniors, though what is really the opening match is to be played to-day on the ground off Wilderspeol Causeway, between the well-known Swinton team and the Warrington first team. Altheugh no special announc,ment had been made of Saturday's match yet there was a considerable 'attendance of spectators who were rewarded by witnessing a very closely contested match. The ball having been started the first part of the game was somewhat adverse to the seniors. In a couple of scrimmages that took place the large number, of the juniors gave them an advantage, which Ran(lane, Apple- ton, and Boardman, the three-quarter backs, fully availed themselves of. Randalls securing the ball gained some ground for the juniors, and Appleton by smart play im- proved the position. Speakman, however, did some good service to the seniors by his saving tactics, and eventually passed the ball to Jolley, who forwarded it to the centre, and soon after Antrobus was the means of getting it into the juniors quarters. The large numbers of the latter, however, rendered it difficult to make headway, and the leather was again taken towards the goal posts of Ashton's men, and it was found necessary to concede a touchdown to the juniors. In the play which followed Whittle's team again had the advantage, and Buxton was more than once caned upon to defend his goal line, which he did with his accustomed dash. Ere long a second minor was conceded to the juniors, who were only pre- vented from again scoring in the first part of the game by same fine play on the part of their antagonists. In the early part of the second half Speakman, Hough, Heyes, and Bux- ton, for the seniors, and Whittle, Appleton, and Boardman showed good play for their respective sides, and Boardman, from a pass by Whittle, at length secured a try, from which Walsh obtained a goal. The first team now strove hard to equalise matters, and eventually a minor point was placed to. their credit, and later on Buxton got hold of the ball, punted, and following up gained a try behind the posts. Speakman, who attempted the goal, was not successful, and the game ended in favour of the juniors by one goal and two minors to one try and one minor. It should be men- tioned that the form displayed by the players was of a promising description, though the first team was deprived of Barnes and Gilbert, who were playing for Tyldesley against Beswick's Swinton team, Massey, Rigby, and Dillon. In the ranks of the juniors, setting aside such well-known hands as Whittle, Walsh, Appleton and Boardman, who certainly held out no signs of falling off, but the contrary, there was some capital material which will no doubt render good service in future matches. The teams were—Seniors : Back, Buxton ; three-quarters, Hough, Fair. Turner, and Jolley: half, Antrobus and Speakman; forwards, F. Turner, Povey. Hayes, Dillon, E Nevins, Littlewood, Davies, and Ashton (captain). Juniors : Back, Bibby ; three-quarters, Handles. Appleton, and Boardman ; half, Whittle (captain) and Walsh; forwards, Ceagan, Thornley, Fair, Eyes, Bate, Rigby, Ashurst, McEvoy, Howarth, Telford, Evans, Jones, and Savage. Umpires, Messrs. Barns and Wright. Referee, Mr. T. Pemberton. it should be mentioned that the headquarters of the club have been removed to the Roebuck Inn, Bridge-street, where rooms have been admirably fitted up for the pur- poses of the club. On the top floor three rooms are set apart, one for the home team, one for visitors, and a third for washing purposes. On the second floor the large club room will be used for dinners, &c., and is very suitable for this purpose. In the washing room there are six bowls fitted up on the patent system of Messrs. Maoferlane and Co., Glasgow, and tnppli!d. by Mr, ca,1,4w01; pf Warring- ton.

. , ASSOCIATION RULES. HAYDOCX V. WEST MANCHESTER.—Haydock commenced their season en Saturday with West Manchester, at Hay- dock, and as the visitors had obtained a high reputation for last season's performances considerable interest was manifested in the match, which Haydock won by ten goals to one. EARLESTOWN CHESTER ST. OSWALD'S.—The first teams of these clubs met on the ground of the first-named, the Alesnes, Earlestown, on Saturday afternoon. There was a large attendance of spectators, who were rewarded by wit- nessing an even game. The resnit was a victory fer Earles- town by two goals to one. RUNCORN ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL CLUB V. BARNTON BOYERS —The first match of the newly-formed Runcorn Association Football Club was played at Runcorn on Satur- day. Owing to the late arrival of the visitors, the kick-off did not take place until 4-15. After a fast and pleasant game the visitors won by four goals to nil. EARLESTOWN WANDERERS V. SPRINGS BRANCLI STEAM- MED.-The Earlestown Wanderers visited Wigan on Satur- day to play the above match, and defeated the home team by eight goals to three. J. Shaw, the Earlestown captain, scored six, and J. Ogden and J. ljearden one each. The game was agreeably contested, but the home team were slightly outplayed. The second team of the Wanderers opposed the Common Rangers on the ground of the latter, and a pleasant game resulted in favour of the visitors by three goals to one.

div.head: STATE OF IRELA:ND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELA:ND.

Tralee, the centre of the area in which agrarian and moonlighting offences have been most prevalent of late, was visited by Sir Redvers Buller on Saturday, in company with Colonel Turner and County Inspector 31oriaty. It was market day, and many of the country people were in town, bat General Buller passed among them quite unknown. His presence, however, was soon afterwards a matter of common knowledge, and there was a deal of humorous " chaff " in- dulged in. At Belfast Police Court, on Saturday, William Kitchen was charged with being concerned in a disturbance. which took place on Queen's Island on August 13th, and assaulting a man named Walker. At breakfast time, while the prose- cutor was smoking, about a hundred men came to him, and it was alleged he was asked by the prisoner to curse the Pope. He declined, whereupon he was severely beaten. The prisoner was stated to have kicked him on the legs. He was attacked on several subsequent occasions by other workmen, the p-isoner, it was stated, being the principal as• gallant. Walker received several contusions on the face and bead. The prisoner was committed to the assizes for

trial. The tenants on the Kilshannick estate of Lord Fermoy, in the county of Cork, have arranged for the nurchase of their holdings on terms which average about 15 years' purchase of judicial rents. A circular has been sent te all the tenants on the estate of Sir John Marcus Stewart, Bart , of Ballygawley Park, offer- ing them the sale of their holdings at twenty years' pur- chase. It is notified that no less sum will be taken, and that all tenants must buy or none will be sold. Rioting was renewed on Sunday night at 11-dlymacarrett. The mob attacked four policemen, who took refuge in a dwelling-house. The mob wrecked the house and reached the bonstables, who were severely mauled. The military rescued them eventually, and two arrests were made. It is announced at Belfast that fever has broken out in one of the police barracks in that town, probably induced by the crowding of reinforcements in the building which has been necessary during the last month, as well as by the physical strain undergone by the men during the riots. The Dublin correspondent of The Times writes :—The re- ports which are received as to the condition of the county of Kerry represent it as generally deplorable. The people are miserably poor, and there is but little stock in the country. The fields are covered with hay, which is selling at very low prices—as low as LI a ton, and even under. The so- called Moonlighters are farmers' sons and farm labourers, who have nothing to do. They sleep all day and prowl about at night, plundering and doing mischief of all kinds. If they had employment, they would probably be induced to give up their criminal pursuits, )ut without employment they are hopeless and reckless. The priests have little or no influence over them. Most of them would be very glad to emigrate if they had the means. But will anyone venture to propose the formation of a " Moonlighters' Emigration Society ?" It would have to be done, like their deeds, in the dark.

At Bantry, on Monday, the charges against Mr. Gilhooly M.P., of assault, intimidatiOn, and unlawfully assembling, were to. have been heard by the local trench, but were post- poned in consequence of the absence of the defendant, who as attending to his Parliamentary duties. Similar charges against two other persons were likewise postponed. The Roman Catholic Biehops of Ireland have just held their annual meeting at Maynooth. At the close of their deliberations the Bishops unanimously adopted a series of resolutions in reference to the Home Rule controversy and the land question. They record grateful appreciation ef Mr. Gladstone's labours and services to Ireland, and the conviction that it is only by the recognition of Ireland's right to make and administer her own laws that genuine union can be secured. The allegation that the Catholic majority would use its power unjustly is indignantly denied. The Bishops express deep anxiety in regard to the harsh exaction of unearned rents, a course of procedure which, they fear, will lead to grave social disorder. They also complain that the educational grikvancesof Catholics are still unredressed, and they ask again that in every grade of edu- cation Catholics, in common with other sects, shall . enjoy the advantages derivable from the public education grants.
