div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 11, 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 11, 1886.

THE Trades Union Congress has come to be recognised as one of the most important of the bodies that assemble year by year with a view to discussing the problems of life and resolving upon measures for ameloriating the lot of humanity. It is true that its basis is not as broad as that of the British Associa- tion or of the Social Science Congress; but it cannot be regarded as narrow, seeing that it extends to the great mass of workers. It has, further, the advantage of being able to operate directly upon Parliament. That is the position, at any rate. i which the Con- gress stands to-day, though when it Com- menced operations eighteen years ago its resolutions were regarded as extravagant and as entitled to small consideration. Who could have thought then that, within a score of years, its principal members would develop into Government Inspectors, Justices of the Peace, Members of Parliament, and that its Parliamentary Secretary would become a member of a Liberal Ministry? Yet all this has happened, and, as events are likely to move as quickly in the future as they have moved in the past, we may look forward to the doings of the Trades Union Congress occupying a still greater share of the attention of the nation. It is significant that all political parties are disposed to be hand and glove with these once despised trades union- ists; and it is greatly to the credit of the Congress that every care is taken to prevent its becoming an instrument for-mere party purposes. Both Liberals and Tories have done a little angling in the past, and it is not long since the Protectionists made a deter- mined attempt to " nobble" the Congress; but their plot was exposed in good time and it failed. The delegates include men of all sections and sects both as to politics and re- ligion, and this being so, it is of the utmost importance that there should be no playing into the hands of any one party —that the resolutions of the Congress should be the honest and independent outcome of matured conviction. So long as this is the case, and so long as the Congress remains united, it will continue to be a power in the land, and leave its impression on the legislation of the country.

The Congress for the present year has been held during the past week at Hull, and the opening meeting on Monday was graced by the presence of the Sheriff, who in the ab- sence of the Mayor through indisposition, most heartily welcomed the delegates to the town. The retiring President, the Report of the Parliamentary Committee, and the new President, dealt with the difficulties of the labour question as revealed by the fact that through the depression in trade, a large num- ber of workers continue to remain unem- ployed. The problem is—how to keep the toilers regularly employed, and secute them a

fair share of the fruits of their industry. The opinion held by the ex-President (Mr. J. AIAWDSLEY), and by the new President (Mr. F. MADDrsoN), is that the solution is to be found in reducing the hours of labour. Mr. MAWDSLEY said: In his opinion working men were at the present time working too many. hours. Not that they were Producing too much, but that the production was by the hands of too few people. They could not have too much production, but the result of the Present system was that many men, being excluded from a share of the labour in the market, were un- able to purchase their share in the produce of the World. MADDISON followed in the same track, for in his official address on Tuesday he Said: Personally, I think that one of the first steps taken by the Congress should be in the direction of the eight-hours movement. I am aware that this Will not be easily accomplished, but this is no reason for refusing to fake it up. We shall be opposed from all quarters', and stigmatised as agitators who have lost what little sense they once possessed; but no amount of abuse or opposition prevented those who Won the ten-hours and the nine-hours fights, and it thould not prevent us. A proposal of this kind is, it need hardly be said, an attractive one on the face of it. There are few of us who are engaged in daily tasks who do not think that if less time Were spent in drudgery and more in leisure, life would be better worth living. It may be admitted that the country as a whole, and the Working class in particular, have greatly benefited by the adoption of the nine hours System of labour; but the question remains Whether we can still further, and beneficially, reduce the hours of labour. It is obvious that there is a point in the reduction of time Worked which c- ould not be reached without Its proving utterly disastrous to employers, and consequently to the employed. It is near, for instance, that if the British artisan Worked six hours only per day, and received as much for his labour as the conti- n. ental workman who put in twelve hours, it would not be long before the Bri- tish employers would be ' nowhere in the race, through being so ' heavily handi- capped. The case would be altogether dif- ferent if the six-hours labour was a factor Which remained the same all the world over; and the same may be said of an eight-hours system. The danger, as it appears to us, is that, if the English workman succeeds in another agitation for a reduction of the hours of labour, his immediate gain may be fol- lowed by an irreparable loss. The depression In trade has been felt, it must be remem- bered, by employers as well as the employed. Indeed, workmen have in many cases suffered no reduction of wages, whilst it has been notorious that the employer was losing Money year by year. The cry of capitalists has been that they were losing ground in the World's markets, because on the Continent Workmen were content to work longer hours, and receive less pay. What if this difficulty in this country, instead of being lessened Should be increased by a still further reduc- tion of the hours of labour? Is it not Possible—nay, does it not come within the limits of probability—that the workman might by this means kill the goose that lays his golden eggs? Granted that his object is to divide the eggs more equally—to en- sure as far as he can that there shall be work for everyone—he must perceive, if he looks at all at the matter, that his project may fail, and fail terribly, because of its being attempted to be carried out in one country and not in every country. We know that it is part of the programme of time Trades Union congress to induce con- tinental workmen to follow the example Which has been set them in England, and We congratulate the leaders on the efforts they have made to lead French Socialists to take a mbre rational view of trade pro- blems; but as yet they have met with only Partial success. Long hours and low wages are still the rule upon the continent, and, Until both hours and wages are brought More nearly on a level with those common to this country, it seems that it would be imprudent, to say the least of it, to enter Upon an agitation in this country for still further reducing the hours of labour. We are not saying that eight hours is not suf- ficiently long to work, or that if adopted the world over it would not be .a good thing, but what we do urge is that English Workmen, already ahead of their fellows in . this respect, may go too far, and produce a strain which will be a breaking strain to , the employers in this country. It is sug- gestive that the Parliamentary Committee of the Congress have had to confess that they see no hope of inducing the Government ever "to make eight hours the maximum working day in all their departments and Workshops." The whole question, they can- didly admit, is involved in complications-- complications, we contend, so great, and in- volving results so far-reaching, .that no Go- , vernment would be justified in breeding disorder and dislocating trade by taking the, lead in such a matter. The Trades Con- gress is doing good work in many ways; it may do good work in discussing the question of the hours of labour; but it will make a huge blunder if it should force a crisis on this issue until the workmen of other coun- tries are ripe for the change.

"THE Revival of Trade by the Develop- i ment of India" is the title of an address which has just been published, and which was recently delivered by Mr. W. BIRKMYRE, of Calcutta and Port-Glasgow, to the members of the Glasgow Chamber of Commerce. Mr. BIRKMYRE does not advance any new theory; but he brings forward some new facts and re-states old arguments in a most forcible manner. India is suffering from lack of inter- communication ; the resources of the country are excellent, but they are not utilised as they should be because there are so few railways. The grain-growing capacity of the country would appear to be incalculable; but what is the use. of growing grain when it cannot be conveyed to those who are willing to purchase it? Sir LEPEL H. GRIFFIN, in addressing a meeting in London on 15th June, 1883, stated—" In the neigh- bourhood of Bhopal and Bhilsa, the produc- tion of wheat is so enormous in good years that it lies rotting on the ground because there are no means of exportation." It is notorious that during the famine periods there was plenty of grain in some parts of India; but it might as well have been in the moon so far as the starving natives were concerned ; there was no means of bringing it, in time, to their doors. Evidence has been given before a Parliamentary Committee that there is no country in the world that requires rail- ways more than India ; whilst the committee itself reported that " the present limit of borrowing powers for the construction of public works in India might be safely en- larged." But our great Eastern Dependency is far away; and gets very little attention at the hands of Parliament ; nor will it get more until either the natives of India unpleasantly

assert themselves, or the people of this country, recognising their own interests insist upon the construction of railways and other public walks. When an issue of this sort is raised, the question is always asked—Where is the money to come, from? As to this, we think there would be little difficulty if the Government were to set themselves about the task. India is, we know, poor, but money can always be found when it is required for war purposes. • India was poor when the Afghan war was com- menced ; but we managed to spend over twenty millions of money, with nothing in the end to show for it. How much better would it have been if these twenty millions had' been applied—extending over a few years' time-=towards paying interest upon capital borrowed for the construction of railways! It would have greatly stimulated the iron trade of this country, and would, indeed, have stimulated trade generally, for, as sections of the railway were brought into use, grain which would otherwise rot in the fields would be converted into cash, no small por- tion of which would be sure to find its way to the United Kingdom. There zso millions of people in India who are customers, when they can afford to buy anything, of this country; but when they are heavily taxed with war in Afghanistan and Burmah, and when, more- over. they have no means of sending their produce to market, they have as much as they can do to keep body and soul together, with- out taking thought of the luxuries of life. It is due to these people who are committ•td to our care to do all we can to develop the re- sources of the country. They are always on the borders of starvation, and we ought to strive to improve their condition, not the less when we know that we cannot improve their condition without improving our own. It is the duty of Parliament to move in this matter, but Parliament will not move except upon pressure from without. Lancashire gave an impetus to her cotton trade by insisting upon the abolition of the tariff upon cotton goods going into India. Why should she not now make another great move, and commence an agitation for the extension of railways throughout our Indian t.i.lpire ?

div.head: " TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: " TOUCH AND GO."

Three additions have just been made to the Warrington borough bench. The present Government have not followed the example of the late Admistration—the new J.P.'s are all Conservatives. There was a wait yesterday for magistrates at the Borough Police • Court. It is to be hoped that the new brooms will not only sweep clean, but sweep early, and sweep often.

For being drunk and disorderly in the Haymarket, London, a clergyman was on Wednesday fined five shillings, with the al- ternative of five days' imprisonment. It is to be hoped that this little experience will have sobered the rev. gentleman, .and that for the future he will keep himself in a spiritual rather than a spirituous condition.

A writer in the "Daily News" seeks to show that the moon rules not only the tides but the earthquakes,and quotes Professor Geikie in support of the statement that "an earthquake maximum occurs about the time of new moon." We seem to be getting back to as- trology, and shall be saying next with " Gloster" in " King Lear "—" these late eclipses in the sun and moon portend no good to us."

There is a dispute amongst Good Tern- plars as to a prohibition on the part of the Grand Lodge of "Kissing games." At Spald- ing, on Thursday, the delegates strongly disapproved of the Grand Lodge in pro- hibiting the indulgence of such games at temperance gatherings. The delegates do not see why the Grand Lodge should abolish such a grand institution. Why, indeed? when as Byron tells us, "Kiss rhymes with bliss in fact as well as verse."

If, as is reported, a number of the Ulster members of the House of Commous are in favour of leaseholders having the benefit of the Irish Land Act of 1881, there will be some chance of Mr. Parnell's Land Bill passing the House of Commons. Mr. Cham- berlain is practically pledged to that portion of it which deals with the suspension of evictions, and as to Lord Randolph Churchill —well, he will go any way.

. - The Liberal Unionists are now talking of having a club of their own in London, and it is stated that the proposal is encouraged by Lord Hartington and the Duke of West- minster. it is hardly like Lord Hartington, however, to commit himself in this way; he has always spoken as if he wished to see the Liberal party united at the earliest oppor- tunity; but the formation of a new club sug- gests closing rather than opening the way to nnity.

Lord Harris did a very foolish thing in suggesting at Manchester that it might be- come necessary to re-impose a duty upon cotton goods imported into India. Several members of the House of Commons have taken the matter,up, and Sir J. E. Gorst, as Under-Secretary for India, has had to make it clear that Lord Harris spoke for himself and not for the Gavernment. Perhaps his lordship, as a subordinate member of the Ministry, will be a little more careful in the future.

Another thing as bearing upon Protection which the present Government have had to confess is that they cannot see their way.to adopting retaliatory duties to meet the wishes of those in this country who are engaged in the sugar trade. Lord Randolph Churchill was frank enough to say that the consumer had to be considered as well as the pro- ducer. Everybody but purblind Fair Traders can see that matters are not to be mended by making sugar dearer. What will the Fair Traders do now? Will they howl at Lord Salisbury's Government as they did at the Government of Mr. Gladstone?

With regara to an alJeged nuisance at a slaughter-house, the Medical Officer of Health for Huyton is prepared to testify that the place is in an insanitary condition, while the Law Clerk expresses his opinion that, if the Board took proceedings, they would not get a conviction. It is not surprising that, under these circumstances, the Board deferred for a month the question of taking action ; but it is surprising that the Law Clerk should have sought to anticipate the decisio4 of a Bench of .Magistrates. In a case of this kind, if a nuisance be proved to exist, a conviction must follow.

Replying to the Directors of the Scottish Protestant Alliance, who recently passed a resolution protesting against the elevation of Roman Catholics to positions of power and trust in the British Empire, Lord R. Churchill expresses his "astonishment and regret that in this age of enlightenment and general toleration persons professing to be educated and intelligent can arrive at conclusions so senseless and irrational as those which are set forth in. the aforesaid resolution." We are glad to be able to agree, for once, with his lordship. Whether he is quite consistent in inciting Orangemen to fight, and then slapping them in the face by promoting the appointment of a Catholic as Hom'3 Secretary, is, Of course, another matter.

THE FARNWORTH AGRICULTURAL SHow.—This important annual agricultural fixture will be held on Thursday "next. The arrangements are being carried out on the usual complete scale, and with fine weather a most successful show is anticipated. 1 The 'entries number about 1,300, being considerably in excess of recent years, and the value of the prizes offered is about £6OO. Lord Lionel Cecil, the president. is expected to preside at the luncheon. CHESTER SHOW.—The "McCormick" harvester and binder has been awarded the silver medal for improvements in binders by the Rcyal Manchester, Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society, being the only medal awarded to the binders exhibited at the above show. The Longford Wire, Iron and Steel Company, Limited, have been awarded a Silver Medal at the Royal Show, Chester, for Wood's patent double woven steel spring wire mattresses. The Company were awarded a Silver Medal at the Birkenhead Ag- ricultural Show. ST. HELENS AND WIGAN JUNCTION RAILWAY BlLL.—This bill, which provides for the extension of existing and authorised lines, and has passed the House of Commons, came before the Duke of Buck- ingham in the House of Lords, on Friday, and passed the committee stage.. The opposition offered to the bill in the Lower House was with- drawn, and Mr. Belt, the agent for the promoters, explained the clauses. The proposed new connect- ing lines are in the townships of Haydock, Windle, Lowton, and Walton-on-the-Hill, and will give im- portant connections between the colliery district and existing railway systems. LANCASHIRE ANNUAL SESSION.—The adjourned annual assembly of the justices of the county of Lancaster was held on Thursday at the County Hall, Preston. After the re-election of chairman and vice-chairman, and the appointment of com- mittees for various county purposes, there was sub- mitted a letter from the Home Secretary. with a copy of the regulations made under the Riot ! Damages Act of 1886 with regard to claims to com- , pensation for losses by riot. -Various pensions and gratuities were passed. There was also submitted to the court the annual report of the General Fi- nance Committee of the county. Among the notices of motion was one to the effect that all bills of costs for Parliamentary and litigious busi- ness be taxed before being paid by the proper taxing officer. Sums were granted for new police stations. THE ESTABLISHED CHURCH. The Bishop of Liverpool s statement that " no respectable insu- rance office in London would insure the life of the (Church) Establishment for twenty years," havi,pg recently gone the "round of the Press," the " Re- cord " endeavours to take off the edge of it by say- ing"that "it was written by Dr. Ryle seventeen) years ago." That is quite true; but the " Record ' omits to add that the Bishop has repeated the state- ment in the " Manchester Courier" so recently as the 16th March last. It forms, in fact, a part of the appeal which the Bishop is making on behalf of Chur-.th Reform, as a means of saving the Establish- ment, which he maintains is in serious danger from many causes. "There is," he says, " a current set- ting in towards the disestablishment of all national , Churches, and we are already in it." He adds, "A few—a very few—years, and, unless we exert our- selves, we shall be over the falls."—The Liberator. CHILDREN'S TREAT AT CROFT.—ThiS treat took ' place on Saturday afternoon under most auspicious 1 circumstances. The children assembled at the 'Board School at one o'clock, and, about half-an-hour ' later, a procession was formed, headed by the ban- ner of the school, and several members of the School Board, the Rev. T. P. Kirkman, and the Lowton Brass Band and the Croft Drum and Fife Band. They paraded the village, under the guidance of the Committee, and afterwards went to a field) kindly lent for the occasion by Mr. Sankey, one of the members of ths School Board, where games were indulged in until half-past three, when the children sat down to an excellent tea in an adjoin- ing field. Afterwards the members of the bands, members of the School Board, Committee, wait- resses, and friends partook of tea in the schoolroom, which was thoroughly enjoyed. All then again ad- journed to the field, when the various games were resumed, and the bands played a choice selection of music for dancing. .. THE ISLE OF MAN.—Those of our many readers who are interested in the above pleasant and popu- lar place of resort will find in another portion of this paper the prospectus of a new Manx line of steamers, setting forth the advantages which a second and independent line of fast-sailing steamers to the island will undoubtedly possess. The emi- nent firm of shipbuilders, Messrs. John Elder and Co., of Glasgow, have entered into a provisional contract with the company to build the steamers on the most improved plan and on exceptionally favourable terms. The builders of such magnifi- cent ocean-going " greyhounds " as the Umbria, Arizona, Etruria, and Alaska are not likely to turn out work of a second-rate character, so we may safely conclude that the steamers of the Isle of Man, Liverpool, and Manchester 1 Steamship Company will be second to none in re- spect to safety,speed, accommodation,and equipment. It is worth noting that a daily double service is arranged for passengers leaving Manchester, Liver- pool, and other large and adjacenttowns during the season summer months, and that a similar service will be in operation from the Isle of Man. Passen- gers at a distance can be booked through to the Island and vice versa by fast trains, thus saving loss of time, and occasionally annoyance. We may point out that the shares of the present monopolist company are quoted at a premium of over 200 per cent, and are paying a large dividend. The gross receipts from passengers and goods by the present company in 1885 were £85,539. The capital of the new company will be £200,000 in £1 shares, and original shareholders of not less than ten shares will have a coupon attached to their allotment notes entitling them to free passages between Liverpool and the Isle of Man during the summer Of next ' year, when the new line will be opened, and holders of fifty shares will be entitled to a reduction of 50 ' per cent. on the ordinary passage rate. There is no doubt that the new company will supply an urgent . want, and we think it will justify a large degree of public confidence. , Buy YOUR GROCERIES from LAWLESS Bnos., 5, Market- place, Warrington.—Advt.

LORD DE TABLEY AND THE CHESHIRE FREE- MASONS.—Lord de Tabley has, owing to continued . ill-health, resigned his office as Provincial- Grand . Master of Cheshire Freemasons. His lordship was installed on August Ist, 1865, at linutsford. by Earl Ripon, and has therefore been in the office 21 years. The resignation has caused the greatest regret on the part of the Cheshire Masons. Lord Egerton of Tatton will probably be his successor. THE HOME IRON TRADE.—A better feeling is maintained in the English iron market, although it cannot be said that any substantial improvement has taken place. Pig-iron continues to be mode- rately bought at the old prices. The Glasgow war- rant market has been somewhat more steady this week, and the fluctuations thitt have taken place have been chiefly due to some of the regular dealers than to anything else. There is no im- provement in the demand for Scotch pia-iron. Closing buyers of warrants were on n ednesd'ay 36s 5d cash and 39s id a month, sellers asking one half- penny per ton more. In the North of England, prices and position of the pig-iron trade have not been so satisfactory this week, but 30s per ton for G.M.B. continues the average quotation, buyers for forward delivery offering 6d to 9d more. At New- ' castle the crude iron business has been dull, and last week's advance in prices has given way to the extent of 3d per ton. No. 3 Cleveland pig is de- livered to the Tyne at 32s per ton, and No. 4 forge at 31s.—Iron. VISCOUNT Cnoss.—The following amusing refer- - ence to Viscount Cross's new position as a member of the House of Lords is from "Punch's" "Essence of Parliament extracted from .the diary of Toby, M.P. ";—" Thuraday.—Thought I knew those Blucher boots. It was the Right Hon. Viscount Grand Cross. Nearly got. between his legs and threw him down. "How do, Toby," he said, handing me two fingers, —" without prejudice, of course." "What do you mean, without prejudice?" I said, looking for his other three digits, which he always wore in the! House of Commons. "Why, the fact is," said his Lordship, "must draw the line somewhere. Don't mind speaking to you, but it can't be expected that every fellow who happened to sit with me in the House of Commons must take advantage of acci-, dental circumstances, and presume on my acquaint- ance now I'm in another sphere; my own sphere, I may say." "Yes, my Lord," I said, willing to humour him, "I think you've reached your level now. You were occasionally something above the comprehension of the House of Commons. "Quite right, Toby," said the Viscount, staring stonily .through his spectacles at Lawrence of Li erpool, who passed with sign of recognition. " You can I always speak to me when we meet." THE ROYAL MANCHESTER, LIVERPOOL, AND NORTH LANCASHIRE AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.—The implement ,•section of this great show was opened on Tuesday, when the adjudications were made. A more appropriate site for the exhi- hibition could not have been chosen than that of the Roodee, which is pretty level, and within easy distance of the City of Chester and its respective railway stations. The .space enclosed is 1,200 by 800 feet, with a main entrance facing the grand stand, the principal portion of the ground extending towards the river Dee. In the department. for im- plements, carriages, and miscellaneous articles and machinery in motion the entries are so numerous as to necessitate the erection of 5,000 feet of shed- ding. A grand stand has been additionally erected, to hold 1,500 people, and the horse ring, which faces it, is very spacious and convenient in every particu- lar for the trials of, the numerous horses which will take place on each day of the show. Seven large shippons are provided, and the refreshment shed is 130 feet long by 100 feet wide; besides which tea and coffee rooms are specially provided for ladies. On Wednesday morning the general show was opened. In consequence of the unfavourable wea- ther the number of visitors was not so large as it: has been on the opening day in some previous years. For the prize money offered by the Society, amounting in the aggregate to over £3,000, there is keen competition. Dairy cattle and dairy produce , are the best features of the show. The exhibition in connection with the Houghton Horticultural So- ciety, open to the inhabitants of the townships of 1, Houghton, Middleton and Arbury, Winwick-with- 1 Hulme, Orford, and Poulton-with-Fernhead, was opened on Friday last week. The exhibition was, , by permission of Mrs Comber, held in Middleton Hall Park, and, in point of exhibits, was very suc- cessful, as the classes with one or two exceptions were all well filled. The exhibition was declared open by Miss Hopwood, and amongst those present were the Rev. Canon Hopwood, the Rev, J. Carson, and Mrs Carson, Mr. George Comber (president of the society), Mrs Comber, the Misses Comber, Mr. and Mrs W. Beamont, Mrs Wilkinson (Warrington), Rev. W. H. Williams (Padgate), Dr. White (War- rington), Messrs. W. H. J. Jenkins, Swinton, T. Tyldesley (Poulton), Owen, sen. (Croft), S. Southern, &c. The band of the Warrington Union Industrial School was present, under the leadership of Mr. H. M. Mines, and played selections of music. The judges were: Flowers, fruit, and vegetables, Messrs. Green (Warrington), Jephson (gardener to Mr. W. Beamont, (Orford Hall), and W. Baker (gar- dener to the Rev. Canon Hopwood) ; farm produce, Messrs. James Halton (Padgate), and John Southerns (Springfield, Croft). The judges were as- sisted by Messrs. Barber and Dixon. The show was continued on Saturday when there were 450 visi- tors there having been 400 on Friday. On Saturday afternoon Mr. W. Stirrup's (Warrington) quadrille band played music for dancing. In the evening the prizes were distributed to the successful exhibitors by Miss Comber, of Middleton Hall, and the usual , votes of thanks were passed. APPOINTISENT OF CHAIRMLif.-Mr. Dobson said under circumstances of which they were all aware, Mr. P. Speak- man had had to vacate the chair, and seek re-election, and he begged to move that Mr. Speakman be re-appointed chairman. His past experience and the able and efficient manner in which he had conducted the business et the Board for the past six months, gave them encou- ragement for the future. Mr. Speakman • would take that position by the voice of the ratepayers, as he was at the bead of the poll—Mr. Lightburn seconded the motion with pleasure, and it was carried rmanimously.—Mr. Speakman then took the chair, which bad been occupied by the law clerk pro, tem., and said it gave him great pleasure to re- occupy that position. This would be the third time succea- 'lively that he bad been elected to the chair under circum- stances that would be fresh in their memories, and he thanked them very much for the confidence they had again reposed in him. He hoped he should continue to merit their confidence, which he should hold as a sacred trust. He felt sure the Board's business would go. on as It had done in the past if he had the confidence and support of the members, and there would be no effort spared on his part to conduct the Proceedings to the advantage of the Board and the Public.

div.head: •U CAL NEWS.
div.p: •U CAL NEWS.

FATAL ACCIDENT AT WIDNES —Lloyd Robinson, who was struck on the bead by a falling derrick on Tuesday week at the Desota Chemical Works, succumbed to his in juries on Wedneselty night. An inquest will be held at the hospital to-day. SLEEPING IN CHEMICAL WonKs.—J ames Millington, a convicted thief, was, on the evidence of P.C. Thompson, sentenced to 14 days' hard labour by Mr. Brundrit. at Run- corn Tatty Sessions, yesterday. His offence was sleeping on the works uf Messrs. Wigg Bros. and Steele. THEFT AT WlDNES.—Before Mr. T. S. Tiremis, at the Widnes Police Court, Catherine Matthews, an old offender, was charged with having stolen a saucepan, worth 34 3d, the property of Frederick Taylor. The prisoner pleaded guilty, and was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. 1.0.G.T. WIDNES SAMARITAN LODGE.—The members of this lodge on Wednesday evening celebrated the anniver- sary of the introduction of the order of Good Templars into England by a tea party and entertainment. About 40 per- sons were present, and a pleasant evening was spent. NELSON-STREET BAPTIST CHAPEL, WIDNES.—The anni- versary of this chapel was celebrated on Sunday. when ser- mons were preached morning and evening by Mr. J. Robin- eon, of Widnes. There were good congregations, and the services were rendered attractive by specially selected music.

FOOTBALL AT RIINCORN.—A football match was played on Wednesday night between the Runcorn Recreation anl the Weston Point Football Clubs. The Weston Point team .won by two tries and five minors to one miner.—ln the match Runcorn against Manchester Rangers to-day, Run- corn will be represented by T. Wood, full back ; E. Lunt, H. C. Speakman, and T. Davies, three-quarter backs; H. Hughes, and H. Andrews, half-backs; W. Wright, W. Hughes, J. Dean, J. Barnes, J. Lewis, J. Gatler, Faulk- ner, Wainwright, and Andrews, forwards. Reserves, Dolan and Joule.

THE REV R. YEATMAN, OF WIDNES —The third anniver- sary of the residence in Widnes of the Rev. R. Yeettnan, the pastor at the Baptist Chapel, was celebrated on Thurs- day evening. About 80 people partook of tea that had been provided by Mesdames Hinglev, Hallding, Robinson, Bailey, Edwards, Thompson ; Misses Passey, Makereth, Thompson, Willing, and Bailey ; and Messre. T. Smith, and Willing. Subsequently a meeting was held under the presidency of Mr. E. Carey, who delivered a brief speech. Addresses were delivered by the Pastor, and the Revs. D. Davies, R. G. Hughes. and R. Burdon ; and Mr. Passev. The proceedings were rendered very enjoyable by anthems and sacred songs sung by the choir and several friends. CRUELTY TO A. HORSE AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, James Brown, a young man, of Gerrard-street, West Bank, was charged with cruelly ill- treating a horse. Ore Tuesday afternoon, the 31st ult, PC. Grimshew saw the defendant riding a horse at a rapid rate along Victoria-road. He was lashing the animal with a heavy driving whip. He took no heed of the officer's com- mand to stop; but when he pulled up at the butcher's shop opposite the Central Hotel the constable examined the horse, which appeared to be thoroughly winded. Under the saddle he saw two raw wounds, each about two inches in length and a inches in width. The cotton cloth which covered them was saturated with blood and matter, which bad run down the horse's sides.---Inspector Wood, who had also seen the horse, said it was a case of gross cruelty.— The defendant said the horse did not belong to him nor to the person for whom he was riding it.—He was fined 20s and costs, 13s. FLAT ROBBERIES AT WESTON.—At Runcorn Petty Ses- sions, on Monday, Walter Barker, a ticket-of-leave man, was charged with breaking into a boat and stealing a pair of trousers, a cardigan jacket, and two caps, belonging to Samuel Lydiate, and a pair of trousers belonging to Peter Cawley. He was also charged with breaking into the flat Mary Ellen, and stealing two coats, a pair of boots, two shirts, a vest, four handkerchiefs, a pair of braces and a razor, the property of Alfred Gates, and a pair of trousers belonging to Thomas Vernon. On Saturday. the 28th ult, the flats were lying in the canal at the Weston Chemical Works, and during the abeence of the prosecutors, the cabins were broken into and the articles stolen. On Thurs- day, P.C. Bennett, was on the canal hank at Stockton Heath and saw the prisoner on board a flat. He boarded the boat, and opened a bundle which the prisoner claimed as his. The bundle contained all the stolen articles, and the prisoner was taken into custcdy. He subsequently admit- ted his guilt to Sergeant Booth. He was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. TEE WIDNES INTERWORES FOOTBALL COMPETITION.— The Widnes Football Club has struck upon a novel idea for increasing the popularity of the winter game in the district. Teams representing the various works in the town have been invited to enter a football competition for 15 gold centre medals, and a capital entry has been made. The first match took place on Thursday night, when 15 employes of the Widnee Alkali Works met 15 employes of Messrs. Sullivan and Co. in the first round. The latter team were the vic- tors by one goal, two tries, and five minors to Widnes Alkali nil. The following are the teams :—Sullivan's: Full back, Crosby; thretequarter backs. Minton, Abrams. and Flynn; half-backs, Barber and P. Boyle; forwards, Meagher, Bur- rill, Bate, Hewitt. Clare, Gaskell, Knowles, J. Boyle, and T. Ridvard ; umpire, Mr. J. Latham. Widnes Alkali: Full back, W. Neil; three-quarters, E. Evans, W. Lewis, and W. Ryan: half-backs, W Devenport and G. Tumbity •, for- wards, P. Kenyon, A. Kennion, W. Gregson, Farrell, E. GordoncA. Owen, Daley, Starkey, and Clarke; umpire, Mr. Farrell; referee, Mr. Rose. St. Helens. RECEPTION OF A WESLEYAN MINISTER AT WIDNES.— On Tuesday evening a reunion was held in Lacey-sireet Schoolroom for the purpose of Inaugurating the appointment of the Rev. J. Bryant to the Widnes circuit. The proceed- ings commenced with a tea, of which about 300 people Par- took, visitors from all parts of the district being present. Subsequently a meeting was held under the presidency of the Rev. R. Burdon. There was a capital attendance. On the platform, in addition to the Rev. J. Bryant, were Messrs. J. Robinson, R. Jones, D. Timmins, W. Brown, J. Shaw, dm. Addresses were given by the chairman and other gen- tlernen, in which Mr. Bryant was given a hearty welcome to the circuit, and confidence was expreseed that he would lend his abilities and experience to carrying on the good work that was being done. Mr. Bryant delivered a speech in reply, and reciprocated the good feelings expressed. The usual votes of thanks concluded the proceedings.—The Rev. J. Bryant preached his first sermon in the Widnes circuit on Sunday in Hartland Memorial Chapel. There were good congregations, and collections were made in aid of the treat funds. Opeer AIR CONCERTS AT RUNCORN.—The last open air concert of the present season will be given in Devonshire- square this (Saturday) evening at 5-30 by the Mill Brow Brass Band. The programme will, besides other interest- ing pieces, consist of last year's Belle Vete contest piece, " Nabucodonosur ;" " Gloria in Excelsis," from Mozart's 12th Mass; " The British Patrol," a descriptive piece, and a grand National Scotch Fantasia. During the past summer the Mill Brow Sand has delighted hundreds of lovers of music by its admirable performances. and the members are deserving of every Praise for so unselfishly coming forward to gratify the musical tastes of the public. The Band has also received high enconiums upon its playing at Birken- head, which place they have visited several times by desire, and they are becoming well-known beyond their own local sphere as a skilful set of musicians. The expense the bind has been put to in connection with their concerts at Run- corn has been very considerable, and it is to be hoped that the large audience which will assemble in Devonshire-square this evening will generously help to foster local talent when the collection is made. ATTEMPTED BURGLARY AT WIDNES,—At Widnes Police Court on Monday, before Messrs. Holbrook GaSkell, jun., T. S. Timmis. James Jackson, a stranger in the town, was again brought up on remand charged with having on the 18th ult. attempted to break into the lock-up shop of Mr. David Brooks, tailor and outfitter, Waterloo-road. Inspec- tor Wood, said about a quarter to three on Wednesday morning, the 18th of August, P.C. Laing was standing in front of Mr. Brookes's shop, when he heard a dog bark, and immediately afterwards saw the prisoner come to the end of the side street near the shop, and look into Waterloo-road. On seeing him he went back. The constable followed, and on getting up to him searched him, and found in his posses- sion the hammer key, and knife produced. He afterwards found that a square of glass in Mr. Brookes's window bad been broken, and the rust on the glass corresponded with that on the hammer. Prisoner could eive DO account of himself. Byrom Brookes. Albert Farber, labeurer at the Salamanca works, and P.C. Laing having given evidence. prisoner made a long and rambling statement, saying that he was intending to go to the Salamanci Works to see if they would let him stop there all night by the boiler. The things he had in his possession he had picked up on the way from St. Helens. The magistrates did not consider this a sufficient excuse, and prisoner was committed for a month.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. DlONonr. --Bef,,re Alderman Holmes and Mr. J. Greening. DayNkENN-zss —Mary Hulse was fined 53 and casts, or seven days, for having been drunk aad disorderly in Butler- maalket-street, on Saturday night.—For a like offence in Horsemarket-street on Saturday night, Margaret Johnson was fined 103 and costs or 14 days.—James McNamara was fined 5s and costs, or seven days, for having been drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road on Saturday—John Dutton, drunk and disorderly in Irlam•street, on Saturday night, was tined 5s and Costs, or seven days —John Lewis, drunk and disorderly in Haydock-street, on Saturday night, was fined 5s and costs, or seven days. It was stated that prisoner, whilit drunk, went to a strange house, put off his clothes, and went to bed.—A youth named John Thomas Meeks or Cronan, drunk and disorderly on Sunday morning in Win- wick-srreot, was fined lOs and costs.—Daniel Kenny, drunk and disorderly in Buckley-street, on Sunday. 105 and costs, or 14 days.—Tnomas Troy, a youth, drunk in Winwick- street, on Sunday, 103 and costs. or 14 days.—Charles Elli- son, drunk and disorderly in Manchester-road, on Sunday night. was fined 55 including costs.—John Bryan, of Pen- keth, druak and disorderly in Sankey-street, early on Mon- day morning, 53 and costs, or seven days.—Mark Crayon, drank in Sankey-street, on the 30th ult., was fined 5s in- cluding costs.—Joseph Henshaw, a young man, was fined 2s 9el including costs, for having been drunk a.hd disorderly on the 27th ult., in Old Gardens.—Michael Hawkins, drunk and disorde;ly in Lord-Nelson-street, on the 28th ult., fined 5s including costs. THE CATAPULT NUISINCE. —Henry Clarke was charged with having thrown stones with a catapult in Latchford, on the 29th ult., and was fined is. OBSTRUCTION.—Thomas Nixon, ot Upton Rocks. near Widnes, was fined 103 and costs for having allowed a horse and cart to stind in the Market-place, longer than was necessary to unload, viz, an hour and an half. SCHOCL CASES.—For not sending their children regularly to school the following persons were fined, viz. :—Joseph Newne, Chorley-street (of° children) 103 ; Elijah Page, Wakefield-street, ss; ;:ohn McCowyne (12th appearance), 5s ; Thomas Pemberton, Kerfoot-street (two children), 103 ; Thomas Allcock, Hall-street, 53; Peter Garlan,l. Bewsey- street, six strokes were ordered to be given tr the boy ; William Mapp, Wellin,,ton-street, 5s ; Pete: Woodall, Stamford-street, 53 ; Simon Thomas Bank Quay. sa; William Backhonse, B@wsey-street, the lad, who was des- cribed as an incorrigible, was sent to the ship Clio, as was also the son of James Fairhurst.—William Clark was sum_ mooed in respect of two children, but it was stated that the non-attendance of the children was due to the drunken habits of defendant's wife, who, it was alleged, spent the school money of the children in drink.—Mr. Greening re- marked that thechildren looked to him to le half-starved._ Defendant : They are sir; whatever I buy them goes in drink.—The case was adjourned for a month. TUESDAY.—EIfore Mr. E. J G
Monks.

SLBEPING..—Patrick McDermott was charged with sleep- ing in a brickfield belonging to Messrs. Roberts and Lucas, in Bewsey-road, the same morning.—He was sent to prison for seven days. DRUNKENINESS —James Ward, charged with being drunk In Bewsey-road the same morning was fined 5a and costs or. seven days' imprisonment. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. H. Bleckley at3d Alderman

Holmes. NEGLIGENT APPBENTIcEs.—A. number of appren'tic.s in tbe employ of Mr. Platt were summoned for absenting themselves from work. In mcst of the cases the migistratts ordered the girls to fulfil their contracts. Warrants were issued for the apprehension of several who did not appear in answer to the summonses. Mr. A. Browne appeared on be- half of Mr. Platt. ALLEGED Asstart:r.—Mary Roscr..e was summoned by a _ • _ _ _

girl named Mary Smith for assaulting her on the Ist of September. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the complainant. It was alleged that Mrs. -Roscoe struck complainant on the face. She was ordered to be bound over to keep the peace.

div.head: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Major Haziehurst and Mr. James Handley. _ • _
div.p: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Major Haziehurst and Mr. James Handley. _ • _
NON-PAYMENT OF POOR RAT-E.—Twenty. three persons were summoned for non-payment of poor rate, and, on the evidence of Mr. W. Sutton, assistant overseer, the usual Orders were made.

DISORDER AND DRUNICENNESS.—Henry Green and John Cavanagh, young men, were convicted of fighting in Bridge street on the 28th August, and were each bound over to keep the peace.— Peter Farrell and Thos. Costello were each fined for drunkPnness.
GAma LIChNSH —Mr. Peter Sinnott, Regent-street, was granted a license to sell game. TRANSFER.—The license of the Cornwall and Devon- shire Arms was transferred from Thomas Page to Williim Doyle.

CONTROL OF DOGS.—William Farrell, jun., Egerton- -street,• was on the evidence of P.C. Boyle fined is. and costs, 9s fid, for having on the 2nd September permitted Hs dog to be at large in contravention of an order of the justices. A WOMAN'S WRANGLE —Sarah Clarke was summoned for having assaulted Mary Littlemore, and there was a cross- summons charging Littlemore with assaulting Clarke.—Ttas ?tales live in Robert-street, and a disagreement arose about the manner in which Littlemcre had cleaned her yard, and according to witnesses were "as bad as one another."—Each defendmat was bound over in her own recoanisancc,s to h,2ep the peace for six months, and pay costs, lie al each.

div.head: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. TirußsDAY.—Before Messrs. F. W. Earle and W. N. Heald.
div.p: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. TirußsDAY.—Before Messrs. F. W. Earle and W. N. Heald.

BREACHES OF THE PEACE.—WiIIiaM Cain, James Gag- ban, Elizabeth Murray, Ann Hignett, James Duff v, and Ann Duffy were each charged with committing 13,eaches of the peace, and, with tbe exception of Ann Duffy, were each bound over. DEFAMATORY LANGrAGE.—For using defamatory lan- guage to Elizabeth Francis, John Kruze, a young man, was bound over to be of poi behaviour. _
AN OLD OFFENDER.—Rose Kelly, who did not appear, was sentenced to a month's hard labour for being drunk and disorderly in Ann-street West on the 20th ult. This was the woman's 54th conviction.

Dnrma.s.—The following were each fined for drunken- ness :—Cicely Riley, D. Moran, H. Murphy Catherine Keenaghan, Philip Burke, Thomas Carney, William Dun noghan, Patrick Brien, Thomas Com6skey, Thos. 13ro efn, and Bernard Collomb. Margaret Redmond, a married woman, was summoned for using defamatory language to Andrew Quinn. Mr. J. T. Knowles appeared for the complainant. The woman, when under the influence of liquor, had called Qiina a murderer, alleging that he had s'arved his wife to death. The woman was bound over to keep the peace. ROBBERY. - Harriet Burns and Ellen Smith, were charged with stealing a shirt, worth 28 6d, from the shop of Mr. F. Neil, pawnbroker, Anne-street, on the 6th inst. Burns had been in the shop several times during the day, but made no purchases, and in the evening the shirt was missed from a shelf. Afterwards the prisoner pledged the article with Mrs. Jameson, Pawnbroker, for 2s. They were sub,equently apprehended by P.C. Savory, and were now each sentenced to a month's hard labour.

Mr. S. Smith, M.P., in a letter to a Wrexham correspond- ent on the tithe question in Wales,seys the only logical issue ' out of the present state of things is the speedy disestablish• menl and disendowment of the Episcopal Church in Wales. Mr. Smith counsels the Welsh farmers to exercise patience. EXPLOSION OF FLOUR Drst—Two men named Charles Kane and William M'Pherson were severely injured on Thursday morning by an explosion of flour dust in the drying store of the starch manufactory of Messrs. Brown and Co., Govan, Glasgow. The woodwork of the room took fire, and the windows were smashed, hut the fire brigade turned out and speedily extinguished the flames. Both 1 men are in the hospital. Mr. Parnell presided, on Wednesday night, at a banquet to Mr. Justin M`Carthy on the occasion of that gentleman's visit to America, and in proposing Mr. M'Cai:thy's health pronounced a eulogy upon the services he had rendered to Ireland,declaring that he had never wearied in coueteract- ing the prejudices of Englishmen against Ireland, and had not shrunk from going through the worst period in modern Irish history. FriXE LAND LEAGUE The annual meeting of the Free Land League eves held on Thursday in London, the chair being occupied by Mr. Arthur Arnold, the president of the League. In his opening address Mr. Arnold contended that there were no questions of general concern more ripe for legislation than these which the Free Land League was engaged in promoting. Referring to the tithe agitation, he was of opinion that the payment of tithes by tenant farmers ought to cease, and he anticipated that the Government would be forced to introduce a bill restricting the payment of tines to the 0 smira of len6, by whom the tithe could redeemable. After Mr. Arthur Arnold had been re-elected president of the League, it was resolved that it was desira- ble to take and support action in Parliament upon the ob- ject of the League at the earliest practicable time.

At 'the conclusion of the service cial to workmen than this Act, but many other the "D delegates replied that the Act had been beneficial not merely or the money compensation it procured for injured workmen, or for their relatives in case of death, but from the increased carefulness on the part of employers and their managers which the existence of the Act induced. It was also urged that, as employers were insuring themselves against claims under ',the Act, workmen should have some organisation for securing legal assistance from a central body in preferring their claims befOre the courts. Eventually the motion was carried. The Congress also passed resolutions calling for a considerable increase in the staff of inspectors to prevent the Factories, Workshops, and Mines Act becoming a dead letter. The Parliamentary Com- mittee were instructed to urge the Government to appoint practical workingmen and women as in- spectors. By another resolution the Congress advocated some Government test of fitness in persons in charge of steam boilers. It also adopted one in favour of relatives of deceased persons under coroners' inquests having power to examine witnesses. A vote of .condolence with the family of the late Mr. Samuel Morley was passed. On Wednesday, the principal subject under dis- cussion was the representation of labour in the House of Commons. A resolution was submitted declaring that "the direct representation of labour in Parliament was necessary in the interest of the working population and the kingdom at large." In the course of the discussion the question arose as to what relation a labour party ought to stand in with regard to political parties in the House of Com- mons. Some speakers considered that a labour party should stand aloof from politics; others main- tained that this could not be done. Mr. Jos. Arch asked whether it was likely that agricultural labour- ers would at Parliamentary elections feel ne respect or gratitude to the party which had given them the franchise? Mr. B. Pickard, M.P., expressed the opinion that working men had got more from the Radical party than they ever did from the Conser- vatives, who were a party of privilege. This de- claration was objected to by several delegates, and a lively discussion occurred, which was brought to a close by a speech from Mr. Shipton, who vigor- ously defended Mr. Henry Broadhurst, M.P., from the attacks which have been made upon that gen- tleman from some Conservative quarters. The mo- tion in favour of direct labour representation in Parliament was afterwards carried unanimously. The Trades Union Congress at Hull resumed on Thursday morning the discussion on the land laws and their effects on the labour market. A resolu- tion was submitted by the agricultural labour dele- gate in favour of such reform of the land laws as should enable the peasantry to acquire proprietary rights, while at the same time arrangements were made with the colonies to receive our surplus agri- cultural population and give them grants of land there. An amendment was proposed by the delegate of the Sheffield trades that no emi- gration should be sanctioned until the land laws have been reformed so as to afford more em- ployment for the people at home. A lively debate ensued, many delegates arguing that no reform of the land laws can be obtained so long as labourers consent to leave the country. They should insist on reforms that will enable them to remain at home. Landlordism was stigmatised in very strong terms. Mr. Joseph Arch made a powerful speech on the sub- ject, contending that the resolution was the most delusive ever submitted to the congress. Our aris- tocracy had in late years bought large estates in the colonies, and we were now asked to send out labourers to improve those estates. With better land laws our labourers.would be much larger pro- - ducers of food .and larger consumers of manufac- tures. The amendment was carried by a large ma- jority, 87 voting for it and 11 against. At Thursday's sitting of the Trade Unions Con- gress at Hull a resolution on the land question, which included clauses recommending emigration, was rejected, and an amendment was adopted which declared that while "the most drastic reform of the land laws is needed, the Congress could not lend itself to any scheme of emigration, State di- rected or otherwise, until that reform was brought about, seeing that defective and injurious land laws reduce the agricultural population, throw land out of cultivation,.and bring general distress upon the people." Mr. Joseph Arch and Mr. J. Wilson were among the speakers. The latter gentleman, who formerly sat for Durham in the House of Commons expressed his conviction that nationalisa- tion was the only righteous mode of dealing with the land.

div.head: FAILURE OF A ST. HELENS
div.p: THE FAILURE OF A ST. HELENS
ALDERMAN. PUBLIC EXAMINATION.

At the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, on Thursday, before Mr. Registrar Bellringer, Edward JOhnson,. wholesale and retail provisiox 'dealer, carrying on business in Church-A.. St.Helens, Market-st., Earles- town, and Widnes ,Warrington, Sc., and resident at West Park House, St. Helens, came up for public) examination. Mr. Ring, deputy official receiver, and Mr. Robert W. H. Thomas, solicitor, appeared for the creditors; Mr. Roclway appeared for Mr. 3. T. Davies, of the Swan-lane Colliery, and Mr. H. L. Riley appeared for the debtor. The statement of affairs showed liabilities of £10,839 14s, and assets of £3,307 4s. Jo reply to Mr. Ring, the debtor said he com- menced business 30 years ago in Church-street, St. Helens, and had continued in that business and in that street ever since. For some years his takings had been about £50,000 a year. He had been alderman and mayor of St. Helens. His capital on commencing business was about £3OO, part.of which was borrowed, but this had been paid off. The busi- ness had been a very profitable one until the last eight or nine months, the profits being £1,500 a year for ten years since, and occasionally £2,000. About ten years ago he purchased the freehold of the Swan-lane and the Long-lane Collieries, as well as some brickworks adjoining, the properties coating altogether about £BO,OOO. He could not at present show any entries in his books in respect of those collieries, but he knew from the monthly returns that they paid. He sold the Swan-lane Colliery and the brick- works for about £15,000. When asked why he sold for such a small amount what had cost him £60,000, he replied that he did so because he was pressed for money at the time. The Long-lane Colliery.coat about £16,000, but it was not now in his possession. He was not now liable for any debts of these collieries. Up to last Christmas he had not given any orders for goofs for the collieries. All his drawings for salary, die., were shown in the books ; he never drew a shilling but what was entered.—The Deputy Official Re- ceiver here drew attention to the fact that since the 10th of May the cash book had not been added up.—The Debtor said ha was not aware of this. His instructions were that it snould be done. Questioned as to the payment of cheques, he said when he drew a cheque he never had it entered in the cash book, but every cheque drawn could be seen by the counterfoil.— The Deputy Official lleceiver : Was that the only account of these cheques that you made payments with? Yes.— The Registrar: And that was your loose way of doing busi- ness?—The Debtor: Well, sir, if I sent out a cheque I knew what it was sent out for, and the cashier sent money to pro- vide for the cheque ; therefore we knew what every cheque was used for. The debtor stated he had had a privae meeting of his creditors on the 23rd August last. Before that date he had been served with two writs for amounts of money which he 'could have met hat that he thought it would be taking the money from some one else.—The deputy official receiver said an entry in the cash book showed that a sum of £BO had beetle paid to one of the debtor's sans, although at that time he must have been in- solvent—in fact, it, was on the very day the meeting of creditors was held. The debtor said that amount should have been pail several days before, but had been delayed. It was a matter of borrowed money to prevent a distraint in one of his places, which he was bound to repay. He had thre- sons in the business at one time, and owed them all considerable sums for wages, and he paid them £l5 each about the 23rd of August on account of wages. They had pressed him for it, as they owed bills. He had transferred his egg business to his son Charles about three weeks before the meeting of creditors. There was no goodwill attached toil, and Charles paid him £35 for two horses and carts. Charles had money of his own, his mother and uncle having made hirn presents of £lOO each on his 21st birthday. At the time of his marriage, some 25 years ago, he had some furniture, and other furni- ture had been bought from time to time since; but it had been bought by Mrs Johnson in her own name. She had private means—£soo to £OOO a year. Some of the old furniture had been sold, and he now valued what re- mained at only £B. The value of the furniture now on his premises was from £3OO to £4OO. In accounting for his deficiency he put down £6,000 as against the collieries four years ago ; but he calculated that his interest in the collieries would be worth £lO,OOO to £15,000 at least. As- suming that he bad no interest he was then insolvent. The payments he had made since on account of the collieries amounted te £5,000 or £6,000. He had taken the money from the grocery and provision business. He estimated hie deficiency on the grocery and provision business at £4,000 ; but he had assumed all along that he ret tined the interest in the collieries.—Exarained by Mr. Thomas : Some five years ago, when he disposed of the collieries, he transferred one of his ebops into the name of his son Charles,but it was afterwards transferred back again. —Examined by Mr. Rodway : The reason he gave up the collieries was that he was short of meaneaend wanting money for wages, he applied to Mr. Davies, to whom he then owed £3,700, and told him it was his intention to sell up, pay all his creditors, and pass through the court for the leases. Mr. , Davies thought that would be a disgrace, and it resulted in an arrangement b2ing made with Davies and Dobell for
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 11, 1886.

them to buy. A valuer was offered from Wigan, who valued the moveable plant, ,to., at the Swan-lane Colliery at .£21,500, and he sold for the £15,000 on the understanding that he was to have a partnersnip, and to take the manage- ment of the colliery, as he knew most about it. He under- stood that his share was to be one-third. That was named several times. No articles of partnership were drawn up, though he wished it, the reply being that they were gentlemen, and he might rely on their word. He considered that they had abundant value in the one colliery,. only for what they paid, and for his third itherest, but they had now also got possession of the Long-lane Colliery for nothing. He con- sidered that the plant if sold now by auction would realise more tban Messrs. Davies and Doh-di had paid, He did not think, however, that they bad made any profits of late. He admitted having received some moneys on account of the collieries, but hs had also paid mosey or had a counter- claim for more than the amount so received.—Mr. Riley said as there must be an adjournment be would postpone his re-examination —The Deputy-Official Receiver then asked for several accounts, showing the state of his affairs at the time be sold the colliery, his personal drawings, and his receipts and payments sine tat date.—The learned Registrar made an order, and adjourned the extmination for a month.

div.head: TERRIBLE FALL 10OWN A PIT SHAFT AT ST. HELEN.
div.p: THE TERRIBLE FALL 10OWN A PIT SHAFT AT ST. HELEN.

The inquiry into the circumstances attending the death of Thomas Percival, who, on Monday week, was jerkPd out of the cage in the shaft of the Alexandra Colliery, and, falling seventy yards, was almost imme- diately killed, was resumed before Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, at the Lamb Inn, Mr. Hall, Government Inspector of Mines, was present. Mr. 0. Swift represented the St. Helens Collieries Company, and Mr. Thomas Glover, miners' agent, watched the pro- ceedings for the society. Jesse Taylor, runner-in at the Little Delf, or Bette mine, said that when a cage wanted to stop at the Rushy Park mine, which was seventy yards higher up, it usually came to the bottom, and then in ascending it was stopped, catches were put out, and it was lowered on to them. There was a semaphore in the engine-house which showed the engineinan the position of the catches. Oh Saturday morn- ing witness heard something falling down the ehaft' and moved away. On returning he found two planks of the scaffold over the dlb-hole broken, and deceased lying on it. There was a piece of iron nine of ten inches long (a piece of a catch) lying on the scaffold. The cage was three of four yards above.—ln reply to Mr. Hall, witness said he knew somebody was coming down in the descending cage. De— ceased had signalled to him from the top, and be had sig- nalled that he could come down. There was nothing to inform Rigby, the runner-in at Rushy Park, who worked the catches, that anyone was coining down, because they always went to the bottom. The man at Rushy Parkcould knock to witness at the bottom, but witness could not knock back again. His mode of communication was to shout up. The cage had not sernck the catches before to his knowledge.—By Mr. Swift: Goulding,, the engineman,. had worked there for many years. He was a careful man, and the winding was done properly,---By Mr. Glover Witness had no signal to tell him when the catches were out.

Mr. Francis France, general manager for the Collieries Company, put in plans. He examined the catches after the accident, and tested the semaphore, which was in per- fect order. Goulding had been there over twenty years, and there bad not been an accident in his hands before. Edward Rigby, haring been cautioned, said he did not pull the catches back as he oaght to have done. Robert Goulding, the engineman, having also been cau- tioned, gave evidence. He said be had no instructions from deceased to stay at bushy Park, and in the absence of such instructions be took it to be his duty to send him to the bet- I torn. He lowered him at half-speed. During tbe descent bee heard a thud on the drum, and brought the engine to a stand. He then noticed the signal arm was out at danger,. but whether it was danger or not before he commenced to wind he did not know.-In reply to Mr. Hall, witness-said with hav- ing his attention on the man going down he could not say that be did look at the semaphore.—By Mr. Swift : • He had to hold the regulator as well as the reversing lever, so that his attention was concentrated on his engines. Mr. Hall, Government inspector, said he had elamined the machinery caref ally and the shaft arrangements, and could not say there was anything likely to conduce to an accident of that kind. There had been some omission about the signal, but at present he did not see that that, had any bearing tipen the accident. His (Mr. Hall's) opinion was that if Rigby and the engineman had used ordinary care the accident would not have happened. The Coroner said he felt certain that the jury would be able to coma to an honest verdict, because they had done everything they sould possibly do to arrive at the facts of the case. They had taken the trouble to go to the colliery and inspect the semaphore and its working, and they had listened attenti% ely to the evidence. The simple question was whether they thought there had been °minim on the part of both Rigby and Goulding, or on the part of either of them, that would lead them honestly to say that they ought to take their trial for having criminally caused the death of Percival. He (the coroner) thought the jary would admit that there hall been an omission on the part of both of them. After summing up the evidence the coroner and officials left the room. The jury, after ten minutes' consultation, returned a vet', diet of "Manslaughter " against the engineman Robert Goulding; and while censuring Rigby, did not think his negligence was sufficient to say he was culpable.—Goulding was then committed for trial ripen the corner's warrant.— The coroner allowed bail, Goulding in MO; and one surety of £5O. The Rev. H. S. Bolton, vicar of Raysnhead, entered into his recognisance for Goulding. The coronor afterwards censured Rigby, and told him he was very for- tunate in not then standing in the same position as the engineman. Go-aiding, who lives at Thatto Heath, was then taken Into custody by Inspector Whittaker and removed to the Town Hall, where he was later in the day brought before Alderman Harrison, J.P., who granted a remand until Mon- day next, and allowed the prisoner out on the same bail as that fixed by the coroner.

On Thursday Sir E. Malet,the British Ambassador to Ger- many, arrived unexpectedly in London, and in the after- noon had an interview with Lord Iddesleigh at the Foreign Office.

Mr. Ira D. Sankey, of Moody-Sankey fame, arrived in Liverpool on Thursday morning in the National steamer America. Mr. Sankey, who is accompanied by his wife, visits Europe to recuperate. The contract for the construction of the Manchester Jubilee Exhibition building has been let to Messrs. Robert Neill and Sons, of Manchester. Their tender amounted to £34,350, and was the lowest of the fourteen received. AN ENOINE-HO'CSR DESTROYED EX FIRE.—On Thursday morning the engine-house of the Lady Blanche coal mine at Dysart, the property of the Earl of Rosslyn, was des- troyed by fire. The damage to property and machinery is great, and many miners will be thrown ont of employ- ment.

div.head: SFIAM BAILIFF AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: A SFIAM BAILIFF AT ST. HELENS.

At the Town Hall, on Wednesday, before Dr. Gus- hell, James Owens, a cripple living at Pocket Nook, who pushes himself about the streets in a wooden car- riage, was brought up charged with "acting under a false colour and pretence of the process of the CourAy Court of Lancashire, hoiden at St. Helens." Mr. Garner (from the office of Messrs. J. 0. and W. Swift) prosecuted, and stated that on the 26th May a judgment was obtained by Messrs. Price and Sons, furniture dealers-, against Benjamin Scott,- of 3, City, Wincile, for goas sold and delivered, for him to pay 1 IS3 by monthly instalments of 43. Mrs. Scott seemed to have made her payments regularly, and as late as the 23rd August paid an instalment. The same evening the prisoner called upon her and said; he had brought her trouble, ard that unless she paid him, a sovereign he would "clear her house out." She said she had that day paid an instalment, but he repeated his threat, and called up the road to two men who were standing there. Mrs. Scott became terrified, and, thinking they were really bailiffs and had come to clear the house under a warrant from the County Court, she procured a sovereign. He (Mr. Garner) would call evidence to prove that prisoner was not an official of the St. Helens County Court, and that he had no right to make people believe he was.--Mrs. Scott then detailed the conversation which ensued in reply to prisoner's demand for a sove- reign. He said she was two months behind; in her payments, and that be had two men with him to take the furniture. He went and called "Charley," but as she went for the sovereign he taAld " Charley "to stop. She eerrowed a sovereign from her niece and offered it to him. He then said, "Now, if I:take this will it hurt you?" ehe then said, "What do you think when I have borrowed it ?" and then he said, "Then won't take it" She gave him 4s. because she was afraid•of his taking the things and for the sake of quietness, because* he made such a row in the neighbourhood. He gave her a. receipt for the 4s on the County Court form upon which receipts were given at the County Court offices.,—Dr. Gas- kelt asked the Clerk (Mr. Brewis) if the charge would be ono of false pretences.—Mr. Brewis remarked that giving a re- ceipt on a County Court form by an unauthorised kerson was a serious offence, and one that must be tried at the assizes.—Mr. Garner asked for a remand of the prisoner un— til Monday, which was granted.
PRESCOT.

VAGUANCY AT WHISTON.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, four rough-looking characters, named William Johnson, William Judd, James Kenyon, and John Heap, were charged with sleeping in an outhouse at Whiston, and having no means of subsistence. P.C. Orrnerod stated that at half-past one o'clock that morning he found the whole of the prisoners lying in a cabin at Old Curs Colliery, Whis- ton. He hid had many complaints as to men sleepin there. They were each sent to gaol for seven days with hard labour.

LOCAL POUCH Casas.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, a rough-looking fellow named Thomas Brawn, was charged with stealing three shirts, value 121, the property of Fred Allanson, a clerk, residing in Picton-road, Waver- tree. He was sent to gaol for three months, having been previously convicted—James Critchley, a labourer, of Tar- bock, was summoned for refusing to quit the license 1 pre- mises of Mrs Perch, the Hare am.: Hounds, Tarbock, and he was farther summoned for assaulting Annie Bellew Calder, on the 29th August. The defendant, who said he was ex- tremely sorry, was discharged with a caution.—Ed ward Edwards and John Forrest were summoned for creating a breach of the peace at Huyton Quarry, on the 13th ult, opposite the Seel Arms. They were discharged with a can- tien.—Ann Kelly, a married woman, of Prescot, who made her 4th appearance in court, was fined lOs and costs for being drunk and disorderly.—John Scotson, for committing a breach of the peace at Prescot, was hound over to keep the peace for three months, himself in £lO, and one surety of LC

TERRIBLE DEATH AT WITISTON WITH RWO MSS. —On Friday morning,auout a quarter to eleven o'clock, an acci- dentof a shocking character occurred at Mr. William Long- ton's dolt Lane Quarry Waterworks, near Whiston, which supply the Prescot Union Workhouse. Whilst the engi- neer, Thomas Haworth, assisted by Peter Jones, was chan- ging the bucket of the pump, the block saspended from the tripod became twisted, and for the purpose of righting it they climbed up, bat when they had got no about four feet it snapi3ed suddenly, and the whole weight fell upon Howarth, crushing his head in a fearful manner and killing him on the spot. Deceased, who was 47 years of age, in addition to holding the position of engineer at the quarry was landlord of the White Hart Inn, Prescot, and leaves a widow, and four children. On Monday, an inquest was held on the body of the deceased at the Royal Hotel, Prescott' by Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy-coroner. Mr. T. Dyson was present on behalf of the relatives of the deceased, and and,Mr..W. Mackensie represented Mr. William Longton, proprietor of the quarry. The jury returned a verdict of "Death from misadventure."

Cxsua AGAINST A PEESCOT WATCIIIIAIMI.—At the Prescot Petty Sessious, on Tuesday, before Mr.H. Bright and Major Pilkington,Edward Preston, a watchmaker, residing in Derby-etrest, Pres.cot, wag summoned for stealing fruit from the garden of Mr. Arthur F. Evans. The defendant pleaded guilty.. P.C. Fisher stated that at ten minutes past four o'clock on Saturday morning he saw the defendant walk in. He walked round the vinery and peach house and tried the doors,, but found them locke4. He then walked down the garden to a. peer tree where he plucked some of the fruit and put it in his pocket. He then walked to an apple tree sad also took; fruit from it. He then spoke to the defendant and took him into custody.—Mr. Andrew Murray, occa- sionaligardener to Mr. Evan., said the value of the fruit taken by the defendant was twopence, and the damage done would be tenpenee.—Superintendent Barker said the defen- dant was in a good position in the town, was a watchmaker, and he.might oily he had had great complaints of gardens being robbed in Present. It showed clearly from the evid- ence of the officer wkat the man's intention was in trying tke door of the vinery. The tlefendant had a big garden of his own, and he was a man, be was sorry to say, who took a great deal of drink, far more than he ought to de.—The beneh inflictel a fine of 20s and On 6,1 costs, and allowed the witness Murray f.la (scl for his expenses.

PRESCOT HIGHWAY BOARD.—The monthly meeting of this beard was held on Tuesday, when there were present Mr. Lowe, in the chair, Mr. Willis, Mr. Tyrer, Mr. Sumner, Mr. Newton, Mr. Cross (clerk), Mr. Goldsworth (surveyor), and Mr. W. Goldsworth, jein. (assistant surveyor).—Sur- veyor's Eryenditure Mr. Goldsworth reported that his ex- Peoditure for the five weeks from July 29th te September 2nd was as under :—Bold, £l5 4s 8d; Knowsley, £22 7s 7d; Reinhill, £ll lie 6,1 ; Whiston, £2l 17s lid ; team labour, £57 4s 6d ;. new materials, £63 12e 10d ; incidentals, £l5 Os Id ; total. £206 193 Id. The Erection of lelephone Poles at Rainhill : The Clerk said with reference to the erection of telephone poles at Rainhill, he had received a letter from Mr. Owen, who stated You are doubtless aware that representatives of the petitioners, Mr. Goldsworth aud Mr. Lowe, met the two engineers of the telephone company at Rainhill in the month of April last, and at that meeting it was arranged that the poles then erected in the roads should be removed, and an-alternative route was agreed upou. which would not be objectionable, and so far as I was concerned consent was given for poles to be erected over the land for the purposes of that route.. Not having heard from the company for more than a month, I concluded that the alternative route was to be adopted r but instead of this I, op the 15th June;received a letter from the company asking permis- sion to erect three poles across the Lawton House Grounds. As this had been refused prior to the company's applica- tion to the Highway Board, it must have beep pretty evi- dent: that the permission would still be withheld. since writing to that, effect on the 21st of June last, I have heard nothing further from the company. The petitioners hope that the Highway Board will not allow the poles to be erected ea desired by the company, for they will unquestionably be an injury to the place, and 'so reluce the value of property at The Chairman said he had told Mr. Owen that he had not raised any objection against the erection of the poles, but that he wee quits willine that the alternative route selected by Mr. G-oldsworth and himself (the chairman) should be adopted. As there was no opposition put in the way, ha thought this route should be the one adhered to.—The Sur- `Yeyor was of opinion that if a copy of Mr. Owen's letter was sent to the Telephone Co., then the company would eee how the matter stood.—The Clerk was then instructed, to send a copy of Mr. Ovven's letter to the Telephone Company. —The Steam Road Roller: The Surveyor said that they were doing excellent work with the steam road roller, and he hoped to get it working in a regular way, say two (Nays in one township and two days in another township. He also brought before the notice of the meeting that it was possi- ble that before the next meeting the London and North- Western Railway Company would reclaim the roller for the , purpose of making the road over Platt's bridge at Whistm. He would like the Board to fix a price per day for he loaa of the machine. It was decided that the sum of 35s per day be charged for the use of the roller should tke company require it.—The Condition of the Roads: The Surveyo-r said that the county surveyor had been over the roads within the Board's jurisdiction since the last meeting, and had expressed himself satisfied with them. Ife (Mr. Golds- worth) had to ask the Board to consider the point he brought before them a few, years ago in respect of making application to the county authorities •to adopt certain roads as main roads. Two of these roads would be between Widnes and St. Helens and one through Knowsley township. The advantage would be that in the first place the county would pay one half of the cost and the Government would pay a fourth. The fact of the matter was they would get three-fourths back again. —Mr. Newton. propose and Mr. Tyrer seconded that the necessary application be neade.—The resolution was adopted. land the meeting terminated.

SCALDED TO DEATH WITH Tit. -• Mr. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at the Oddfellows Arms, Parr Stocks, on Saturday morning, touching the death of John Stirrup, son of a collier named Thomas Stirrup. The mother of the deceased stated that on the 19th ult she was pouring out some hot tea into cups stanaing on the table. She had filled all the cups, sad was in the act of putting the pot upon the hob when the child, who was sitting upon his sister's knees, pulled the contents of one of the cups over him. The child sustained serious injuries, to NO:Ade he succumbed soon afterwards. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death,"

There were present— Messrs. W. R. Burdis. M. Rirlrhea6l, C. Kelly, JAB. Rutter, Jshn Ball, , Dr. Foulson, F. Willis, L Morris, Joseph Davies, JOhn Clarke, W. Younger, F. A. R. Neill (Bolt!), and I'. Morris (hon. sec.) Afttr tea, the chair was occu- pied by F. A. R. Neill. The loyal toasts, drc., were duly honoured, after which Mr. W. McEvoy proposed the toast of the "'Health of the Right Hon. W. E.
