It was decided that important steps should be taken to make it still more attractive to the. inembA-s. The proceedings were of a very pleasant charac- ter throughout.

A MinNIGHT', ST272IOGLE AT NiIVTON —At Newton Town Hall, on Monday, before Colonel George AlcCorquo- dale, Thomas John aoslin, a stiiker, living at Wargrave View, Earlestown, was charged with being drank in Church-street, Newton, at half-past twelve on Saturday night, and also with assaulting P.C. Spencer whilst in the execution of his duty.--i'.S. Cotumins stated that Police- constable Spencer found the prisoner drunk and asleep on the footpath in Church-street. He awoke him, but the prisoner refused to more fur a time. He eventually jumped up aud struck the constable a' severe blow with his fit under the right ear, knocking him against some railings. The constable closed with him, and both fell to the ground. The prisoner struck the officer several times, but be was at last hand- cuXed. On the way to the police office he again struck the constable. P.S. Commins asked for the prisoner to be re- manded until the Petty Sessions to be held at Newton to- day (Saturday). T;(3 magistrates granted the remand, and admitted prisoner to bail, himself in .-EllG; and two sureties of £6 each.

EAMLESTOWN BOWLiNG,CLI7I3.—The members of this club played a handicap of bowls on Saturday for a prize, value £2 10s, presented by Mr. 117. Melling,-of Etrlestown. The greOn was in first-class condition, and the game throughout was very exciting. Thirty-six members took part. After a'splendid afternoon's engagement the game was brought to a close by the first prize being awarded to James Foster, second prize to J. Bod worth, end third to W. Morris,. Great credit was due to each player for the excel- lent manner in which they bowled throughout the contest. The presentation of the first prize took place at Mr. Mel- hog's New Market Inn, on Wednesday evening. The prize consists of a splendid silver coffee service. Mr. W. Clare was calfect upon to preside. The proceedingawere of a very enjoyable character, tongs being rendered r.,y Messrs. By. Stanton,..Finch, and others. Vctes of thanks were given to the gentlemen of the town who had so kindly supported the club by offering prizes during the past season. Outing the evening the presentation we made to Mr. Forster by the chairman on behalf of the club, who warmly com• plimented the winner upon his success. GooD, TEMPLARS' ENTERTAINMENT.—There was a good attendance of the members at the weekly session of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Tensplars on Mon- daY evening. Brother J. Macdonald w.0.T., presided. After lodge business had been transacted Brother Bolton, of the Sir Wilfrid Lawson Lodge, Cockermouth, who attended , as a visitor, gave an excellent address, and concluded with a song in the northern dialect, entitled "Sandy's a templar now." Tlet lodge tendered hearty thanks to hint and for- warded fraternal greetings to the Cockermonth lodge. An open entertainment was afterwards held, and several friends attended. Brother IT Walker sang " Dublin Say.", Bro. E. Newman read "The pink boots," Brother F.:'.Uren sang" When the war is over. Mary," Sister Barnard recited "The little dove." Sister E. Day recited 66 The last minstrel," Sisters E. and J Clarke gave the duet "No one cares for me," Brotl,er W. Harding read " Little Maggie's mother; " Brother J. McDonald sang 'The honest heart," Sister Barnard recited " Why the poor com- plain." Brother George Clarke read " A•ourious companion," and Brother John Taylor read 'When is the time to sign ?" The proceedings were very enjoyable.

div.head: NEWTON IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: NEWTON IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS.

A meeting of the Newton Improvement Commtssionets was held at the Town Hall. at Newton, on Monday after• noon. The chair was occupied by Mr. Wt F. Gooch, and there were also present Colonel McCorquodalai Messrs. T. Stone. T. Hunt, T,Forster, J. Fairclough, Woreley (law-clerk), and R. Brierley (surveyor). HIGHWAY' Commirrrin.—A meeting of the Highway, Public Works, and Sanitary Committee was held on Mon- day, the 23-rd August. Mr. T. Stone was elected chairman of the committee for the ensuing year. The surveyor submitted anew plan of the sonth end of Wargrave-road, Vulcan-brow, relative tolhe sowering, paving, and digging, of same, and it was ordered that the same be considered at a special meet- ing to be held immediately following the next Board meet- ing, the law-clerk to be present. Mr. Weyer gave notice that be should at the next meeting move—" That, inasmuch as Mr. Molyneux and his adjoining owners have not com- plied with the following minute of the 16th November, 1885, the oarne be rescindei, viz., Having further con- sidered Mr. Molyneux's application for a footpath opposite his new property on the west side of .Wargrave-road, it was ordered that a footpath be formed and adopted by the Com- missioners on Mr. Molyneux and adjoining owners agreeing to pay one-half the cost of curbing,.gaggieg, and paving the same?' On the report of the surveyor it was ordered that tv.N& storm grids be provitled for Crow-lane, near the Rock Pit, one at Cross-lane, and one at Wargrave Bridge. It was also ordered that the law-clerk and surveyor wait upon the County Highway Committee at Preston, on the 31st inst., as to the Commissioners' claim on the recent action, and as to their adopting the Bolton and St. Helens roads, and Golborne Dale and Parkside roads, under section 15 of the Highways and Locomotives Act, 1878, as main roads.—The minutes of the committee were approved without discussion.

GAS /Ali> WATER COMMITTEE.--A meeting of this com- mittee was held at the Town Hall, on Monday, the 234 nit Mr. Brierley read his correspondence with Messrs. Vicars and the railway company respecting the gas mains under the old railway crossing in Chemical-street, when it was ordered that steps be taken to. examine and repair the pipe joints, and adopt other means to secure an efficient supply of gas to Messrs. Vicars' works.—The minutes were can firmed.

bt,CZ.OOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. -- Mr. Emmett was elected chairman of the School Attendance Committee at ,af meeting held on the 23rd Aueus4 Mr. Ball read a report in whi3h he submitted the following return of attendanae at each school for the quarter endinz June, 1886 :—S•. Peter's 282,:Cras-street 65, \Vargrave 210,Earlestown District Infant 217, Wesleyan 492, Roman Catholic 237, Vulcan 91. varions 86, making a total of 11T86, as compared with 1745 last year.—Mr. Ball was directed to report on the most re- fractory cases of irregularity.:—The Board adopted the re-- port without discussion.

TRH MEDICAL OFFICER.—The Lao, Clerk read a.. letter that had been received from the Local Government Board ' 'sanctioning the re-appointment of Dr. Watkins as medical officer for the term for which be was at the last meeting appointed. THE RECENT FIRES. Mr. Stone said that within the last two or three weeks there had been three fires in that neighblurhood. Several people bad suggested the ad- visability that something should be done in the,way of pro- viding a fire engine or procuring some provision in case of .fire. He believed that water was laid on throughout the whole of the township, and, if they did not go so far as to have a fire engine, they might have a sufficient length of lu:se-pipe to attach the hydrants in case of fire. It was time that something was done in the matter,--TheZurveyor said that the Hoard. had already sufficient .hose,pipe.—Mr. Stone asked who, In the case of fire, was. going to. use it. He suggested that the staff of men should be doubled.—The question was refeued to committee for csnsideration.

A VIOLENT: CUSTOMER.—At St. Helena, on Mon- day, John Tobin (Windle) was charged with being drunk and disorderly, assaulting P.C. Clarkson,andalso damaging his uniform to the extent of is Clazkson said on Saturday night. at the bottom of Liverpool-road, he beard a crash of glass. Immediately afterwards he saw the prisoner come out of a shop. He was drunli, and cursing and swear- ing. He went to the shop, and saw that a large plate glass window had been broken, and a large. crowd had collected around the place. He took Tobin into custody, whereupon he becawe very violent, and struck and kicked him several times. He also tore his trou,sers.—Tobin, who pleaded guilty, was fined £1 and costs for the assault, is Gd for damaging the uniform, and he was also ordered to pay the amount of the damage, or in default 23 days' imprison- ment, Row BETWEEN NEIGHBOURS. At St. Helens, on Friday, Frederick Ratclifle and William Cash, both of Gerard•gtreet, were summoned for assaulting a neighbour named John Burns. Tba complainant stated that on, the previous Sunday afternoon be was proceeding to his work, when the two defendants met him in Gerard-street. They cried out "Now we have him," after which Ratclige struck him and knocked haat down, and Cash kicked him severely on the eye whilst he was upon the greund. They also threatened what they would do with him when the nights were dark —Ratcliffe said Burns had knocked a flower ,out of. his coat by striking him roughly on the breast, and Cash stated that Bums bad keen insulting him and a young lady for a long time, until he could not stand it any longer.— They were both bound over to keep the peace for three months, themselves in £5 each and out suety for a similar amount, et wren dap' imprisonment.

MARRIED OR NOT MARRIED? EXTRAORDINARY CASE. An extraordinary cage came before Col. Gambl,e and Mr. 11. S. Hall, at the Town Hall, on Mumlay, what a young man named John Haled], of Eccleston La•ne-ends,vras sulfl. monad under the Igiarried Women's Maintenance AM, ISM, tashow cause why he should not contriute towards the maintenance of his rife, who was not at prment living with him. •

Mr,John 0. Swift aelpeared for complainant and said the parties were married on the 16th February laete and went to live at Eccleston Lane-ends. They appeared to have got on comfortably until June or July, and then defendant begat; to abuse her. In the week beginning the 16:h August, der fendant appeared to have made up his mind that he would get rid of her, and next dear he assaulted her and turned her out. She got in the house again at night, and he -.Yent an& slept away. Next day hc-threatened her and turned her out, and threw her clothes into the street. On the following Saturday he cleated oat the furniture, and had gone away altogether. He had told her he would swing fer her, and also told her father he would net support her. Mr. Swift coetinued to say that deNndant earned £1 a week on the railway. His wife was expecting to be confined shortly'', and it was for the magistratee to fixethe amount that de•-• fendant should pay. Under the circumstances Bs. a week would be a reasonable sum. Mrs. Helsel' was then put in the box, and she corrobo- rated the statement made by Mr. Swift: —Defendant: Are you married ?—Complainant: Yes;. you know that.—De- fendant: Where were you married at ?__Complainant: was married at St. Peter's Church, Liverpool.—Defendant Where are your marriage lines ?—Ccernplainant : You kept them in a box.—Defendant: Your worships, we were never married. She is speaking false. (Astonishment in court.) —Complainant: our sister stood for me. Defendant: Where are your marriage :lines ?—Complainant: I have not got them, but I can get them. His sister and a young man were there. I have nobody in court who was present at the wedding. I have seen the marriage lines. They were in a box upstairs. He has them now.—The Chairman (to de- fendant): Do you still say you are not married? Defen- dant : Yes.—The Chairman: Would you like to come into the box and give evidence :)=-Defendant : Mr. Swift then called complainant's mother,. Mrs kieyeee who said defendant was courting her daughter, and they' arrangedto be married. he remembered. them going down to :Liverpool to be married. When they come back he said they had got married. Witness had not seen their marriage lines. Defendant and cemplainant lived as man and wife until the 21st of August, but had not been back since. They bad been looked upon as man and wife. Mrs Heyes continued to say that defendant said he had married here:but she didn't know bow they were married, whether by banns or not.—Defendant (after being cautioned by the chairman) said he was prepared to go into the witness.box. He knew what he was doing. He was prepared to tell the truth. Complainant had been epeeking false all the time. —Mr. Swift asked that a note should be taken of defendant's evidence. Tbis the clerk proceeded to do, and the defend- ant was then sworn. He said he now lived at Thatto Heath. worked on the railway, and earned .£1 a week. He bad courted Sarah Heys (complainant) for about two years. He did not arrange to be married ; it was never mentioned. He told her be would not marry her. She kept coming tO him night after night crying, and saying that her mother would turn her out. He said be would not marry her, but he would take her ao his housekeeper. They went together to Liverpool, and when they got back they said they were married. Defendant was again reminded by Mr. Swift that he was on oath, and defendant said he knew it. He did not know whether it was the 16th Februaryabut it was at the begin- ning of the year that they went down. He had had his . breakfast previeusly at her mother'i. His sister did not go with them ; nobody went with them—they went alone and came leack alone. They did not go to St. Peter's Church, or to any church. He did not go through any ceremony of marriage on that day. He had never gone through any ceremony of marriage with her. He did not know where Sc. Peter's Church was. He had never been inside a church with her. He did not get a licence. On their return she told her mother they had been married, but he did not. -- Complainant (astonished): You didn't ?—Defendant : I didn't.--Complaioant : Why, he told my father and mother as well.—Defendant : I pretended to be her husband.' have not had her marriage lines nor seen them. I have told my mates that I was married. Mr. Swift: What did it cost you the day you were itt Liverpool ?—Defendant: We bought a ring in London-road. and put.it on, and from there we went to the station, and to my sister's at Woolton. She put on the ring herself. I didn't put it on, nor find the money to buy it.—Mr. Swift: How mach did it cost you that davq.:--Defendant : I don't know.—Mr. Swift: £2 ?—Defendant: Not that by a great deal. I have not been married to :ter nor anybody else, and there was no pretence at a marriage. . Mr. Swift asked the magistrates to grant an adjournment for a fortnight, so that they could come prepared with direet evidence of the tnarriege.—Defendant said it would only be wasting time, as complainant had been speaking false.—The Chairman (to Mr. Swift): You can take an adjournment to the 27th inst.

Nothing has been seen of the boy or the five pairs of boots he ob.' tamed. Ilysaoll TEMPERANCE] ASSOCILTION. The members of the above opened the weekly series of meeting i on 'needs! evening at the Hayten Park school. There was a great muster, the president, Mr. E. S. Eccles, in the chair, and he gave an address on "Perseverance in the temperance cause," illustrating his remarks by the history of Russia in her endeavours to obtain a position on the Mediteranean. An address was also given by Mr. J. B. Leach, and an enter- taining programme of songs, ctc., was rendered by Dr. Bd. mand Capper,. an old favourite, Mr. H. Capper, and Mr; P. Capper. Miss Capper played a solo on the pianoforte and the accompaniments. Several persons signed the pledge at tho.close of the meeting. Elb-OTRNING OF THE CONGREGATIONAL CHI:IRM On Sunday the above church, which had been closed for siz weeks during which time it has undergone considerable ' alteration, cleaning, and painting, was re-opened, and the services were conducted by the Rev. W. A. carter, of Ttled- dingworth. The church and school buildings have been coloured and painted throughout, the seating of the church has been modernised, and a uniform appearance given by re-cushioning with a velvet pile carpeting. A great im- provement has also been eff,cted in the ventilating. Messrs. Hughes and Stirling were contractors for the alterations, and Messrs. S. R. Henshaw were the decorators, while Messrs. TJrquhart and Adamson, of Liverpool, and Mr. Bishop, of Roby, were entrusted with the upholstery. The whole of the work has been carried out in a tasteful and satisfactory manner at a cost of about £lBO, which has nearly all been subscribed. A collection:was mads,..-nornicg. and evening Ici give an opportunity to those wha,had not been asked previously to contribute.

• The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday evening at the Public Offices, Blacklow-brow, Mr. J. Siddely in the chair. Present—Messrs. J,,E. Parker, It. Brown, G. Banner, JL Makinson, neer W; Dame, T. Pinnington, T. Evans, •E.. J. Grimshaw, T. Dated', W. Swift (clerk), E. F. Hall (medical officer), and J. Worrell (surveyor). fiIitALTH REPORT —Tho,rninutes having been read and passed the medical officer's report was read showing the deaths for the month to . be, Huyton 3, Huyton Quarry 2. Roby 0. One case of scarlet fever had occurred, but every :precaution has been taken to prevent it spreading. ; BALDWIN SLAUGHTM,HOUSR.—Mr. Dalzell wished to know if the Board bad power to grant or withhold licenses to slaughter-houses in their district —The Clerk said they could not interfere with the slaeghter-houses in question, but they might in tha.ease of a new application. The Board could only deal with any nuisance complained of.,—The Chairman inquired of the surveyor if t.t3 nuisance had abated, and if the alterations that had been suggested had been carried out.—The Surveyor said the place had been whitewashed and theoffal removed, but the floor and drains had not been done.—Mr. Grimshaw wanted to know -what the doctor thought of it, when he saw it.—Dr. Hall: It was in an insanitary state.—Mr. thimshaw Then I suggest that we compel them to remedy this state of things at once.—Mr. Swift I don't think we coald get a comiction• —Mr. Dalzell: I don't think Mr. Swift should say such thing; it is more a question for the medical officer than the law clerk.—Mr. Swift (warmly): Then lhope Nem will get some one else to appear in court if you won't take my ad- vice—Mr. Dalaell, moved, And Mr. 'Grimshaw seconded, that legal proceedings be taken to enforce the order of the Board.—An amendment by Mr. Banner, seconded by Mr. Evans, that the matter be deferred for a month was carried by five votes to three, several members not voting. ) ANOTITEII. IsinsaercE.—A lettee. was read from Mr. E. ißrereton Williams, "drawing tho attention of the Board to a stench emanating from the barracks opposite to Mr. Reichardt' e shop, believed to arise from a defective midden, and calculated to engender disease." As a matter requiring immediate attention it was referred to the surveyor. HIGRWAT AND LIGHTING.—The Surveyor reported that a. bracket larep might be advantageously planed in Wigan - street, Huyton Quarry. It was. resolved to place one there and one near to the Catholic chapel in Huyton Hey-road. Mr. Parker complained of the bad state of Roby-road,naus,sa by the re-haying of telegraph underground wires.—Toe ;Chairman : We know nothing of it.—The Surveyor: I re" ceivecl due notice, but did not acquaint the Board, as it was* only a renewal of the pipes, and the Government hav6, power to take up the road at any time on giving forma, notice.—Mr. Grimshaw called attention to the dangerous state of a wall near Huyton Quarry station.—The CleT replied that he was incommunication with Major Seel, the owner, in the matter.. AUDITOR.—A letter was read from Mr. S. B. Frovis, CI the Local Government Board, showing that from the report of the auditor, there were certain omissions of minutes. which the clerk described as of trivial moment. PLANS. A plan of shed submitted by Mr. Thomas Birchall for Mr. Bleale, was referred back for alteration. Feereezcc.—A halaice in band of £1,020 12a 7d was d.e. ciared, and accounts were passed for payment amounting £595 lOsfli, It was resolved that lel days' notice be sent t. these in arrear previous to summonses being taken out, arl.a_ that a lietbi pre?ared of defaulters for usAt meeting of 04 , Boat*.

AND HUMOUR.,

Coming to grief—Meeting trouble half way. The tool that keeps a newspaper going—The "adze." Why should tailors always be able to please their cus- tomers?—Because it is their especial duty to suit people. The man who went to the country for "rest and change" says the waiters got most of his change and the landlord the rest. AT THE PALAIS ROYAL.—Jack (who has just treated his friend to the dinner of the establishment): Pretty good dinner for two francs and a half, eh ?—His friend: First rate. Let's have another. HEARD AT THE Zoo.—Wife, before a lion's cage, to husband: What would you say if the bars were to break suddenly, and the lion to eat me up ?—Husband, drily I should say he had a good appetite. "You have plenty of reading her e," said a visitor to the editor of a literary journal, pointing to a pile of books on the editorial desk. "Those are not for read- ing," replied the editor.; "they are for reviewing?' Friend, to young writer: I see that your publisher has failed, and has been sent to an asylum hopelessly insane. —Young writer, bitterly: Just my luck! It was only last week that he accepted a story of mine. "I say, Jones, how is it that your wife dresses so mag- nificently, while you always appear almost out at elbows ?" "You see, Thompson, my wife always dresses according to Le Follet, and I dress according to my _ _

ledger." - Master-builder, to member of United Order of Hod- carriers out on strike: Pat, you ought to be at work, instead of loafing about the streets, and your family half starved at home.—Pat: Shtarved, is it? An' sure it's meself that's trisurer av the ordher ! SHE WOULDN'T PLAY HOUSE THAT WAY.—Mother : Why, Harry, you haven't got through playing house down on the beach, have you ?—Harry: Yes'm.—Mother : What's the matter? Didn't you have a good time ? Barry: No'm ; that Carrie Judson is a mean old thing. She wouldn't fight a bit like you and papa, and when I hit her on the head she-cried. She's no fun. TILE WORKING MAN'S FILIEND.—" Yes, sir," yelled the Socialistic agitator, "I am the working man's friend." "Oh, go 'long," said a real working man, "you haven't done an honest day's work in two years." "Of course I haven't. That's where I show my friendship for the working,man. I keep my hands off so that he can have the job.' 0 CO3IPAN-Y MANN-ERS.—Mrs. Converse (to neighbour's nurse girl) : I wish I had such a polite, well-behaved girl for my children. I notice that you always address your charges as 6. Miss " and "Master."-,Nurse girl (spoiling the illusion) : Yes, ma'am, I get paid extra for that; the missus thinks it looks big to have me use such terms in company. A SPICY PARISI:CIO:CDR.—A prominent member of a church not a thousand miles from this town was talking with his pastor the other day about an excellent but somewhat aggressive lady of the parish. After descant- ing at lendth on her virtues, he concluded by saying, "In fact, she may be calied the salt of the earth." "Yes," responded 'the clergyman quickly, "and the pepper, too." A REVELATION.—After a fashionable dinner the other day at which many of the guests were authors, a well- known society-man said to a friend in confidence, " I can imagine one wanting to know an author after read- ing his book; but I cannot HOW imagine any one de- siring to read a book after knowing its author. A SHORT MEMORY.—A lady once had such a short memory that she scarcely knew what she read. A friend, knowing this, sent her the same book to read seven times in succession. On being asked how she liked it, she replied, "1 think it is a first-rate produc- tion, but the author sometimes repeats the same !" At ''a place called Erinelo, in the Transvaal, there was lately brought before the magistrate a man charged with horse-stealing. The evidence was conclusive; but, as the case was proceeding, thc magistrate stopped it with these words—" Prisoner, it is quite clear that you are guilty, and I shall have to commit you if the case goes on. But there are no public funds to keep you alive in prison; therefore I should have to keep you myself, which I cannot afford to do. Therefoie I ais- charge you."

' Kidnapping—a boy asleep. • iCapital fellows—Millionaires. EQUAL TO THE OCCASION.—III a Paris police-court. Judge: "You are charged with being a tramp and a beggar. Have you no trade ?" Prisoner: "Excuse me, your honour, I shovel snow." Judge: "But it is not winter now. What do you do in the summer?" Pri- soner: "I wait for winter to come again, your honour." ALL THE DIFFERENCE.—A well-known land-agent was recently showing some probable investors over a large building estate in the neighbourhood of London which he has for disposal. "Come on to this rising ground now," said he,. "and you can see about how the land lies." "Oh, no !" whispered an irrepressible wag who was present to some of the party. "Come and see how the land-acrent lies!" Mr. Charles Dudley Warner is a warm friend of the Rev. J. H. Twitchell, of Hartford, who has a large family of children, and enjoys a joke at his expense. Not long ago Professor Fiske was a guest of Mr. and Mrs. Warner, and, when speaking of their friend Mr. Twitchell, the professor asked, "How many children have the Twitchells now ?" "I don't know; we haven't heard from there I this morning," was Mr. Warner's reply. HomE, SWEET HOME !—A gallant officer just returned from Egypt had been apparently lost in thought for some minutes, when he suddenly started, muttered "By Jove!" and looked pleased. This outbreak of emotion in one who usually wore a calm exterior caused some one to offer a penny for his thought. Pocketing the penny, the warrior replied hesitatingly, "Well, the fact of the matter is it suddenly occurred to me that nothing was biting me i" A Scotch minister, while visiting the families con- nected with his congregation, began catechising a small , boy thus :—" Well, my boy, can you repeat the twenty- third Psalm ?" Boy: "Na, I canna say that," Minister "Wall, then, can you say the Lord's Prayer?" Boy: Na, I dinna ken it aither." Minister (quite shocked) : "Dear me! Can't you say a hymn or something ?" I Boy: "Ow, ; I can say a grace !" Minister: "Come, let us hear you then." Boy: " Wow ! Hoo can I say a grace enoo—whaur's the brose ?'' The following is a placard in the possession of a naval officer just returned from Egypt. He procured it at a cafe chantant in Alexandria. It was printed in several languages, and this is the English part :—" Every of the consummations of the coldness, one piastre besides. Every of the claim to be addressed directly of the direc- tion. During of the repetitions the price of consumma- tions to be the same that in every the other's coffee.' With the aid of the parallel passages in other languages, the meaning is found is follows :—" All iced drinks, one piastre extra. All complaints should be made at the office. Notwithstanding the performance, the changes will be the same as those of other cafes." Governor Brough was once matched against Corwin in an election for Congress, and, in the midst of his speech, said, "Gentlemen, my honoured opponent him- self, while he preaches advocacy of home industry, has a carriage at home which he got in England—had it shipped across the ocean to him. How is that for sup- porting home industry and labour ?" When Corwin came on the stand, he made a great show of embarrass- ment, stammered, and began slowly, "Well, e-entlemen, you have heard what my friend Mr. Brough has to say of my carriage. I plead guilty to the charge, and have only two things to say in my defence. The first is that the carriage came to me from an English ancestor as an, heirloom, and I had to take it. Again, I have not used it for seven years, and it has been standing in my back- yard all that time, and the chickens have converted it into a roost. Now, gentlemen,"—with a steady look at Brough—" I have nothing further to say in my defence; but I would like to know how Brough knows anything of my carriage if he has not been visiting my chicken- roost."

WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. A meeting of this Council was held on Tuesday evening in the Council Chamber, Town Hall. There were present Aldermen Holmes (in the chair in the absence of the Mayor), Burgess, Davies, Chaudley, Webster; Councillors Greening, Dixon, Barker, Francomb, Whittle, Jolley, Ashton, Bolton, Fleming, Tinsley, W. Pierpoint, J. Pierpoint, Mackie, Wright, Roberts ; Messrs. Brook (town clerk), Whittle (assis- tant town clerk), Dr. Gornall (medical officer), Long- din (borough surveyor), and Chorley (borough trea- surer).

WATCH AND FINANCE COMMITTEES. The minutes of the Watch and Finance Committee., which contained simply orders for payment of accounts', were passed without discussion. STREET COMMITTEE. The Street Improvement and Lighting Committee recom- mended that the following plans be approved :—Plan of al- terations to heuse in Beweey-st., for Mr. Forster ; extension to soap works, Bank Quay, for Messrs. Lever Bros.; additien to house in Stamford-street, for Mr. Naylor ; sculleries to six houses in Tanners-lane, for Mr. F. J. Carlisle ; bake- house in yard off Winwick.street, for Mr. Thomas Sudlow. The committee also recommended that a resolution, that the plan showing the position of three poles of land off Peter- Meet for the Lancashire and Cheshire Telephonic Exchange Company, Limited, be approved subject to payment of an acknowledgment. Councillor Dixoer moved and Alderman CIIANDLEY se- conded the adoption of the minutes. Alderman BURGESS asked as to the amount of the ac- knowledgment to be paid by the Telephonic Exchange Company. Mr. CHORLEY : Five shillings per annum. The CHAIRMAN said the transaction was not completed yet. The minutes were then passed. SANITARY COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee contained the following items :—llesolution, that the tender of Mr. Matthew Chor- ley, for painting, colouring, &c., house at Longford Depot, at £8 10s, be accepted. Resolution, that the slim of £5 2s 6d be allowed John Buckley, as compensation for five pigs slaughtered by order of this committee. lc solution, that Owen Warner be appointed engineer at Longford Depot, and be paid 383 per week, he being allowed in consideration of his watching and looking after the premises to live in the house at the Depot rent free. Resolution, that the whole of the Borough be declared infected with swine fever, and that the following regulations be made and put in force Within the Borosigh :-1. Theis regulations shall commence and take effect from and immediately after the eighth day of September instant, and shall continue in force until the fifth day of October next, unless sooner revoked or altered by the Local Authority of the Borough of Warrington, 2. No swine shall be moved into the Borough of Warrington from the district of any other Local Authority unless a movement license be first obtained, which shall only be granted on a declaration being made ley the owner or his agent to the following effect : (1) That such swine has not been elsewhere than on the farm or lands from which the movement is to be made during 28 days immediately prece- ding the date of the application for the licence. (2) That swine fever has not existed on such farm or lands, or on any adjoining farm or lands. (3) That such swine has not been exposed in any market, fair, exhibition, or public sale within the said 28 days. The foregoing regulations shall not restrict the movement of swine by railway through the Borough of Warrington. N.B.—Licences may be obtained from Inspector Norman, at the Town Hall, who will also supply forms of declaration above mentioned. Alderman BURGESS moved, and Councillor GREENING seconded, the adoption of the minutes. Councillor Dowel moved as an amendment that the minutes be confirmed with the exception of that one having reference to the appointment of Owen Warner as engineer at Longford depot. He (Councillor Dixon) was given to understand that this man had been in the employ of the Sanitary Committee some time ago and was discharged, and as at the present moment they had no machinery ruffling at a high speed he failed to see any need for the appoint- ment. Ant 4 besides he thought there were plenty of men in Warrington who could be got to do what was required at the Longford works. He also understood that Warner be- longed to a firm in Nottingham, and he thought the sooner the knot between that firm and Warrington was cut the better. He ',Councillor Dixon) had been under the impres- sion when he saw the word " engineer "that a mistake had been made; he thought it ought to have been the appoint- ment of a nurse, just to nurse the machinery until a certain time got over. (Laughter.) Councillor Joliet PIERPOINT seconded the amendment. It did appear to hint that 38s a .week and house rent free was a very high sum to pay, and therefore he thought it was a matter that should be discussed, so that they could get the necessary points of information. Councillor Macsta said something had been said about the man being connected with the firm who supplied the machinery, and he should like to know if that was not one particular element in favour of his appointment. He knew it was a common thing that when valuable machinery was purchated and brought to a distance some one who under- stood it was put in charge, at least for a" time. Councillor GREENING said be did not know before that I night that Owen Warner had formerly been in the employ of the Sanitary Committee and bad been discharged for something he had done. However that might be he was one of those who thought that when they had got expen- sive machinery fixed up in a proper manner, and they wanted it kept in good repair they ought to have a man in charge who knew eomething about it. (Hear, hear.) This was a practical man, and he held that it was an important thing for the Borough that the Longford works should be well conducted. (Hear, hear.) Councillor WHITTLE was of opinion that £1 18s. would not pay this man; he was a show man who went round to explain things to deputations, and to Alderman Burgess who had already spent so many thousands of pounds. (Laughter.) Councillor BARKER was sorry that Cauncillor Dixon had used the language he had done about a man who was not present to defend hinase:f. He was one of the Com- mittee who asked Warner to send in his resignation, which was sent ie. But now it was requisite that an eng:ieeer should be appointed for the Longford works, applications were sent in amongst which there was one Irons Warner, and he (Councillor Barker) certainly thought he ought to be the fittest man to look after the machinery. Councillor BOLTON asked why Warner had been dis- charged. Councillor W. PIERPOINT had no doubt that Warner had an extensive knowledge of the machidery, bu; he (Coun- cillor Pierpoint) had such a poor opinion of the machinery that he really thought they ought to have a man who did not know very much about it. (Laughter.) It was a
THE EXAMIN E sATU RD AN. SEPTEMBER 11, 1886.

[singular fact that since they had this machinery tke I receipts for manure at Longford were leas in amount each year. They were receiving— The CHAIRMAN (interrupting): You had better confine yourself to the case of Mr. Warner. Councillor PIERPOINT : I have finished. (Laughter.) Alderman CHANDLEY thought it was a question whether the man was competent to perform his duties, and if he was ; whether it was neceesary to give him in that capacity such , a high rate of wages. It did appear to him that the wages • would amount, with the howe rent free, to something lika 445. or 455. per week, and if he was simply a man to look after the running of the machinery it occurred to him that a man quite competent could be got for less wages. Councillor ROBERTS thought that the Council having sanctioned a large expense in reference to the putting up of machinery at Longford, it would be unwise to withdraw •confidence from the committee on a matter like the present. Tne Council had already swallowed the camel in the matter of expanse, and it was now straining at a gnat. It did ap• • pear to him that the Sanitary Committee Was on its trial at the present time—(hear, hear,)—and it would be a mistake to refuse to sanction this recommendation, to which so much importance was attached by the committee. Alderman BURGESS said with reference to that appoint- ment there did appear to be something on the minds of ,a few gentlemen on that Council. It was not a question of , Owen Warner; there was something more behind it. It had not come out that night, but one night it would come out, and then he would be prepared to meet it. (Hear, hear.) Alderman Burgess then defended the appointment of Owen Warner. some gentlemen. he said, objected to the high wage, but it was very much less than they got for very much less work. (Laughter.) He was told that this was not an excessively hili price, and that if they wented a ccmpeteat practical man thcy wuuld 124tve to pay that prloe, With ieferEnoe to the house Mr. Warner was to live in, his going to live there was an obligation to the commit- tee, for very few men of his position would care to live in a house like that on any terms. The reason he lived there was that some one was needed to leek after the works at nights and on Sundays. He should conclude by saying that they had, as nearly as possible, completed the works. One of the depots which they had been waiting for would be completed next week, and the whole of the works would then be ready for inspection. As soon as they were ready he should take care that every member of the Council was • invited to see them for themselves, and don't let them take anybody's statement. If the committee had misled them let them have the blame, but if they bad not misled them they should not attempt to thwart the committee. (Hear, hear.) If there was to be any blame he was prepared to take the whole of it. On the suggestion of the seconder, Councillor J. PIER- POINT, Councillor DIXON then withdrew his amendment, and the minutes were passed. PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE. . The minutes of this Committee contained the following: —Resolution, that the following apportionment for the paving of Thynne-street be approved :—Williarn Chantrev, £26 18s 2d; Thomas Fletcher, £67 7s 9d ' • William Uns- worth, XS 14s 4; George S. Allen, £9 532 d •, John Long- shave, £2l 7s 10d: Ashton and Woods, £32 10s 2d; Wil- liam Richard Hill, £6 19s 4d; William Richardson, £5 4s 5d ; William Parsons. £5 4s sd; John C. Spinks, £5 4s lid; John Emson, £5 5s 6d ; Isaac Leeson, £5 4s lid ; Thomas Porter, £5 53 ; William Throssell, £5 Ga Od ; Charles Ashurst, £5 6s Od ; Jos. Lawless, £5 5s 6d ; James Muir, £l7 5s o,i ; William Burn, £22 us 7d ; Total, £260 6.3 6d. Resolution that the sewer in Lilford-street be continued to the north end of Mr. Howes' property in Hoyle-street. On the motion of Alderman DAVIES, seconded by Coun- cillor ASHTON, the minutes were confirmed.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCIL The minutes of the School Attendance Committee con- tained the following :—Report of the Inspector that 94 cases had been enquired into by the Board of Guardians, and school fees allowed in 88 cases for 200 children. That 10 cases had been taken before the magistrates, and fines in- flicted in 6 cases. 1 ordered to the Workhouse. and 3 to the ship "Clio." 38 cases were brought before the Committee and dealt with. The average attendance at the different Public Elementary Schools during the month of July was 7,218; corresponding period last year, 6,843; increase, 375. On the motion of Alderman WEBSTER, seconded by Councillor FLEMING, the minutes were passed.

MUSEUM, LIBRARY, AND ARTS COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee were proposed tor adop- tion by Alderman WEBSTER, seconded by Councillor W. PIEHPOINT.—Thev contained a return for July, from which it appeared that the visitors to the museum in that month had been 1,573, the books iseued in reading-room 1,124, and those issued to subscribers 1,456. The Curator reported to the committee the receipt of the following gifts :—From Mr. Percy Davies, 10 eggs of guillemot, drc. ; Mr. J. G. Carter, Colorado beetles and grasshoppers, from Illinois ; Professor Piazzi Smyth, three pamphlets; Mr. R. Pierpoint, "Notes and queries," for 1885, two vols. ; Mr. 'l. Glazebroek Rylands, F.S.A. " Antiquarian Magazine," two vols. ; The Local Book Fund. Lewis', " Materia Medica," Warriugton, 1784, Law's "Serious Call." Prescot, 1806 ; Mr. Beamont. ordnance maps; 29 sheets, parcel of letters, parcel of rub- bings from brasses ; The Cobden Club, " Cobden's politi- cal writings " ; The Provincial Newspaper Society, a pam- phlet; Mr. F. W. Monks, "Report on ;he fauna of Liver- pool Bay." 18O; Mr. G. W. Shrubsole, "Catalogue of Roman stones in the Grosvenor Museum," Chester, 1886 ; Mr. J. Rose, his "Notes on fairs," Leigh, 1886; The Liter- ary and Philosophical Society proceediugs, 1885-6 ; The Owens College," Studies from the biological laboratories," vol. i., 1886; annual reports of the free libraries at Stock- port and Birkenhead. Alderman DAVIES said that he thought the attention of the Council should be called to the extraordinary increase in the number of books issued in the reading-room (50 per cent as compared with July last year.) There was a de- crease of 18 per cent in the number of visitors to the museum. They should congratulate themselves on the increase of the books issued in the reading-room, which must be much appreciated. • Councillor WHITTLE thought that about the worst feature of the whole affair. To him, he said, it clearly indicated that there was no work for the people, and they went to the reading-room to occupy their time. Alderman WEBSTER said that, assuming that to be cor- rect, it was the best thing that could happen that there should be places provided for the people to go to. The institution itself became every year more useful. The minutes were then passed.

CEMETERY COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee included the report of the registrar that the interments for the past five weeks were : Adults 39, minors 47, stillborn and premature 9; and for the corresponding period last year : Adults 28, minors 59, and stillborn and premature 12. The receipts for the past five weeks were £74 12s 9ci ; and for the corresponding period last year £66 68. The minutes were confirmed on the motion of Councillor J. Preete.ouer, seconded by Councillor ASHTON. TOWN HALL, FLEX, AND BATHS COMMITTEE. This committee reported that the income from the Baths for the past six weeks was £43 Os 81, and for the corres- ponding period last year £45 18s 6d. There were also reso- lutions that Mr. Richardson be requested to report upon the general laying out of the gardens and recreation ground ; that the first class plunge bath be appropriated for the use of ladies the whole of each Thursday ; that Mrs. Old- ham, of Leigh, be allowed the use of the swimming bath for one hour every Thursday; that six seats be ordered for the park; anti that the sum of £6 be voted for the purchase of hyacinth and other bulb?. A motion that the minutss be confirmed was proposed by Alderman WEBSTER, seconded by Alderman .CHANDLEY. Alderman WEBSTER, referring to the motion respecting the general laying out of the gardens and recreation ground, said that it was simply a suggestion. Some of the members thought that the recreation ground might be laid out a little more ornamentally. He did not know that much would come of it, but it was now receiving consideration. Many things required doing in the grounds, and they were sadly in want of sheltering places. (Hear, hear.) Councillor FRANCOMB asked if the walk in the Park would be finished between now and Christmas? Ten or twenty yards had been done within the last few months. Councillor BOLTON thought that the work would be done almost at once if the Sanitary Committee would allow the Surveyor a little more time. Alderman WEBSTER replied that there was the question of expense to be considered with regard to finishing the walks rapidly. They were being dune as economically as possi- ble. As the weather got colder, and the influx of visitors decreased, the wales would be proceeded with more rapidly. The minutes were passed. MARKETS COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee, which reported the total income from all sources as being £419 17s 11d, were approved without discussion on the motion of Alderman CHANDLEY, seconded by Councillor JOHN PIERPOINT. GAS COMMITTEE. The minutes of the Gas Committee comprised a resolu- tion that the tender of Messrs. Bournes and Robinson for the supply of 4,000 tons of cannel be accepted; and resolu- tions that the following tenders be accepted :—Messrs. Evans and Co., 5,000 tone of coal; Messrs. The Liarswood Hall Collieries Co., 6,000 tons of coal; Messrs. Pearson Sz Knowles Coal and iron Co.. Limited, 3,000 tons of coal; Messrs. John Brown & Co., Limited, 2,000 tons of coal. The minutes were confirmed on the motion of the CHAIR- MAN seconded by Councillor WRIGHT. GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE.—THE TOWN CLOCK. This Committee had approved the fellowing estimate of expenditure by the Committee for the half-year ending March 25th, 1887, namely; On Borough rate account : Maintainence of beilding; £5O 03 01; rent of open space. Howley, £l9 3s 8d ; sundries, £75 Os 0,1; Municipal Elec- tion Expenses, inclusive of Overseers, Revising Barrister, and Town Clerk's Charges and Expenses in connection with Lists of Voters, £270 Os 0.1; total, £414 3s &I. On Im- provement /tate Account: Half-year's care of frinity and other clocks. £1 Sc Od ; Gas to illuminate dial of ditto, £l5 03 ; New dials for ditto, say £5O Os 01 •, Sundries, £2O Os Od ; totale£B6 5s ; in all. £5OO 8s 81 Mr. F. W. Reynolds, writing from Dalby Villas, Latchford, in a letter which. was entered on the minutes, said :—" About three months ago Mr. Longdin told me that the General Purposes Committee (so I think he called it) had decided not to put new dials to the Town Clock, which is much to be regretted. However, if the old dials are not to be re- placed they ought to be coated behind with some kind of paint or whitewaeh which will not pQel off. The state the dials have been in for full six months past is really dis- creditable to the town. Tee coating Mr. Joyce pat on them just before Christmas bad all peeled off the upper ~part of the dials in three months (caused by the moisture

, condensed from the burning gas), but it still remains on the lower parts. I don't know what Mr. Joyce used, but I think whitewash mixed with size might stick. Opal glass dials would however obviate the necessity of any coating (which must be done periotlically whatever is used)and they would look far better, and show the time better, especially by day. The present dials have no minute graduations en them, and are very ugly looking. The clock is worth the best dials that could be made. I have had the sole ' charge of it for two years and have therefore watched it closely. Since • May it has not varied more than three or four seconds in any one week and often much less. It will not vary five s:•cor,ils a month sometimes, andl has not been more than 10 seconds wrong for 15 months, excepting on two occasions when it was thrown wrong by mismanagement on the part of the winder, and the two oc- casions when it stopped—(lst) for want of oil, and (2nd) because Rigby allowed it to run down. A set of new dials would be a compliment to Mr. Crostleld, and a mark of ap- preciation of his valuable gift.", The committee resolved that the sum of .£5O be included in the estimate for the ensuing half' year, for the purchase of new dials for tee town clock. The following report of the borowgh auditors was ordered to be entered on rtie minutes. It was dated Bewsey Chambers, Warrington, June 17th, 1886, and was to the Finance Committee. It said :—Gentlemen,—We have completed the audit of the borough tret-surees accounts for the year ended 25th March last, and regret that we have had toitake exception to an item of £6 14s 6d charged upon the borough fund in respect of the Mayor's expenses in connec- tion with the Jubilee Banquet of Municipal Corporations. We wrote his Worship on the 3rd instant inlinating our ob- jection to the payment, but have received no reply, and are conseqeently not in a posirion to sign the account relating tn the borough fund. In all other resptCs the accounts are In our opill!On, coirce and in order.—Yours faithfully (signed) John Harrison and J. L. lunsrall, F.C.A., elec- tive auditors. The committee reported that the subject of the Mayor's expenses referred to was considered at its last meeting and disposed of.

SUDDEN DEATH OF A CLERGYMAN. -- Dueng a violent storm which raged throughout North Staffordshire on Saturday night the Rev. Richard Locke. vicar*? Darling- ton, near Stone. was walking, when a flash of lightning caused him to remit and fall senseless to the ground. He never recovered consciousness, and died shortly afterwards. Mr. Locke was 64 years old, and one of the best known clergymen in the county, holding the vicarages of Alton and Darleston.

DEATH OF Mn. SAMCEL MORLEY.—Mr. S. Morley died at his London residence at half-past twelve on Sunday morning. He was attacked soon after ten o'clock on Satur- day morning with faintness, from which he never rallied. Mr. Morley had been ill for many weeks, and some time ago his speedy demise was feared. He, however, survived his acute attack, and from time to time was reported to be making some progress towards recovery, but his long ill- ness at his advanced age gave rise to serious apprehensions, which, unhappily, have been realised. "Men of the Times" says :—Samuel Morley, M.P., youngest son of the late Mr. John Morley, of Hackney, by Sarah, daughter of the late Mr. R. Poulton, of Maidenhead, was born In Wells- street, Hackney, in 1809. He received his Education at a private school, and was introduced early into business. He is now head of the firm of J. and R. Morley, wholesale hosiers. et Wood-street, city. An earnest Dissenter, Mr. Morley has been throughout his public career, both in and out of Parliament, a leading champion of the cause of Pro- testant Nonconformity, which he has promoted by muni- ficent donations for building new chapels. He is treasurer of the college at Homerton, and of the Home Missionary Society. Many years ago, in order to forward the work of the last-named society, he, in conjunction with the Rev. J. H. Wilson, visited most of the counties in England and Wales, held conference meetings, and introduced a new or- der of agency. consisting of " lav evangelists " and colpot- teurs. Towards defraying the cost of the Congregational or Memorial Hall in Farringd6n-street, Mr. Morley contributed £6,000, and his portrait, painted by Mr. Wells, HA, has been placed in the library of that instution, which was founded as a memorial of the 2,000 clergymen of the Church of England who resigned their benefices in the the reign of Charles 11. because they could not conscien- tiously subscribe to the Act of Uniformity. Mr. Morley represented Nottingham in the advanced Liberal interest from July, 1865, till May, 1866, when he was unseated on petition. He first came forward as a candidate for Bristol, on the retirement of Sir Morton Pato, in May, 1868. He lost the election by 195 votes, the numbers being 5,173 for Mr. Miles, and 4,997 for Mr. Morley. Mr. Miles was un- seated en petition in the ensuing June, and Mr. Morley again presented himself as a candidate. At the general election of December, 1868, he defeated his old opponent Mr. Miles, by more than 2,000 votes, and he continued to be one of the representatives of Bristol down to last Novem- ber. Mr. Morley married, in 1841, Rebekah Maria, daugh- ter of Mr. Samuel Hope banker, of Liverpool. div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LoNDON, THURSDAY.

The great and moving drama of "Kidnapped Prince and the Omnipotent Czar "was fitly brought to a conclusion yesterday by the departure of Prince Alexander from Sofia. No play of ancient or modern origin has been better composed for the stage Lnaethis episode in real life. It has been throughout a series of surprises. The kidnapping, the carrying off, the halt, the release, the temporary disappearance from human ken, the return journey, the re-entry of Sofia, the announcement of abdica- tion, and now the final departure through streets thronged with a weeping population—this is enough to make Mr. Druryolanus Harris green with envy. If he had only thought of it first and put it on the stage at Drury-lane what A Run of Luck he would have had! But the Czar, a mightier stage- master was before him, and has carried the play out with a precision, brilliancy, and success that leaves nothing to be desired, except, perhaps, the due ' punishment of the villain of the piece. Here we touch the real genius of the conception regarding it as a dramatic work. The hand which pulls the strings remains throughout unseen. Everybody knows whose it is and from what point it works; but it never openly manifests itself. When the Prince returns his domestic enemies are overthrown, and the whole nation crowd round him with cries of welcome. It seen at incredible that his next move should be voluntary abdication. But there is evidently a power behind the throne of Bulgaria mightier than the throne itself. In obedience to its directions, the Prince was kidnapped, in his own palace, in the centre of his capital. In defiance of that power he returned, and in even more abject submission to it he, after a brief struggle, retires. The House of Commons, having subjected Lord Randolph Churchill, is getting forward with its work with moderate speed. Lord Randolph last week tried a tall with the House and was himself heavily thrown. He attempted to treat it as he treated Sir Stafford Northcote, and as he still con- ducts himself towards Sir Michael Hicks-Beach and his other colleagues. Put he found it would not do, and he had the good sense to capitulate. He dropped his hectoring tone and broke his resolve not to join in discussions raised on various points by members opposite. He went further and pur- chased the goodwill of the Parnellites, by promising to provide their leader with an opportunity of bring- ing in his new Land Bill. Herein Lord Randolph has created for himself fresh difficulties and raised up new adversaries. What pleases Mr. Parnell does not coincide with the views of many influential Conservatives, and has offended the sensibilities of Lord Hartington. The dissentient Liberals gave their support to the Government on the understand- ing that there should be no parleying with the Par- nellites. Now, Lord Hartington declares that Lord Randolph has broken the engagement' and has truckled to the common enemy. There have been interviews and, it is said, recriminatipn. But nothing serious is likely to come of it. The Con- servatives will oppose Mr. Parnell's bill whatever it may be, and with that assurance the dissentient Liberals are fain to be content.

The Irish members are hopeful that Mr. Gladstone will return to give them a helping hand. Tney are prepared, if necessary, to keep things going in Committee of Supply till it is convenient for Mr. Gladstone to be in his place. Mr. Gladstone, has as yet, made no sign, and those in his counsels do not believe that he will intervene at the present time. If this be the case, the sooner the fact is formally communicated to the . Irish members the better it will be for the progress of public business. _ _

It is curious to note how completely Conservative detestation of Mr. Bradlaugh has disappeared, at least as far as outward manifestation is concerned. 'To hear the way they talked Of him, whilst yet he stood at the door of the House, it might have been supposed that they would have found it impossible not alone tdkhold communication with him, but to sit in the same chamber with him. To do the Con- servatives justice, when their grime was played out, they frankly accepted the situation, and Mr. Brad- laugh is treated by them exactly as any other mem- ber of the House. Perhaps it is more exact to say that he receives an exceptional amount of deferen- tial attention. He is always listened to, and Con- servative members who follow him in debate rarely omit to deal with his remarks. Mr. Brad- laugh, on his-part, makes an unexceptional member. He does not thrust himself incessantly upon the attention of the House. But he is always in his place, votes in nearly every division, and says the right thing at the right time. When the Courts meet again next month society will have a fresh sensation in a great divorce case. It will be remembered that some time ago Lady Colin Campbell petitioned for separation from her husband, the case being heard in camera. Now Lord Colin Campbell has laid a petition for divorce alleging adultery against his wife. There are no less than three co-respondents, each well known to fame. The Duke of Marlborough figures almost as a matter of course. The second co-respondent is Colonel Butler. husband of Miss Thompson, painter of "The Roll Call." The third is Captain Shaw, chief of the Metropolitan Fire Brigade, whom it is a little astonishing to find in this gallery. Briefs have been delivered and an enormous amount of evidence has been accumulated. On the part of the defendant and co-respondents the charge is indig- nantly denied, and the war is likely to be carried into the enemy's country. Evidence will be given alleging :that since the former legal proceedings Lord Cohn Campbell has pursued his -wife with a series of persecutions almost sufficient to drive a woman to desperation. Lady Colin Campbell was i well known n society as Miss Gertrude Blood. She is a very handsome woman, of lively manners, and with considerable gifts.. Since this unfortunate quarrel began, Lady Colin Campbell has turned her attention to journalism. She is, I believe, on the regular staff of the "Saturday Review,' which has always affected the collaboration of clever women. The House of Commons has changed a good. deal since Mr. Fawcett first took his seat. But in one particular precise resemblance is curiously main- tained. In Mr. Fawcett's early Parliamentary days a blind man sat in the corner seat, just before the chair of the Sergeant-at-Arms. Ten years ago it was Mr. Fawcett. To-day it is Mr. Macdonald. There is a great rush for seats on the left of the Speaker, where, with adequate paradox, the larger moiety of the House of Commons sit in opposition. But the right of Mr. Macdonald to secure this favourite corner seat is not disputed, even by men like Dr. Tanner or Mr. Matt. Harris. Mr. Mac- donald is led in either by a member or one of the attendants, and is handed round the corner by the cross benches, where he feels his way into his seat. It is strikingly reminiscent of the olden times, when Mr. Fawcett used thus come in. But here the similitude ends. Mr. Fawcett was wont with an unflagging recurrence to rise from this quarter of the House and thunder forth anathema at some one. Mr.ir. i . Macdonald very rarely speaks. When he does it s n a quiet unagressive manner which did not belong to Mr. Fawcett in those days. Later, when he came to take his seat on the Ministerial Bench, the member for Hackney greatly improved in manner, and, though he always spoke in a -voice raised almost to the pitch of shouting, had changed his ag,ressiveness for a persuasiveness of tone that greatly added to the effect of his argument. Visitors to the lobby of the House of Commons will sometimes see a primly-dressed grey little elderly gentleman who carries an umbrella what- ever the season of the year may be. He walks straight up to the entrance of the House, peers in for a moment, and then walks through, taking his i umbrella with him. He s not a peer, and certainly is not a member nf the House. Yet he walks into pri- vileged places with quiet assumption of right that is never called into question by the attendants. i This is Mr. Disraeli, clerk at the table n the House of Lords, and brother of the late Lord Beaconsfield.

I have a copy of a sketch of Mr. Isaac D'lsraeli, by Maclise, done years ago for the portrait gallery of " Fraser's Magazine." One would almost know the present Mr. Disraeli by his likeness to his father, a likeness that extends not only to the face but to the person and carnage. The more famous inheritor of the name did not in the slightest degree resemble either his father or his brother. He was a man as plainly apart from his own family as he was from the average of mankind. The death of Mr. Samuel Morley will be seriously felt by an unknown number of charitable institu- tions and of needy individuals. With respect to the charities, Mr. Morley was almost equal to an additional Hospital Sunday. It is quite amazing to find of how many institutions, he was either presi- dent or vice president, or to which he was at least a regular subscriber. The last time I saw Mr. Mor- ley was in characteristic circumstances. It was on the Saturday before he took to the bed from which he will to-morrow be carried to his last resting place. It was at Charing Cross Station, where he was waiting for a frain to take him down on a visit to his. son in Kent. He told me he was going to stay till Monday. But, I learnt after, he was feel- ing so well whilst there that he remained till Thurs- day, when in returning to town he caught a chill, which was the beginning of the end. As we chatted, a nurse with a little child in her arms passed, and the child recognising, as children miraculously do, the goodness of the man, held out its arms to Mr, Morley and crowed with delight. He nodded and smiled at the child, patted its chubby cheek with his finger, and so the newly- made acquaintances parted. It is a peculiarity of. what is called Mr. Glad- stone's personality that whatever subject he talks about becomes the subject of the day. In politics, of course, this is intelligible enough. But it is true outside the range of political discussion. Just now it is the 25 bites of a bit of meat. I don't for a

moment believe Mr. Gladstone ever said anything so absurd or outrageous. If every guest at a din- ner party were to bite every piece of meat he eats 25 times, why, the dinner would last till breakfast time. But the attribution of this theory to Mr. Gladstone has brought forward for a topic of discussion the subject of indigestion, which is just the one ailment from which Londoners specially suffer. I am told there is no disease which has at once made and lost so many reputations amongst doctors as this of indigestion, and the rea- son is singular. There is no organ possessed by humanity which admits so many variations as the stomach. Now there are a certain number of recognised cures for this derangement. A doctor will sometimes hit on the right one first; some- times he will only reach it very late down in the catalogue of his specifics. And yet that will be attributed to skill, which is generally the result of chance. I heard one doctor say that the reason why Londoners suffer from indigestion more that country folk, and men more than women, is ' the Sunday dinner. The gastric juices are prepared to do their work at certain hours of the day and are extremely punctual. A man in the habit of dining at half-past seven is called upon once a week to eat a heavy meal at half-past one. He does so and reckons without his gastric juices and finds he has to pay the reckoning for the next few days. It is notorious that the English suffer more than any other nation from a derangement which is mainly due to unpunctuality and to bad cookery. There are those who like and those who abuse the French cuisine, but at least a French dinner is digestible. John Bull eats too much meat. All the doctors say so over and over again. The reason he does not eat vegetables is because, cooked as he gets them, they need those 25 bites, and he has not time to go through the process.. He bolts his pota- toes and suffers accordingly.

div.head: NEW TORYISM.
div.p: THE NEW TORYISM.

Sir,—How often de we bear our Tory friends protesting against evolution. Being mostly good sons of the Church. they nave some sort of a hazy idea that it is their duty to protest against anything in the shape of development, yet their every-day conduct proves them to be apt imitators of all that their opponents initiate. If this statement con- tained the whole truth we might rest satisfied, content to let matters slide along, knowing that the Tories, would, in their own good time, remove the brake: but it does not; and the experience of recent years has made it Clear that we pay dearly for the pleasure of educating the Tories. It would be a laborious task to gather and place before your readers, the various Acts of Parliament that have been opposed by the Conservatives. Since the repeal of tbe Corn Laws it seems to have been the duty of the Radicals to initiate, and agitate for measures to which the whole of the energies of the Whig and Tory factions have been united to resist—ab, even to the very point of revolution. Two men amongst the Tories stand out prominent as deter- mined not to be led by their more stupid supporters. I re- fer to Peel and, Disraeli. The former, with the help of Cobden, Bright, and the Liberal party, completely split up the Tory party by repealing laws that were reducing the populations of Lancashire towns to a state of absolute starvation. Sir R. Peel, for thus proving himself a true Englishman, earned the undying enmity of the country party, or antiquated Toryism. His downfall made an open- ing for one not at all slow to avail himself of the oppor- tunity. Disraeli, a true son of opportunism, stept jute the breach, and after fooling the Tories to the top of their bent, made himself so necessary to them that they were forced to confess thern.elves the stupid party and, acknowledging their ignorance, accept the greatest of modern political jugglers as their schoolmaster, bound hand and foot to take as many leaps in the dark as he might think desirable. The Liberal party has two wings, each useful in its way; the Radical party, full of that healthy energy which breathes of life, shows itself very restive at times, more especially when Whigism obtrudes its influence. Together the Whig and Radical wines have carried along the Liberal body in a fairly successful manner. The Tory body, a one- winged, spluttering and fluttering party, is now feeling the inconvenience of having a brutal and bigoted section weigh- ing it down. Orangeism is to-day what it has always been. a sham and a fraud. In its arrogant pride it takes upon itself the right to control the conscience and opinions of others; trying to defend a Church, it makes that Church ridiculous. As the champion of religion, it brings religion into contempt. Championed in the House of Commons by a couple of Ulster fanatics, lookers on may see 'the difference between the cool and calculating Parnellite and the fighting Orangeman.

Toryism under Lord Randolph declares in favour of pro- gress, and quietly snubs Fair Traders. Determined to see which way the cat jumps, it sends Lord Harris to Manches- ter, and then in the House repudiates his statements. Efforts have been made to persuade the world that even working-men could be Tories. How foolish these efforts have 10-en cut be tested by any one who cares to question one of these curios. The present writer has at various times come across men who, as an outward and visible sign of their Toryism, would christen their children after one of Lord Beaconsfield's novels, or would take the great Tory leader's title itself to name a fishing boat with. These men fancy that a noble title or a Primrose badge are evidences to the world of their loyalty to their party, but if you go one step further, and question them on what should be their principles, what a falling off is there! One said quite recently—" Ab ! that Bradlaugh's doing some good work; we should never have objected to him if he hadn't said he would bring in a Bill to do away with the church." "Why, now, look here," I said," what is this church you are so frightened about ?" Is it right that vonr Bishops should have from £3.000 to £15,000 a year, while us poor fellows must work for 15s a week ?" Now mark the answer—" No, and I wouldn't let the Rector have £1.200 a year; he should have as much as I get, and no more." This is pretty fair for a Tory, and when I pointed out, that in voting for a Tory, he voted for a man who would perpetuate the system, he declared be did not, and went on to amsert, " that not only the Bishops, but Royalty and the Aristocracy should have all their screws reduced, so that us workingmen could have a chance."

Tories are annoyed, when they are called the "stupid party ;" surely this is stupidity. They poin to their vic- tories when it is asserted that there are no Tory working- men ; forgetting that, in ignorance, Toryism has its root, that in toadyism it flourishes, and in corruption and evad- ing the law, it cont.ives for a time to be successful. Lord Randolph knows well that the Tories must move, that standing still, or going back to Protection would never be tolerated. As to this, the Manchester Tories have just given him a few straight words. CLIFFORD DIX.
NEW CHAPEL FOR STOCKTON
BETH.

On Thursday afternoon the foundation stones were laid of a chapel to be erected at Stockton Heath, on a piece of land abutting on the Walto a-road. It is the undertaking of a congregation of worshippers who have for the past two years met at what is known as the Barn Chapel, and is not being built for the ac- o-nAalcdation of any particular denomination. The oong,rs?gatiou comprises those whose opinions attach to various Nonconformist creeds, but as, in a village like Stockton Heath, the population is not so nume- rous as to allow of each denomination being represented by a place of worship, a number of, the dissenters combine to worship in the same building. The Barn chapel was opened for divine worship on November 3rd, 1884, and gradually the number worshipping there increased. The chapel was in a dilapidated condition, and application was made to the owner for it to be renovated. The reply re- ceived was that it was the intention of the owner to pull down the building, but that the cosgregation could retain possession until they found another place suitable for their purposes. A subscription was started with the ultimate view of providing a new chapel. The outside public gave generous aid, and subscrip- tions came in freely. It had at first only been ex- pected to raise sufficient money with which to build an iron chapel, but as the success that accompanied the movement , exceeded the most sanguine expectations, a larger tnd more ' substantial building was decided upon. Mr. Perkins, archi- tect, Warrington, drew a sketch of a proposed building, which was submiated to four builders, and tenders were ' made out. That of Mr. Edward Rogers, of Warrington, being the lowest, was accepted. The tender is for the brick work,roofing,and fleoring. When that work is finished prices will have to be obtained for the provision of seata, and there will be other expenses, so that an exact estimate of the total cost can scarcely vet be arrived at. It is not, however, ex • pected to exceed £250. The building will seat 160 persons, and is to be built in the Gothic style. It will be known ae Ebenezer Chapel, and ministers of various denomi- nations are expected to occupy the pulpit. Mr. R. A. Nay- lor, who was unable to comply with a request to lay one of the stones, wrote to Mr. R. Miller, who has taken a great interest in the movement, offering a subscription. Mr. John Platt, J.P.. wrote wishing the undertaking success, and expressing the hope that the new chapel would be a blessing to the neighbourhood, and a letter from the Rev. J. H. Jones also wished success to the enterprise. The stone- laying ceremony commenced shortly before four o'clock, among those present being the Rev. W. R. Parry (Cock- hedge Mission, Warrington), the Rev. E, Moore ( Baptist, War- rington), Messrs: F. Dixon, H. Thornton, R. Miller, Arnold, Brown, Roscoe (Warrington), J. Knowles (Lymm), &c. After there had been singing and prayer the Rev. W. H. Parry referred to the cause of the gathering. He was very pleased to be there to witness the laying of the fotinda- tion stones and to congratulate his friends upon the success that had attended their labour. He was told by those who knew that neighbourhood well that the chapel was much needed. Stockton Heath was a large district, and would probably greatly increase as soon as the Manchester Ship Canal was commenced. The life of the congregation at Barn Chapel had been one of conflict, not internal conflict, but a life of conflict with disadvantages and difficulties. Building chapels was rather an important undertaking, especially in these days of commercial depression, and to build them when they were not really wan- ted was a great waste of stfength and money. But to refuse to build when circumstances claimed was unquestienably a neglect of duty and a sin. (Hear, hear.) He was pleased to see that the chapel was to be a neat and nice one, not very large, but very pretty. He appealed for monetary aid, and hoped that it would be found possible to open the building free of debt.—Councillor DIXON then laid the first stone. Having done so, be made a few remarks. Many present, he said, could remember the time when chapels were not so numerous as now, and when educational institutions were also much less abundant. But at the same time they must feel that when a fresh chapel was built, it would raise and elevate the character of the ' district in which it had been erected. He could remember when to try and get a chapel for dissenting warship was a thing impossible, and they could not bat rejoice that many difficulties had been overcome for them by those who lived in former years. He heartily wished the promoters of the movement success.—Mr. H. THORNTON, after laying the second stone, gave a rather lengthy addrese, in the course of whioh he said he hoped that some time it would be found expedient to remove the stones in order to make extensions that would have been rendered necessary by the increasing prosperity of Ebenezer chapel.—The Rev. E. MOORE also offered bis congratulation, and hoped that the time would come when extensions would be necessary.—Subseauently a substantial tea was partaken of at the Barn chapel, and a public meeting was held in the evening.

HEAVY PENALTY FOR ASSAULTING A LANDLORD._ Wm. Mather, a collier, was, at St. Helens, on Frielay, charged with assaulting George Clare, landlord of the Union Inn, Cowley Hill. The defendant pleaded guilty. Mr. Garner (Messrs. J. 0. and W. Swift) appeared for the e.m.n. plainant, and stated that the defendant lived in the neigh- bourhood of the public-house which the complainant kept. On the previous Saturday night defendant went into the Union lan in a state of intoxication, and called for a drink. The landlord, seeing his condition, refused to serve him, whereupon the defendant became very abasive and wanted to fight with a man who was quietly sitting in the bar. The complainant requested him to leave, but he refused to do so, in consequence of which he took him by the arms, and, without using any unnecessary force, put him out of the house. The defendant then pulled complainant to the ground, and afterwards struck him a violent blow in the right eye. Mr. Clare returned to the house and shut the door, but the defendant burst it open, and again became very violent. He (Mr. Garner) thought that when a man had kept a public-house without any complaint for twenty- eight years he ought to be protected against such roughs as the defendant, and he hoped they would impose a substan- tial penalty.—The complainant confirmed Mr. Garner's statement.—The defendant was deed 40s and coats, or a month's imprisonment in default.

ALLEGED USE OF A GUN WITHOUT A LICENSE. Joseph Tinelev and Joshua Sumner, Moss Bank, pleaded guilty at St. Helens, on Monday, before Col. Gamble and Mr. H. S. Hall, of having used a gun upon Colonel Gamble's land without having a license. Mr. Thos. Heald, supervisor of tne Inland Revenue, appeared for the prosecu- tion. and said that on the 17th July the two men were seen by Colonel Gamble's gamekeeper shooting rabbits without having any license to do so. As Colonel Gamble was in- terested in the case and there was not a third magistrate present the case was adjourned until the 27th inst.
