ITAMILTON STREET NEW SCHOOLS. FOUNDATION STONE LAYING. On Thursday afternoon the foundation stone of the new schools which are in course of erection in , Hamilton-street, off Battersbrlane, Warrington, ' was laid by Mr. W. Beamont. The weather, though rather- breezy, was suitable for an occasion of the kind, and there was a large attendance. Amongst those present were Mr. and Mrs Beamont, Lady and the Misses Greenall, Alderman Crosfield, Alderman 'Holmes, Alderman Webster, the Revs. Morley Stevenson, E. J. Willcocks, S. Wilkinson, G. Allton, H. Gibson Smith, E. C. E. Carleton, J. A. Drummond, and Heath, Dr. Watkins, Messrs. R. Davies, W. Sharpe, R. W. Fra.ncomb, J. E. Wright, IL Isherwood, S. Davies, T. Cawley, J. Fairclough, T. Jolley, &c. These new schools, it may be ex- plained, have been rendered necessary by the in- adequacy of the Crossley-street school to meet the educational requirements of the neighbourhood. The Government inspector of schools for this dis- trict had reported that new elementary schools to accommodate about 500 children must be provided in or near to Battersby-lane to meet the wants of a large and increasing population, and conse- quently a committee was formed for the purpose of carryipg out the suggestion, as otherwise schools would probably have had to be provided through the compulsory actirn of a School Board. The War- rington Training College, being in need of practis- ing schools, offered to contribute £1,600 towards building and furnishing the new schools, provided they were permitted to use the same as practising; schools, and that an additional £1,400 was volun- tarily subscribed. The appeal of the committee has been liberally responded to, and already the build- ing fund, including the £1,600 of the Training Col- lege Committee, amounts to £3,200. It was origi- nally intended to find accommodation for 500 scholars, but the schools, as now designed, will accommodate 650, and it is estimated that the total cost will be about £4,000. The building when completed will be in the gothic style of architecture, and inside the girls' department will consist of a large room and two class rooms, and the boys' department of a large room and another compartment, which, by means of a revolving par- tition, can be divided into two class rooms. The lavatories, cloak rooms, &c., will be fitted up in the most approved style, and there will also be large playgrounds for the children. The building will be of red brick with stone dressings, and around the rooms there will be a glazed brick dado to the height of 41 feet. An excellently fitted up kitchen in which to teach the girls cookery will also be provided. The joint architects are Messrs. J. E. Wright and T. Beesley, of Warrington, and the builder Mr. Gibson, Church-street, Warrington. The building committee consists of the Rev. Archdeacon Barber (Chester), Canon Warr (Childwall, Liverpool), Canon McClure (Rochdale), Rev. J. W. Reynolds (St. Mark's, Cheet- ham, Manchester), Rev. Morley Stevenson, Rev. E. J. Willcocks, Dr. Watkins (Newton), Messrs. W. Beamont (chairman of committee), J. Fairclough. R. Fairclough, T. Cawley, R. W. Francomb, W. Brooks, James Morris, and R. A. Naylor; Mr. J. E. Wright /hon. sec). Mr. BR AMONT, before formally laying the stone, gave a short address. He should like, he said, to say a few words, because he should be able to tell them something that reflected great credit upon the town of Warrington. At the beginning of this cen-. tury there were no public schools, and all the edu- cation which the young had was to be obtained in private schools, which were above the means of the great bulk of the population. (Hear, hear.) In the year. 1839, the Bishop of Chester, whose diocese then included both Lancashire and Cheshire, at the in- stigation of the rector of this parish, the Rev. Mr. Powys, called a great meeting, and the meeting was held on the 25th April, 1839, forty-seven and a half years ago. At that meeting, at which he (Mr. Beamont) was present, there was a very large number of the inhabitants of both counties, and amongst them some of the most emi- nent men in the county who had espoused the cause they were gathered together to forward. There was present one of the most elo- quent speakers Lancashire or the kingdom had ever known, the late Lord Stanley, who afterwards came to be Earl of Derby, and he addressed the meeting in a most powerful speech, after the bishop had opened the proceedings by telling them that he had called that meeting for the purpose of bringing about a more general means of educating the people in the religion of the Church of England than had hitherto existed. A great number of speakers followed Lord Derby, and in the end resolutions were come to of a stringent character praying the legislature to introduce some means that would bring, education better within the reach of the great multitudes of the people. These resolutions passed, and went to the proper quarter in London, and they seemed to be not without effect, for from that date they might date the action of the Privy Council with regard to education, and they might also date the steps that were taken for the purpose of increasing the number of schools in which the bulk of the people might be educated. (Hear, hear.) He did consider that the holding of such a meeting in the town gave an impetus to the education movement, and they had a right to look with some pride upon the town in which such a movement originated. (Hear, hear.) They knew now that there were few places where edu- cation was so well attended to as in Warrington. (Hear, hear.) With regard to that school they might cast their eyes around and they would see a number of respectable houses that had risen up almost by magic, and in which there was already a population ready to take advantage of .the school. They could not have found a better situation for the school, and they could not have found a popu- lation more ready to take advantage of the school they were building. (Hear, hear.) He might say the reason why a school was wanted there was that there was an entirely new population in the neigh- bourhood, and a population which deserved" to have means taken for the education of its children. Everybody who knew the history of Warrington for the last few years knew that there had been an out- cry that if they did not provide new schools they would have to have a School Board, which was worse than a property tax. (Hear, hear, and laugh- ter.) In the school they were about to build, as good an education would be given as they could possibly desire, a better education he dare say than a great number of the people around him had ever known. Referring in detail to the education to be given in the school, Mr. Beamont said the girls would be taught cookery by an eminent expert, Mrs Thwaite, who, he believed, could carry the cookery to any extent. She could even cook a course for the vegetarians, if required. (Laughter.) The vegetarian diet was as old as the prophet Daniel, of whom a poet told them— Daniel ate pulse by choice, example rare, Heaven blessed the youth, and made him fresh and fair. —(laughter)—and he believed there was a good deal more of nourishment in vegetables than many people supposed. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. BEAMONT then proceeded to lay the founda- tion stone, being presented with a handsome silver trowel and a small mallet for the purpose. This over, Mr. J. E. WRIGHT announced that he had received several letters of apology from gentlemen for non-attendance, amongst which was one from Lord Winmarleigh, in which was enclosed a cheque for £l5O, £lOO towards the building fund, and £5O towards the expenses of the school when opened. , The letters of Archdeacon Bardsley, the Mayor, and Dr. Mackie were also read, the latter gentle- men promising a donation of £lO. Mr. R. DAVIES said he was glad to see present gentlemen who differed entirely from him in poli- tical feeling who came to show their interest in the great cause of education. (Hear, hear.) They did not, he said, wish to disassociate education from religion. (Hear, hear.) They believed that if there was anything in Christianity they should do their best to spread it, and it was by the institution of establishments of that sort which imprinted their lessons upon the minds of the young that they sought to accomplish that end. On that occa- sion he congratulated Mr. Beamont on having attained to an age to see so many works flourish under his hand, and he congratulated his fellow- townsmen there assembled on the efforts which had been made to keep Warrington from having a School Board. (Applause.) The Rev. MonLEY STEVENSON, in the course of an address, explained the reasons that had led to the , building of that school, and the steps that had al- ready been taken towards that end. ITe mentioned that the Crossley-street schools •were now closed, and the scholars were being temporarily accommo- dated in a building in Naylor-street. He said tem- porarily because the rector of the parish who had kindly made that accommodation would only con- tinue it to the end of this year. When they started those schools they thought they shouldwant £3,000, but he was now very much afraid they should want £4,000, towards which they had got £3,200. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Stevenson also mentioned that since it became known that Mr. Beamont was to lay that foundation stone the people of the neighbourhood had subscribed their pence and bought a beautiful bible to present to him to show their respect to one

who had done so much for education in. Warring-1 ton. (Applause.) Miss BOYLE then came forward, and, on behalf of the subscribers, presented the Bible to Mr. Beamont, the latter suitably acknowledging the gift. Alderman JOHN CILOSFIELD said he had been asked to move a vote of thanks to their worthy and esteemed townsman, Mr. Beamont. He did not think any town in England had an inhabitant who was so respected as Mr. Beamont was in Warring- ton. (Hear, hear.) And he was deservedly re- spected. His whole life had been devoted to the good of the people. He (Mr. Crosfield) held that no man and no woman could perform a greater charity to people than to promote education, and he was proud that Warrington stood as she stood to-day in the front rank of the towns of England, inasmuch as of her free voluntary will she had erected the schools that have been .necessary to teach the chil- dren. (Hear, hear.) As his friend, Mr. Davies, re- marked, the credit was not due to any particular sect; it belonged to Churchmen and it belonged to Dissenters, as they had all put their shoulder to the wheel and maintained their schools. He hoped and trusted that he should never live to see the day when there would be a School Board in Warrington— (applause)—and he would do his best, as far as his means would allow him, to prevent any such curse coming upon the town. (Applause and laughter.) Mr. Beamont was not only respected, but he was loved by the people of Warring- ton. He (Mr. Crosfield) remembered that when he was a boy, five and forty years ago, his father said there was no man in Warrington he re- spected like Mr. Beamont. Mr. Beamont's life had been a noble example for every one of them, and let them all try to :emulate the example he had set them. (Applause.) He (Mr. Crosfield) rejoiced to be with them there that day in that ceremony, and he was thankful of opportunities when they could sink their political and religious differences and join together in doing a grand and noble Christian work. (Applause.)
, Dr. WATKINS seconded the proposal, ..the vote of thanks was passed, and three cheers given for Mr. and Mrs. Beamont. The proceedings then ended.
CRICKET.—At the drawing of stumps the South of Eng- land's score against the Australians was 90 for four wickets.
It is stated in Paris on high authority that reinforcements are being sent to Madag4scar, owing to the unsatisfactory state of affairs in the island.

Accordiug to special advices from Madrid, it appears cer- tain that the Queen Regent, like her hustmnd, the late King Alfonso, is suffering with pulmonary disease, which is mak- ing alarming progress. _
The ' Gazette " announces that her Majesty has con- ferred the decoration of the Imperial Order of the Crown of India upon Viscountess CfOA3, wife of the Secretary for India.

A preliminary inquiry in the Buckrose (Yorkshire) elec- tion petition shows that whereas Mr. Christopher Sykes has only one doubtful voting paper, Mr. McArthur has eleven. It is therefore probable Mr. Sykes will be declared elected. This wciuld be a gain of one seat to the Conservatives. MANSLAUGHTER —At Uxeridge on Friday a coroner's jury returned a verdict of manslaughter against William Bell, blacksmith, of Fulmer, and William Bell, of Gerrard's Crops, his son, who are alleged to have kicked William Phillips awl struck him with the butt end of a whip with the result that Phillips died. RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT BELFAST.—On Thursday night a serious accident occurred at Belfast terminus of the County Down Railway. A passenger train while entering the sta- tion ran into art engine, smashing the tender and seriously damaging the first composite carriage. Many of the pas- sengers were injured, acme being removed to the hospital, but no deaths have been reported. A. LUCKY WINDFALL.—, furnace man named William Pottney, employed at Tunstall Furnaces, Staffordshire, has just received information that frosts unforeseen circum- stances he has become entitled to a large estate in the south-west of England. comprising over 1,000 acres, to- gether with some £20,000 in money. The windfall is the more welcome since its recipient is a man with a large famil v.

ROYAL MARCHESTER, LiyitßpOOL, AND NORTH LANCA- SHIRE AGRICULTURAL SOClEry.—The show opened at Ches- ter on Friday morning in dull and threatening weather. Notwithstanding this, a great number of persons visited the grounds, the early morning trains having brought very heavy loads from many quarters. No rain had fallen up to noon, and the weather looked more bright and cheering as time went on. MI Thursday night and during the early hours of Friday morning rain cams down in torrents, but the ground was only affected slightly and temporarily. At the General Meeting of the society, held in the show-yard on Friday afternoon, a deputation invited the society to hold its show next year at Manchester. The invitation was accepted unanimously ; and a committee consisting of Lord Egerton, Messrs. Hale, Lonsdale, Rigby, Smith, Scotson, and Weaver, were appointed to make the necessary arrange. meets.

ACCIDENT TO inc EXPRESS TRAIN.-011 Friday morning an accident happened to the ten o'clock London and North- Western Railway express train from the Exchange Station, Manchester, for Wigan, Preston, and the north. Soon after passing Tyldesley the passengers detected a smell as of burning, and clouds of steam were seen escaping from the engine. The train was brought to a standstill, when it was discovered that one of the boiler pipes had burst. The fire- box was immediately emptied of its contents, and all the water and steam was soon out of the boiler. The guard of the train went back to Tyldesley, and another engine was procured, which took the passengers to Wigan. The driver of the damaged engine said that if he had not been pro- vided with an excellent brake the train could not have been brought to a stand so speedily as it was, and something serious might have happened. The men on the engine were drenched and almost blinded with steam, but fortunately escaped serious injury. At Wigan a fresh engine was at- tached, ard the train proceeded on its journey. FUNERAL OF THE LATE Mn. S, MORLEY.—The remains of the late Mr. Samuel Morley were interred on Friday after- noon at Abbey Park, Cemetery, London. Most of the wholesale drapery warehouses in Cheapside, St. Paul's Churchyard, Cannon-street, and other parts of the City of London displayed mourning boards in their windows on the occasion. Rain was falling very heavily at half-past twelve o'clock, the time the funeral procession started from deceased's residence in Grosvenor-street, and consequently the attendance of spectators was limited. Another telegram states : The remains of the late Samuel Morley were taken from his residence shortly before one o'clock on Friday for interment in the Abney Park Cemetery. The coffin was of plain oak. Prior to the departure, a special service was held in the study. Eleven carriages followed the hearse con- taining the chief mourners, among whom were the Rev. Dr.. Stoughton, Mr. Justice Denman, Mr. ' Hope Morley, Mr. Howard Morley, Mr. Charles Morley, Mr. Arnold Morley, M.P., Mr. John Morley, M.P., and Mr. W. W. Morley. Numberless wreaths and floral tributes had been sent to the house sufficient to fill one large carriage. The state carriages of the Lord Mayor and sheriffs followed in the cortege.

THE FIXING OF It tNTS.

Sir,—lt is said that one of the points Mr. Parnell intende to advocate in the bill he is about to bring into the House of Commons is that the rents of the Irish farmers should he fixed according to the average price of the produce of their farms. If this should be so it will be interesting to notice tbe arguments that will be used against such a proposal. When we consider the inconvenience, not to use a stronger term, tbat has been so often experienced through such fluc- tuating commodities as gold and silver being made the measure of value in all sorts of transactions, it is wonderful ' that some such device as that Mr. Parnell is said to favour in regard to rents has not been generally adopted long since. Had this been done those who are legally liable to the pay- ment of fixed sums over lengthened periods would have been relieved from many a hardship. This especially ap- plies to farmers who hold their lands on condition that they are to pay a fixed rent over a lengthened period. When they enter upon their farms the price they can sell their produce for is sufficient to cover their expenses and pay their rents, but if gold, in which they have to pay their rents, becomes appreciated, as it is liable to do, and is doing at present, their difficulties at once begin. Their farms may continue to produce as much as ever they did, but the produce does not exchange for as much gold as it used to do, while they have still the same number of pounds sterling to pay in rent. Were the rent or the value of the land measured in its produce, instead of in gold, as Mr. Parnell, we are told, is coin to propose, these diffi• culties would net be felt. If it were land that produced wheat, for eximole, the rent would be fixed, say, at the price of fifty bushels of wheat, and if wheat declined in price the money rent would decline in proportion ; but if on the other hand, the price of wheat rose the money rent would rise also. A better way still is that of Mr. Parnell, of taking the average of the principal products of land, in- stead of just one commodity like wheat, as the determinatar of rent. If a proposal of tl;s kind he contained in Mr. Parnell's coming Bill, the discussion upon the measure, whethcr it ends in acceptance or rejection, will have one good effect; it will show that the Irish members have a good deal of reason on their side.
JAQUES.

div.head: TRADES UNION CONGRESS'.
div.p: TRADES UNION CONGRESS'.

The Trades Union Congress at Hull, on Friday, passed a resolution in favour of the reintroduction of the Government Bill for efficient inspection of quarries. They then engaged in a long discussion on the evils of the overtime system, which was universally condemned as limiting the number of men in employment in. many trades. The Congress passed a resolution in the afternoon in favour of extending the Employers' Liability Act to seamen, and of representation of shipwrights on Marine Boards; and a resolution was passed in favour of the compulsory registration of properly qualified plumbers. The Congress resolved to accept the in- vitation received from the Corporation and trades of Swansea to hold its meetings next year in that town. Mr. Hemry Broadhurst, ALP., was unanim- ously elected Parliamentary secretary.

ARCTIC EXPEDITION. WINNIPEG, THIIRSDAY.—CoIoneI Gilder has started from this place on is expedition to the Arctic regions with the object of reaching the North Pole. CHOLERA IN ITALY. ROME, FRIDAY.—The cholera returns for the last 24 hours are as follow :—Torre del Annunziata, 9 cases, 2 deaths; Castellamare, 3 cases, 1 death; Putignano, 23 cases, 11 deaths; San Marco in Lamis, 8 cases, 6 deaths; San Gio- vanni "toted°, 3 cases, 1 death; Carrara, 4 cases, 2 deaths; Ravenna, 14 cases, 6 deaths; Ferrara. 16 cases, T deaths; Padua, 6 cases, 2 deaths; and Venice, 2 cases; .otal, 126.

PRINCE HENRY OF BATTENBERG. A Central News telegram says :—Prince Henry of Bstten- berg arrived at Easton at eight o'clock on Friday morning from Balmoral, and at once drove to Buckingham Palace. His Royal Highness will leave % ictoria by the Continental express for Jugenheim and Darmstadt, via Queenboro' and Flushing, where he proceeds in order to meet his brother, Prince Alexander, who, it is expected, will return with Prince Henry to Balmoral on a short visit to the Queen. THE INTERNATIONAL YACHT RACE. Nsw YORK, FRIDAY.-From particulars gathered from those on board the compeiing yachts it has been ascertained that the British yacht Galatea put back yesterday before reaching the turning point, 20 miles out at sea. At that time the Mayflower was believed to be two miles ahead, but the dense fog prevents anything like an accurate record be- ing given. The Mayflower sailed the entire course, but failed to finish within the prescribed time, and conse- quently the yachts will start to sail the same coarse again on Saturday.

THE BULGARIAN CRISIS. A RUSSIAN ENVOY EXPECFED AT SOFIA. PIPLIPPOPOLIB, FIZIDAY. It is believed that a special envoy from the Czar will shortly arrive at Sofia. The de- parture of Prince Alexander caused a strong feeling of dis- satisfaction among the officers here but Colonel Mutkuroff promptly succeeded in appeasing them. PRINCE ALEXANDER INTERVIEWED. Prince Alexander, says a "Daily Chronicle" Vienna cor- respondent, arrived in that city last night from Pesth. Shortly before arriving at Vienna the Prince had a private conversation in the restaurant carriage of the train. Gen. Ulapka has given me the following account of it :'--The Prince said that immediately after his arrival at Philip- popolis be received notes from Russia, Germany, and Aus- tria enjoining him ia the most uncompromising terms not to have a single one of the conspiritors executed, whether soldier or civilian. He was thus deprived of every essence of his power—that of putting the law in force against the very men who had suborned a portion of his army, and who had caused him to be hurried out of Bulgaria like a thief. Being thus deprived of the power to exercise justice and enforce the laws of the country, government naturally became impossible and abdication the only honourable exit from the difficulty.

FRANCE AND RUSSIA. BUCHAREST, FliMAY.—It is stated in high official circles- that recent events have very considerably shaken the triple alliance, and that a Russian alliance with France is highly probable within a short time.

CIVIL SERVICE ESTIMATES. DISCUSSION ON VACCINATION. The House went into Committee of Supply on the Civil Service Estimates, and the vote for Friendly Societies was agreed to.

-On the vote for the Local Government Board, Mr. A. O'CorrNoz opposed, and moved the reduction of the vote by £1.500. being the amount set down for the cost of public vaccination. He strongly objected to the system now in operation.. He contended that the compulsory vaccination was immoral, stupid, and cruel, as it caused unnecessary physical suffering, and was the cause of great anxiety to hundreds of thousands of fathers mad mothers. He also contended that it was opposed to the moral sense of the great majority of the people and that it did not in the least prevent small-pox. Pnblished statistics created doubt as to the value of vaccination. At least one-third of the people were opposed to vaccination, and as he bad already said, the great majority of the population were opposed to com- pulsory vaccination. He deprecated the filthy practice be- ing imposed on the children of those who strongly objected to the operation, which was considered to be neither preven- tative nor palliative ; and he condemned the practice on the whole as a deplorable delusion.—Mr. RITCHIE supported the vote, and' said he should look on it as a national disas- ter if the views of hon. mesnbers should receive the assent of the Muse of Commons. He insisted that vaccination was the means of preventing terrible disease, and quoted statistics in support of his argument. He should use every exertion to secure the end Parliament had in view when the Act was passed and to see that the Act was properly carried out tor the public good. The Local Government Board had no desire that persecution should prevail, but they insisted on the law beina carried out.—Mr. A. O'CONNOR suggested that those who believed in vaccination should be left free to subject themselves to it, but he urged that those who did not should not be com- pelled to do that to which they conscientiously objected.— Mr. Tapling. Mr. W. A. McArthur, and Mr. Molloy were in favour of further inquiry.—Mr. BRADLAUGH pointed out that the rich man who could afford to pay a fine was not compelled to obey the law; but the poor man who could not pay was sent to prison for not complying with the Act. He -supported the reduction of the vote.—Mr. LABOuCHERE held that the principle of vaccination was destroyed when those who were ready to pay the fine were not obliged to obey the law.—After further discussion Mr. RITCHIE said the Government could not consent to any inquiry into the question of vaccination.—The ameadment was negatived withouta division. . Mr. DILLoN called attention to difference in salaries of the Parliamentary Secretary of the Board of Trade and the Parliamentary Secretary for Local Government. He attri• buted the increase of the latter to the exertions of Mr. Chamberlain in the favour of his friend Mr. Jesse Collings_ He moved that the salary of the Secretary of the Local Board be £1,200, and not £l5OO per annum.—The CHAN- CELLOR of the EXCHEQUER explained that the salary now paid the two officers was the same.—Mr. DILLON was glad to hear it. Mr. PICKERSOILL called attention to the difference of coat of rations in different Unions in the metropolis.—Mr. RITCHIE said the subject was now under investigation. Mr. F. S. POWELL urged increased inspection of canal boats.—Mr. W. LONG said directions had been issued to inspectors to do everything possible to improve the con- dition of tthe boats and the people who lived therein.— Mr. Dillon's proposal was accepted, a:nd the vote agreed to. [LEFT SITTING.]

OUTRAGE UPON A LITTLE GIRL, - Before Aldermen Y. Harrison and Mr, 13. Biram, at St. Helens, on Sat- urday, a half-witted middle•aged man, named Patrick Rey- nolds, of Prescot, was charged with indecently assaulting Ellen Fenney, aged seven years, living in Sutton Heath' road:—Superintendent Johnston stated that the prisoner had been in the habit of startling opposite the house of the complainant's father, near which he had been engaged stone breaking. He asked the Bench to commit the prisoner Or trial. The girl. Finney then stated that about seven o'clock on Friday night she was playing along pith two other little girlerin a lane close to her father's house. The prisoner came to her and committed an assault upon her. The other little girls ran for assistance, and the prisoner was aporehen• ded.—Mrs. Fenney stated that from what she was told she went to the door of her house on Friday evening, when she saw the prisoner. She asked him what he had been doing to her daughter, when he replied—" I have not done her, any harm, forgive me this time and I wilt not do it again.' He tried to getaway, but she held him until her husband arrived.—ln reply to the cliarge the prisoner pleaded not guilty, and stated that the complainant and two other little girls had followed him. All he did was to slap the coT- plainant and tell her to go back home again.—The maga" trates committed the prisoner for trial at the next Quarter Sessions in November.—On hearing this., decision the pri- soner exclaimed—"Oh, my God, I'll not stop in prisoa un- til then."

This company is formed for the purpose of carrying passen- gers and merchandise between the Isle of Man and adjacent parts of the United Kingdom and Ireland. The Isle of Man as a place of resort has year after year grown in popular favour, and the enormous increase of visitors is shown by the table of returns appended herewith. Independently of the holiday seekers and visitors, the general traffic has kept pace with the remarkable develop- ment of the trade and resources of the Isle of Man, conse- quent upon the construction of railways, harbours, and piers in different parts of the Island, the practical effects of which are evidenced by toe great rise in the value of buildiaag land. It is not surprising that under such altered conditions the requirements of the public should have outgrown the capacity of the existing means of communication, and this company accordingly proposes to meet the demand for ircreased and improved aecommodation by the immediate construction of two first-class paddle-wheel steamers. William Pearce, Esq.. M.P., of the Fairfield Shipbuilding Company (Messrs. John Elder and Co.), Glasgow. the eminent builders of the greyhounds of the Atlantic, embria, Etruria. Alaska. and Arizona, also the magnificent " paddle-wheel steamer Victoria, just placed on the Dover and Calais service, has entered into a provisional contract with the company to build the steamers on highly favourable terms, and that they shall be ready for the station in May, 1887. The steamers will attain a speed of 21 knots an boor, and will be fitted up with all the recent improvements. havipg special regard to safety and comfort. The time for entering into such contracts is exceptionally favourable, for while the business of this company is strictly "Passenger Traffic." and 1' is in no way a.yrected" by the ...fluctuations of rates in the Ocean Shipping Trade," the man- aging directors are entitled to avail themselves of the excep- tionally low prices of material and construction, and will thus acquire these vessels on very advantageous terms for the share- holders. A Daily Double Service is arranged between the Isle of Man, Liverpool. and Manchester, passengers leaving Manches- ter by train at nine a.m. and three p m. to catch the steamers leaving the Liverpool Landing-stage at ten a.m, and four p.m. Steamers will also leave Douglas at ten a.m. and four p.m. This-double service will be run from the Ist of June until the 30th of September, these being the season summer months. These advantages, combined with special arrangements for the benefit of visitors, round the island and from one seaport to another, together with an increased rate of speed, supplying as they do an urgent want, justify the conviction that this undertaking will secure a large degree of public confidence and support. Through fares by fast trains will be arranged with this com- pany's steamers between London and the principal cities and towns and the Isle of Man. A daily service will also be arranged with Ramsey. Arrangements are made with the railway companies where- by the passengers and their baggage will be conveyed by omni- bus from the stations in Liverpool to the Landing-stage, where the steamers start frcm, free of charge. The progress and present financial conditions of the existing Isle of Man Steam Packet Company, which originally started with a capital of £B,OOO, and one small boat, and the £25 shares of which are now quoted at from £75 to £BO, may well serve as an indication of the prospects of this company. A recent issue of new stock in £5 shares has been allotted at £l4 each £5 share. Looking at the market value cf the Isle of Man Steam Pac- ket Company's shores, quoted at * premium of over 200 per cent. and paying a large dividend, it is reasonable to calculate that this company will pay a handsome dividend, and the shares will quickly command a considerable premium with the great advantages cffered to the public, by becoming shareholders at par in new steamers of the highest class, TABLES SHOWING INCREASE UN s RAMO.
